title: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder
author: Will Grant
content:
![Argentine President Javier Milei, wearing a leather jacket, stands smiling with a closed fist raised against a black backdrop.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/819/cpsprodpb/4547/live/523d1300-a88f-11f1-96fc-dd627484b0e6.jpg)
Argentine President Javier Milei enjoys a warm relationship with President Trump
- Published
The tone over the Falkland Islands dispute has been sharpening in Argentina from well before President Javier Milei's late-night national address on sanctions earlier this week.
It's tempting to see a visual representation of the tension in the jubilant Argentine players celebrating their hard-fought win over England at the Fifa World Cup this summer holding a banner which read "Las Malvinas son Argentinas" - the Falklands are Argentine - in front of their deliriously happy fans. However, the ill-feeling has been fomenting for much longer.
President Milei began his Thursday address with a brief history of the Falklands, very much from the Argentine perspective. He repeated the refrain at the heart of their position: the islands "rightfully belong" to Argentina. The British had invaded and colonially occupied the islands in 1833, he said, violently wrestling the territory from Argentina's hands.
The UK Government would say he conveniently overlooked a few details: the islands â over which the European powers had interchanged control throughout the 17th and 18th centuries â were uninhabited at the time the British reoccupied the land. The Argentine settlement had been forced out two years earlier, not by the British but by the Americans. A warship, the USS Lexington, destroyed a fort established there in December 1831 amid a dispute over local fishing and sealing rights.
Still, if the Americans had a hand in forcing the Argentines out two centuries ago, they may now play a central role in strengthening the Argentine claim. President Milei certainly thinks so.
"Winds of change" were blowing, he assured the Argentine people, after President Trump said he was "re-evaluating" the US position on the Falklands.
![US President Donald Trump (R) shakes hands with President of Argentina Javier Milei during a bilateral meeting at the 80th session of the UNâs General Assembly at the United Nations headquarters on September 23, 2025 in New York City. The men are both wearing dark suits and sitting on chairs. Milei is smiling with his mouth closed, while Trump, looking at him, has a serious expression.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/9664/live/dedd3490-a88d-11f1-96fc-dd627484b0e6.jpg)
The US recognises Britain's rule over the Falklands - but Trump has suggested he is "re-evaluating" the US position
That position has traditionally been one of neutrality - albeit while recognising Britain's rule over the territory. "Neutral" is relative, of course, given that President Reagan provided material support to Margaret Thatcher during the Falklands War in 1982 â an act which reinforced the long-standing alliance between London and Washington in times of conflict.
For Trump, however, that mutual support â the "Special Relationship" â was eroded by Sir Keir Starmer when the UK Government chose not to join the US war on Iran.
"You weren't there to help me", the president retorted in an interview with GB News this week. The Falklands were "a long way away", he said. The Falkland Islanders â who voted almost unanimously to remain a British overseas territory in 2013 â would point out that distance from London to the Falklands is fractionally shorter than the distance between Washington DC and the US territory of Guam, in the western Pacific.
Still, Trump's words have undoubtedly galvanised Milei. As have the opinion polls. He urgently needs a boost ahead of a presidential election next year in which one of his challengers, his former vice-president, Victoria Villarruel, has presented herself as a tougher defender of national sovereignty and attacked Milei's diplomatic approach on the Falklands as failing.
![Football players, some with their shirts off, stand or jump while smiling on a green football pitch. Two of them hold a white banner that says in black writing "Las Malvinas Son Argentinas" - the Falklands are Argentina's.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/b6d6/live/8cdaa330-a88d-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Fifa fined the Argentine Football Association after players held up a banner claiming the Falklands, breaching rules against political messaging
Domestic politics can rarely be ruled out of the equation when the Falklands issue flares back up. However, Buenos Aires argues that the matter has become urgent: "A clear and urgent danger", as Milei put it.
With two energy companies â the Israeli-owned Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration from the UK â due to undertake exploration work on the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, the issue has new impetus. Argentina "cannot allow" the companies to "appropriate the oil reserves under our sea", he said. "We will not stand by with our arms folded," he added.
On Saturday morning Milei's office said on X that it was launching sanctions proceedings against 45 people and companies. The announcement did not identify those targeted and it is not yet clear what impact they will have.
In his speech, Javier Milei painted Argentina as a reliable and "trustworthy partner" to Washington and he enjoys Trump's support, both ideologically and personally.
The two men are close allies in a vision of the Western Hemisphere which Trump calls the "Don-roe Doctrine", a play on words on the 19th Century 'Monroe Doctrine' which exerted American domination over the continent. In essence, the two presidents want to see only like-minded leaders in power in the Americas.
Within such a new partnership and a reordering of the spheres of influence, it's more than conceivable that Trump favours the Argentine leader over the British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, even if the issues at play transcend personality and party politics.
Perhaps the key question for the coming months, then, is whether the strength of the so-called "Don-roe Doctrine" outweighs the lasting history of the "Special Relationship".
summary: Argentine President Javier Milei has intensified demands over the Falkland Islands, arguing the territory rightfully belongs to Argentina and citing upcoming energy exploration as an urgent threat. Milei has been emboldened by US President Donald Trump's suggestion that he is re-evaluating the US position on the islands amid strains in the UK-US relationship. Argentina's renewed focus on the sovereignty dispute also comes as Milei faces upcoming presidential elections and political pressure from rivals.
key_points: President Javier Milei addressed the nation regarding the Falklands, stating the islands rightfully belong to Argentina and announcing sanctions proceedings against 45 people and companies.
US President Donald Trump stated he is re-evaluating the US position on the Falklands following strains with the UK government.
Upcoming energy exploration on the Sea Lion oilfield by Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration has given new urgency to Argentina's claims.
Milei faces political pressure ahead of next year's presidential election from challengers like former vice-president Victoria Villarruel, who criticize his diplomatic approach.

title: UK weather: Weekend heat for parts of UK before more rain next week
author: Elizabeth Rizzini
content:
![A seaside scene in Skegness with a big wheel and a funfair, the skies are blue](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/a83e/live/b8175640-a777-11f1-b2d5-535b3b3d379f.jpg)
- Published
Temperatures are on the rise again in time for the weekend with areas of the south experiencing 27C on Sunday.
However, before that, wet and windy conditions are in the Friday forecast for many across the northern half of the UK.
Low pressure systems continue to roll in from the Atlantic across the far north of the UK, affecting mostly northern and western Scotland.
Meanwhile, high pressure will block and weaken these fronts across the southern half of England and Wales, where drought conditions and hosepipe bans continue.
Sunshine and showers on Friday
Friday will feel cooler across central and southern areas of England and south Wales with a brief spell of rain in the morning, followed by sunny spells into the afternoon.
It should also feel less humid, but temperatures could still reach 22C (72F).
By contrast, northern England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and north Wales will have a breezy day with sunny spells and a scattering of showers which could be heavy in the west.
There will be fewer showers and more sunshine for eastern Northern Ireland and eastern Scotland.
Gales are expected for exposed coasts and hills in western Scotland.
Weekend warmth
![Map of UK and Europe showing orange and red colours where temperatures will be highest.  South or south-westerly wind arrows show warm air approaching the UK. Meanwhile low pressure is shown sitting to the north-west](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/726e/live/14b29770-a6a1-11f1-b048-153395f36aa1.jpg)
The UK will import some hotter air from France and central Europe this week, whilst rain-bearing weather fronts approach from the west
Saturday is looking fine and dry for England and Wales as hotter air from France makes its way to the UK.
In Scotland and Northern Ireland there will also be a lot of dry weather with the chance of a few showers in the west and more cloud through the afternoon.
On Sunday it will be cloudy and damp for many in Northern Ireland and western Scotland.
South-westerly winds will scoop up more warm, humid air from Europe and it's likely to feel hot again in the best of the sunshine for England and Wales. Eastern Scotland is also likely to stay dry with sunny spells.
Temperatures could peak at 27C (81F) in south-east England. Northern England, south-west England and Wales could reach 24C (75F), while Northern Ireland and eastern Scotland could see 20C (68F).
How is next week looking?
There is some uncertainty about how long the warmth will last beyond the weekend.
It looks most likely that Atlantic weather-systems will continue to bring westerly winds and areas of rain at times.
On Tuesday there is a chance that a deep area of low pressure will bring stormy conditions but it is currently too far away to predict if it will happen with any certainty as well as where the strongest winds and heaviest rain will be.
Check the BBC Weather app and website for the latest hour by hour forecast.
And keep an eye on the monthly outlook for our latest thoughts on the weather longer range.
summary: Temperatures are rising ahead of the weekend, with parts of the south expected to reach 27C on Sunday. However, Friday brings wet and windy conditions to the northern half of the UK, while drought conditions and hosepipe bans persist in parts of England and Wales. Looking ahead to next week, Atlantic weather systems are likely to bring returning rain and westerly winds.
key_points: Southern areas of the UK could experience temperatures of up to 27C on Sunday.
Wet and windy weather is forecasted for the northern half of the UK on Friday.
High pressure continues to block rain fronts in the southern half of England and Wales, where drought and hosepipe bans remain.
Atlantic weather systems are expected to bring more rain and westerly winds next week.

title: Farage seeks to shore up damaged leadership as scandal engulfs Reform conference
author: Rowena Mason; Pippa Crerar; Ben Quinn
content:
Nigel Farage sought to shore up his damaged leadership on Friday as he attempted to distance himself from two of his most senior officials reported to the police for apparently plotting to evade the law on foreign donations.
As the scandal engulfed Reform UK’s party conference in Birmingham, Farage was forced to suspend close aides Dan Jukes and head of policy James Orr after an undercover investigation by reporters from a group called Verbatim.
He later acknowledged Jukes and Orr had made “human error” and were “not authorised” to act in the way they did when trying to orchestrate donations to benefit the party from a fake US businessman, who was not permitted to give money.
![Dan Jukes, wearing a wax jacket, talks to Farage](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/2cad9221591dc08843aa6252d545b8132beb1868/0_0_8192_5464/master/8192.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The Met police are now assessing the evidence after a complaint that Farage, Orr and Jukes may have broken political funding laws, with sources suggesting a full investigation is highly likely to be launched. They all deny wrongdoing.
One possibility would be for the police to extend an existing Met investigation into whether Reform took donations channelled through an intermediary from potentially impermissible sources, which the party and donors deny.
Orr is an associate professor of divinity at the University of Cambridge who had been working for Reform, reporting directly to Farage, since February. In relation to the undercover footage of Orr, a spokesperson for the university said Cambridge was “looking into these matters”. Jukes is Farage’s closest aide, and has been at his side for more than a decade working on communications and strategy.
Farage had been introduced by Jukes to the would-be donor from the US promising to give £500,000 despite not being eligible, who was really an undercover reporter. The Reform leader then appeared to endorse the scheme for the impermissible US donor to give money through his son, a UK intermediary, by saying “thank you, both” and “all above board”.
After dismissing the sting as a “hoax”, Reform began an organised campaign to limit the damage to Farage personally before his main conference speech, after a summer of scandals over his finances, including an undeclared gift of £5m.
Addressing the allegations, the Reform leader responded by reading out a legal statement in which he dismissed the allegations as “a little local difficulty” and described the reports as “an exercise in entrapment”.
Farage claimed Orr and Jukes had merely been “contractors” who engaged in “loose pub talk, including a couple of boasts that simply were not true”. One party figure, Nadine Dorries, claimed Jukes had merely booked transport and carried bags, despite being a senior adviser integral to Reform’s operations and success for many years.
![A man in chainmail and a crown poses for the camera.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/575d32933bec94a0e4ba68de9bb0a684e6c138f6/0_0_8640_5760/master/8640.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
When it was put to Farage that he had thanked the bogus donors and understood what was going on, he said: “It was the middle of the byelection. I was told I had to go and meet these people. I didn’t have to, but I did. I was told they had a global family trust headquartered in London. I asked the question: is this all above board?”
The Reform leader also insisted that the party’s internal processes would have stopped any impermissible donors and said neither Jukes nor Orr should have been carrying out fundraising. He said a suggestion by Jukes in the footage that other foreign donations had been channelled through UK intermediaries was not true and the donors did not exist.
The pair were caught out after being filmed by undercover reporters from the group Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, and broadcast by Channel 4 News on the eve of Reform’s party conference.
![A woman is hauled away by security personnel after protesting at the Reform UK conference.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/88ac30b8ee16c5c3e45a58196928fcde1d27965b/0_0_8640_5760/master/8640.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In the footage, Orr and Jukes appeared to help orchestrate an impermissible donation of £30,000 from the fake US donor, which was used to pay for polling that would benefit Reform and made front pages of national newspapers. The money from an American company was transferred to the polling company JL Partners after being organised at the behest of Reform to boost its policies and political narrative. It was not declared to the Electoral Commission.
Jukes went on to discuss whether the US businessman could give £500,000 through a UK intermediary, who was an undercover reporter, and introduced the would-be donors to Farage at a lunch in Clacton over oysters and champagne.
Jukes issued a statement: “This was entrapment over a prolonged period of time by individuals using selective editing who had their own agenda to discredit Reform UK.”
Orr said: “I have agreed to step down from my current role at Reform UK pending the outcome of the party’s internal investigation into the conduct of the program, with which I will cooperate fully.”
The Lib Dems have asked the standards commissioner to investigate Farage’s conduct.
The row comprehensively overshadowed the first full day of the party’s conference with every Reform politician repeatedly questioned over the scandal.
It also exposed splits at the top of the party, with Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, strongly distancing himself from Jukes and Orr. He told reporters “anyone who supports Reform is disappointed”, and added of the investigation: “It’s just not something I am personally involved in.”
He also launched a personal video about his backstory, leading to speculation he could attempt to run for the leadership as a rival to Robert Jenrick or Richard Tice if Farage were to be forced out over his financial scandals.
However, some Reform insiders are convinced Farage will part company with Yusuf before long, partly over his ambition and combative style on social media, including one post on X that saw him accused of racism towards a Somalia-born Labour councillor. Farage is understood to have used a rude term about Yusuf recently in relation to his troublemaking on social media.
One senior Reform figure said they believed Yusuf would have to go as a precondition for some sort of reconciliation with Rupert Lowe, whose party, Restore Britain, has eaten into the party’s voters on the hard right. Farage has recently condemned Lowe as vindictive, but some of their friends believe a rapprochement could be possible if Yusuf were no longer in the party.
Reform had wanted the main event to be Farage announcing a deal with the hard-right French National Rally president, Jordan Bardella, to return small boats crossing the Channel if both parties achieve power. However, a press conference was dominated by questions about the foreign donations scandal.
![Jordan Bardella and Farage shaking hands](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ae1611190ede43cbde4999289cd5a86795fe0c98/1256_103_5793_4634/master/5793.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Farage’s main speech was later delayed by security concerns after climate protesters disrupted Tice’s stage appearance. More activists later repeatedly interrupted his address. While waiting to go on stage, the Reform leader danced and sung with the crowd.
He began his speech by calling for Andy Burnham to hold a general election and accusing Labour of planning to put up taxes.
The speech was light on policy but Farage at one point hinted he could look at the way judges are appointed in future – suggesting the party could look at a system of political appointments as is the case in the US.
summary: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage faced a leadership crisis during the party's conference in Birmingham after an undercover investigation caught two of his senior officials allegedly plotting to evade foreign donation laws. Farage suspended aides Dan Jukes and James Orr, dismissing the sting as entrapment and "loose pub talk," while the Metropolitan Police assess evidence for a potential full investigation. The scandal has overshadowed the conference, prompted calls for a parliamentary standards investigation, and exposed internal party tensions.
key_points: Reform UK officials Dan Jukes and James Orr were suspended following an undercover investigation by Verbatim reporters regarding foreign donations.
The Metropolitan Police are assessing evidence to determine if Farage, Orr, and Jukes broke political funding laws, though all deny wrongdoing.
The undercover footage showed officials orchestrating an undeclared £30,000 donation from a fake US businessman and discussing a larger £500,000 contribution.
Farage defended himself by calling the incident entrapment and "human error," while dismissing the allegations as a hoax.
The scandal completely overshadowed the party's conference, disrupting Farage's scheduled announcements and exposing internal party splits.

title: Queen's joy at 'happy ending to a terrible story' at riot-hit library
author: Paul Burnell
content:
![Queen Camilla in a dress of white circles on a black background talks to a boyu and two girls in green school uniform.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1152/cpsprodpb/f2d2/live/c63e9e90-a862-11f1-ae45-e9984fc27c77.png)
The Queen praised the local community for its resilience
- Published
The Queen visited a library rebuilt after being destroyed in a riot, telling the children she met that "you can never have too many books".
Her Majesty had donated a box of books to Spellow Library in Liverpool after it was burned down in widespread unrest in the summer of 2024 following the Southport attack in which three children died.
She was at the library earlier to unveil a plaque, and brought with her more books to donate.
Queen Camilla said seeing the library rise from the ashes was a "happy ending" to "such a terrible story".
After unveiling the plaque, she said: "You can never have too many books. I've brought some more and it's so wonderful to see this place rise from the ashes.
"Congratulations to all of you who made it happen."
Ahead of the plaque being unveilled, children's author Frank Cottrell-Boyce read a poem about the library.
He told the Queen he had done a workshop with children to come up with a new name for the County Road site ahead of its reopening, but that the children wanted it to remain as Spellow.
![Queen Camilla in a dress of white circles on a black background sits next to Sean McEvoy as he reads a children's story from  a large illustrated book.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/946/cpsprodpb/d377/live/58f5bcb0-a86c-11f1-bbad-43eaf67b94b6.png)
Library staff member Sean McEvoy read to the children
The library was rebuilt after more than Â£250,000 was raised through fundraising, and a host of celebrities donated books to help restock it.
Alex McCormick, who set up the fundraising campaign, said: "It is is amazing how far we have come, and that the Queen wanted to see what we had done.
"I set it up the fundraising page in anger on the night [of the fire] to raise just Â£500 and I never dreamed we would be where we are now."
![Staff, students and dignatories with the Queen viewed from on high](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/0681/live/6b9112c0-a86c-11f1-bbad-43eaf67b94b6.png)
A plaque was unveiled by Queen Camilla
Library assistant and information officer Sean McEvoy was joined by the Queen as he read Giraffes Can't Dance by Giles Andreae to the children.
He said: "It's not something I expected to do on a normal day in work. The children were fantastic."
![Queen Camilla in a dress of white circles on a black background is presented with a book by a child in a wheelchair wewaring a red T-shirt](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/c6a1/live/ad9bcfc0-a86c-11f1-bbad-43eaf67b94b6.png)
After donating a box of books, the Queen received one herself
Resident Lyndsey Crowther-Jones said of the royal visit: "It's brilliant. I can't believe she has come here.
"It was lovely to see the kids from St Francis De Sales school go over all dressed up."
The Spellow Lane Community Hub and Library originally opened in 2023 to serve deprived communities.
McEvoy said the Queen's visit was "great for the community, the library", adding: "It's what somewhere like this deserves the way the community has come together."
Listen to the best of BBC Radio Merseyside on Sounds and follow BBC Merseyside on Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external. You can also send story ideas via Whatsapp to 0808 100 2230.
summary: Queen Camilla visited Spellow Library in Liverpool after it was rebuilt following its destruction in the summer 2024 riots. During her visit, she unveiled a plaque, donated more books, and praised the community's resilience, calling the rebuilding a "happy ending to a terrible story." The library was restored after raising over £250,000 through a fundraising campaign launched by resident Alex McCormick.
key_points: Queen Camilla visited the rebuilt Spellow Library in Liverpool to unveil a plaque and donate more books.
The library was originally destroyed in widespread unrest and riots in the summer of 2024.
More than £250,000 was raised through a community fundraising campaign to rebuild and restock the library.
During the visit, the Queen listened to a reading with children and praised the resilience of the local community.

title: Investigations launched into polling firm at centre of Reform UK allegations
author: Geraldine McKelvie
content:
A polling firm at the centre of allegations that Reform UK breached electoral law is being investigated by two industry bodies.
JL Partners, which is run by former Conservative aides, has been accused of breaking transparency rules by failing to declare that three separate polls had been commissioned by the party.
The company is a member of the British Polling Council and the Market Research Society, who say the identity of a client commissioning a poll should be disclosed when the results enter the public domain.
Both organisations confirmed on Friday that they had launched inquiries into JL Partners. The reviews have come after Channel 4 News broadcast footage gathered by undercover reporters during a year-long investigation into Reform’s finances on Thursday night.
Investigative journalists from Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, posed as a Reform donor and his American father, who paid for more than £30,000 of polling from JL Partners that generated positive headlines for the party.
Nigel Farage, the party leader, was filmed saying the polling was “amazing” and provided “bang for buck”.
In the footage, Farage appeared to welcome the suggestion of a larger donation to the party. He was told the UK-based son could be registered as the official donor, despite the money originating from his father. Farage said: “Both of you, thank you.”
In the UK, only those registered on the electoral roll are permitted to donate to political parties, meaning the polls and the proposed larger donation could both be classed as illegal.
On Friday, as its annual conference got under way in Birmingham, Reform said it had suspended two senior officials who were filmed as part of the Channel 4 News investigation.
James Orr, the party’s head of policy, and Dan Jukes, a senior adviser to Farage, were both recorded apparently plotting to bypass electoral laws.
The first poll, conducted in January, related to the Labour government’s aborted plans to cancel some local elections, which Reform strongly opposed. The poll indicated Labour would face heavy defeats if these went ahead.
The second, published in April, suggested that two-thirds of voters wanted the then prime minister, Keir Starmer, to resign. The third, released in June, appeared to show that support for Reform among trade union members was drawing level with Labour.
JL Partners’ co-founder James Johnson was covertly filmed discussing the Reform polling, telling one of the reporters that his company had done “a little bit of informal rule-bending” in relation to one survey. He admitted that it “should have disclosed who the client was” when publishing the data.
after newsletter promotion
The results of the polling appeared on the front pages of the Times and the Daily Telegraph. Both newspapers said they had not been aware that the polling had been commissioned by Reform.
The British Polling Council said on Friday that “all data and research findings made on the basis of social or political polls conducted in the United Kingdom … must include reference to the client commissioning the survey”. It added that it was clear its rules had been breached in relation to the polls paid for by Reform.
“According to the programme, this may have been deliberate,” a spokesperson added. “We are seeking further information from the BPC member concerned and expect them to make information available after further consideration.”
The Market Research Society said: “MRS is aware of the Channel 4 reporting involving an MRS Company Partner. The matter is being referred to the Market Research Standards Board (MRSB) for review in line with its established complaint procedures.”
JL Partners told Channel 4 News: “Despite there being no concern about the accuracy of our work, the report did reveal weaknesses in our procedures. For that reason JL Partners is reviewing those procedures in order to eliminate possible grey areas and ambiguities and strengthen our safeguards for the future.”
The company did not respond to follow-up queries from the Guardian.
summary: Two industry bodies have launched investigations into the polling firm JL Partners following allegations that it breached transparency rules by failing to declare Reform UK as the client behind three separate polls. The inquiries follow an undercover investigation by Channel 4 News and Verbatim, which also raised questions regarding political donations under UK law. In response to the broadcast, Reform UK suspended two senior officials, while JL Partners stated it is reviewing its procedures.
key_points: JL Partners is being investigated by the British Polling Council and the Market Research Society.
The firm is accused of failing to disclose that Reform UK commissioned three separate polls.
Undercover footage broadcast by Channel 4 News prompted the inquiries and led Reform UK to suspend two senior officials.
UK electoral rules require political donors to be registered on the electoral roll and mandate transparency regarding poll commissioners.

title: Drumcree: Parades Commission to consider Orange Order march
author: Mark Simpson
content:
![A large procession of Orange Order members being blocked by police from walking down a road.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/a62e/live/44214f80-a069-11f1-a9ee-9bb6b032b6a3.jpg)
The Orange Order Drumcree march has been turned away from going down the Garvaghy Road every year since 1998
- Published
The earliest date for a decision by the Parades Commission on the planned Drumcree march by Portadown Orange Order is 23 September â four days before the scheduled parade.
The route the Order hopes to take - including the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road - has been published on Parades Commission website, external.
It states that on Sunday 27 September the Order intends to start at 13:00 BST on Drumcree Road and finish in Portadown town centre by 14:30.
The commission has posted that the date that the parade is "to be considered" is Wednesday 23 September.
However, it could be later in the week before the decision and the reasons are published.
The contentious part of the route is along the Garvaghy Road, which is in the early part of the planned parade.
The order says that with only 60 members taking part, it should take 15 minutes to pass through that area.
They say they will march in silence with no music.
Once they are beyond the Garvaghy Road and close to the town centre, they say they will be joined by two accordion bands and other members of Portadown Orange Order.
Portadown Orange Order have appealed to residents on the Garvaghy Road to engage in mediation.
They said the Parades Commission had written to them about taking part in a process overseen by an independent mediator.
An order spokesperson said: "We have swiftly confirmed our agreement to participate in talks without precondition."
They called on Sinn FÃ©in and residents to support a talks process.
The spokesperson said: "In our view, the independent chair should be someone with judicial experience, given the issue being considered is at its heart one of human rights law.
"It is welcome this matter is now very much on the table and we stand ready to go into the talks process immediately.
"This is not about the rights of our district prevailing over the rights of those who oppose us, but nor is it sustainable that the rights of those who oppose us can continue to prevail over our rights."
![An older man with grey hair and glasses. He is wearing a green fleece with a black and white shirt underneath.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/97eb/live/d4747e20-a6e2-11f1-9e4c-79c1c0e340c6.jpg)
BreandÃ¡n Mac Cionnaith is a spokesperson for Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition
Speaking on Thursday, BreandÃ¡n Mac Cionnaith, a spokesperson for the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition, said, "a number of years ago" the group had put forward a proposal to complete the parade.
He said it would have saw 32 Orangemen parade down the Garvaghy Road "accompanied by 32 young people from this community, each wearing their county GAA tops".
"The Orange Order rejected that outright on the grounds that only a fully paid-up member of the Orange Order could take part in their parades."
Mac Cionnaith said this demonstrated the Orange Order "wants no association with this community, it wants no inclusion by this community, and if anything, it wishes to exclude this community".
He added that the offer was still on the table.
summary: The Parades Commission is set to consider a planned Orange Order march in Portadown, which includes the contentious nationalist Garvaghy Road, with a decision expected around 23 September. The Portadown Orange Order has agreed to participate in an independent mediation process without preconditions and called on residents to engage in talks. However, Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition spokesperson Breandán Mac Cionnaith criticized the Orange Order's past rejection of a previous local proposal, stating the offer remains on the table.
key_points: The Parades Commission will consider the planned Drumcree march by the Portadown Orange Order, with an earliest decision date of 23 September.
The proposed route for the 27 September parade includes the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road.
The Orange Order stated that 60 members would march in silence through the Garvaghy Road area before being joined by bands later in the route.
The Orange Order has agreed to participate in an independent mediation process, though past local proposals involving GAA-wearing youths were previously rejected by the Order.

title: Golden retrievers to gather at the breed's ancestral Highland home
author: Steven McKenzie
content:
![People stand, some of them holding up phones to take a picture, as hundreds of golden retrievers stand in a grassy arena next to the ruins of Guisachan House.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/651/cpsprodpb/c037/live/05404410-a7d0-11f1-809e-25fc74c1ec7d.png)
A gathering in 2023 involved almost 500 dogs
- Published
A mass gathering of golden retrievers and their owners is to return to the ancestral home of the breed in July 2028.
The event will mark 160 years since the first golden retriever puppies were born at Guisachan House in Glen Affric, near Cannich, in the Highlands.
Meetings to celebrate the breed have been held in different formats by the Golden Retriever Club of Scotland since the late 1990s, with larger events taking place since 2006.
The last gathering held at Guisachan in 2023 involved almost 500 dogs from 12 countries.
The Golden Retriever Club of Scotland said a date for the 2028 gathering would be announced later.
![A close up of a golden retriever showing its neck and head. The dog is a golden colour, has its mouth open while it looks up to the right of the image.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/498f/live/f84c1900-a6ee-11f1-9e4c-79c1c0e340c6.jpg)
Today's golden retrievers are descended from dogs bred in the Highlands
![A golden retriever stands with its tongue out next its owner.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/5dc4/live/5852a130-a6f3-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
The last event at Guisachan involved dogs from 12 countries
Golden retrievers were bred by aristocrat Sir Dudley Marjoribanks, who wanted a gun dog suited to Scottish Highland terrain.
The first litter was born in 1868 to a Tweed water spaniel, a breed now extinct, and yellow wavy-coated retriever.
The puppies were called Primrose, Cowslip and Crocus. Some histories of the breed report the litter having four pups.
More than 40 years later in 1913, the golden retriever was officially recognised as a breed by The Kennel Club, the UK's largest organisation concerned with dog health, welfare and training.
Guisachan House had fallen into ruin by the 1960s.
![Four well-behaved golden retrievers sitting looking at their owner on a grassy area below the ruins of Guisachan House.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/718/cpsprodpb/ddb9/live/f30b4870-a6f4-11f1-97e2-55b9ef1865bd.jpg)
Guisachan is the ancestral home of the breed
![A golden retriever sits looking at the camera on a grassy area below the ruins of Guisachan House.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1552/cpsprodpb/2f7a/live/b7713730-a6f3-11f1-97e2-55b9ef1865bd.jpg)
The Victorian mansion has been a ruin since the 1960s
summary: Golden retrievers and their owners will return to Guisachan House in the Scottish Highlands for a mass gathering in July 2028. The event will celebrate 160 years since the first golden retriever puppies were born at the estate in 1868. Organized by the Golden Retriever Club of Scotland, the gathering follows previous successful events, including one in 2023 that drew nearly 500 dogs from 12 countries.
key_points: A mass gathering of golden retrievers is scheduled for July 2028 at Guisachan House in the Scottish Highlands.
The event marks 160 years since the first golden retriever puppies were born at the estate in 1868.
The breed was originally created by Sir Dudley Marjoribanks to serve as a gun dog suited for Highland terrain.
The Golden Retriever Club of Scotland hosts these celebrations, with a 2023 event featuring almost 500 dogs from 12 countries.
The golden retriever was officially recognized as a breed by The Kennel Club in 1913.

title: President Javier Milei says ‘winds of change’ support Argentina’s claim to Falkland Islands
author: Tiago Rogero
content:
President Javier Milei has said “winds of change favourable” to Argentina’s claim to the Falkland Islands were “blowing around the world” in a televised address, citing signs that Donald Trump might reconsider the US position on the islands’ sovereignty.
“Recently, President Trump declared that the US is re-evaluating its historic position in relation to the Malvinas,” he said, using the Argentinian name for the islands.
The Argentinian president said the UK was facing “multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. It is clear that they are on a path of decline. Argentina’s future, however, is flourishing and will prevail.”
Earlier on Thursday, Trump was asked by British outlet GB News if he would “come to the UK’s aid” during a potential territorial dispute over the Falkland Islands with Argentina, and hinted that he would not, adding that the UK “weren’t there to help me [with Iran]”.
Supporters had expected Milei to use his address to the nation on Thursday night to announce an unprecedented US endorsement of Argentina’s sovereignty claim over the Falkland Islands.
Instead, the self-styled libertarian, when asked whether he was reviewing the US position on the islands, repeated the US president’s words, saying: “I always review every position. That’s just one of many.”
The far-right president then portrayed Trump’s response as a “threat” that was “not innocuous”.
“The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come,” he said.
The US has formally recognised the UK’s de facto administration of the islands but has not taken a formal position on sovereignty. The first reports of a possible revision emerged in April, when an internal Pentagon email reported by Reuters raised the prospect of Washington reconsidering its stance as one possible way of punishing Nato allies that declined to join the Iran war.
In Thursday’s interview, Trump said of the UK: “Your country was not there to help me. We didn’t need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader [Keir Starmer], ‘why don’t you send a couple of ships?’. He said, ‘We don’t have any’. It was pretty sad, the whole thing.”
Despite the expectations created by Milei and his supporters – the president summoned all his ministers to stand alongside him – the main new elements of the speech were a few decrees announced by the president.
One of them is to speed up sanctions “against those participating in oil extraction initiatives”, specifically citing an offshore oil project in the North Falkland Basin led by the Israeli company Navitas alongside its British partner Rockhopper. Milei claimed the project violated a UN call for neither Argentina nor the UK to take unilateral action in the territory.
Despite his “radical” austerity policies, Milei also said he would sign an emergency decree to increase resources for the defence ministry, prioritising the construction of an integrated naval base in Tierra del Fuego. The project to build a base there predates Milei, and construction began in 2022.
The UK said earlier this week that its position on the Falklands was “long-standing and unwavering”. It said in a statement: “Sovereignty rests with the UK, and the islanders’ right to self-determination is paramount. The UK’s position is clear. The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory.”
Some analysts had already viewed Milei’s recent embrace of the Malvinas cause as another attempt to create a “smokescreen” at the lowest point of his popularity since taking office. He is expected to seek re-election next year.
Amid corruption allegations involving members of his government and poor economic results – his “chainsaw” austerity policies have brought inflation under control, but unemployment and poverty have risen – the far-right president has increasingly turned up the volume on controversial measures, including claims of an anti-Argentina campaign dating back to the World Cup, attacks on Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and an immigration crackdown modelled on the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
Many have also noted that his interest in the issue is recent. Milei had long described himself as a great admirer of Margaret Thatcher, the British prime minister during the 1982 Falklands war, and only began adopting a public pro-sovereignty stance a few months ago, after reports emerged that the US might be reconsidering its position.
The far-right leader also dismissed the principle of self-determination invoked by the UK – in a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of the islanders voted to remain a British overseas territory.
Echoing the same phrase used by Argentina’s national team on a banner celebrating their victory over England in the World Cup semi-final, Milei said that “The Malvinas are Argentinian.”
summary: Argentinian President Javier Milei stated in a televised address that global "winds of change" support Argentina's claim to the Falkland Islands, citing potential shifts in the U.S. position under Donald Trump. Amid domestic economic and political challenges, Milei announced decrees to accelerate sanctions against companies involved in North Falkland Basin oil extraction and to increase defense resources. The UK maintains that sovereignty rests with the UK and that the islanders' right to self-determination is paramount.
key_points: President Javier Milei claimed that international conditions are increasingly favorable to Argentina's sovereignty claim over the Falkland Islands.
Milei announced decrees to speed up sanctions against entities participating in oil extraction initiatives in the Falklands.
An emergency decree will be signed to increase defense resources and prioritize the construction of a naval base in Tierra del Fuego.
The UK reiterated its unwavering position that sovereignty rests with the UK and that the islanders' right to self-determination is paramount.

title: Trump hints US may not back UK over Falklands over Iran support
author: Greta Ruffino
content:
The US recognises Britain's administration of the Falkland Islands but remains neutral over the competing sovereignty claims.
US President Donald Trump has suggested Washington may not support the United Kingdom in the event of a future conflict with Argentina over the Falkland Islands.
Speaking to GB News, as reported by the BBC, Trump criticised Britain over its response to the US war with Iran, saying the country had "not been there to help me". He later acknowledged that the US military had not required British assistance.
Trump's comments come as Argentine President Javier Milei renews his country's longstanding claim to the islands, known as the Malvinas in Argentina.
Milei said he would address what he called the "SACRED issue for Argentines: the Malvinas cause" in a televised speech on Thursday night.
"What cause more important and strategic for the vital interests of the Nation could there be than the Malvinas cause?", he wrote on X.
On Monday, Trump said the US was reassessing its position on the Falkland Islands, following reports that Washington could challenge Britain's sovereignty over the territory unless the UK increases defence spending.
The reported move was among measures being considered by the Pentagon to encourage NATO allies to meet their defence spending commitments, the Daily Telegraph reported last week.
"I always review every position. That's just one of many," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office when asked if the United States was reviewing its position on the Falklands.
Asked whether he wanted the government of newly appointed British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to increase its defence spending commitments, Trump said: "The UK's got some problems but they'll get solved."
More than four decades after the 1982 Falklands War, the sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina remains a source of tension.
The issue resurfaced at this year's World Cup, when Argentina players displayed a banner reading "The Falklands are Argentine" after their 2-1 semi-final victory over England. FIFA later fined the Argentine Football Association $321,000 (€276,000).
The 1982 conflict began after Argentine forces invaded the British overseas territory, prompting then-UK Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher to send a naval task force to retake the islands.
summary: US President Donald Trump suggested the United States might not support the UK in a future conflict over the Falkland Islands, citing a lack of British assistance during the US war with Iran. Trump also confirmed that the US is reviewing its position on the Falklands sovereignty issue, while reports indicate this pressure is tied to encouraging NATO allies to increase defense spending. Meanwhile, Argentine President Javier Milei has renewed his country's claims to the islands.
key_points: Donald Trump hinted the US may not back the UK in a potential conflict with Argentina over the Falkland Islands.
Trump criticized the UK for not helping in the US war with Iran, though he acknowledged American forces did not need British assistance.
The US is reportedly reviewing its position on the Falklands as a measure to encourage NATO allies to increase defense spending.
Argentine President Javier Milei has renewed his country's longstanding sovereignty claim to the islands.

title: Farage senior aide filmed suggesting way to avoid donations law
author: Chris Mason; Harry Farley
content:
Watch: Undercover reporters posing as party donors meet with Nigel Farage
- Published
Nigel Farage's senior aide suggested a way to get around electoral law to secure a foreign donation of Â£500,000 for Reform UK, according to undercover filming broadcast by Channel 4.
Dan Jukes was filmed meeting a man posing as the British-based son of a rich American businessman.
Electoral law sets out that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.
In this instance, the son would be a permissible donor, his father would not be.
The undercover filming was done by a group called Verbatim Investigations, which was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting. Channel 4 News say they have verified the material they were given and chose to broadcast.
Reform UK denies any wrongdoing and claims to have "been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign funded climate change activists".
The reporter posing as the son of the American donor is filmed raising a concern that his father wouldn't be able to directly donate to the party within the law.
Filmed standing outside a pub in Westminster, Jukes said "you do realise that you can do it?"
Channel 4 say Jukes was suggesting that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.
"Actually that does strike me as a solution," Jukes continues.
He then claims they have done it several times before, in exchanges bleeped out but which appear to refer to other instances where this mechanism had been used before.
"That's one of the ways in which we do it," he is recorded as saying.
Reform UK have launched an internal investigation into Jukes. They would not confirm if he remained a party spokesperson.
Later, Channel 4 broadcast footage from a lunch in Clacton in Essex, with both the reporter posing as the UK-based son, and an actor â his supposed American father. Opposite them are both Dan Jukes and the Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.
Farage says "it's all above board" after the son has told him he has been in discussions with both Jukes and Reform's Head of Policy, James Orr about it for some time.
"I'll be the registered donor," the son says. "But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that's done and all those conversations are had the money is available."
"Thank you. Well, both of you. Thank you," Farage is heard saying.
Orr is also now the subject of an internal Reform UK investigation.
Watch: Farage senior aide filmed suggesting way to avoid election law
Earlier in Channel 4 News's film, prior to the suggested half a million pound donation, Channel 4 says Orr suggests to the undercover reporter that perhaps his father could pay for opinion polling to aide Reform's campaigning.
The poll would cost Â£18,000 plus VAT â and Orr suggests that perhaps the polling company could send the bill to the undercover reporter.
In all, Channel 4 News says Reform commissioned three polls costing Â£32,500 in total and that the public was not told who commissioned or funded them.
Not disclosing such funding would be illegal and accepting this kind of foreign funding would also be illegal.
A Reform spokesperson said: "Reform UK has been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded, climate change activists posing as would-be party donors. The party denies any wrongdoing.
"Reform UK has a robust vetting process for prospective donors approved by the Electoral Commission.
"The hoaxers are 'Verbatim Investigations'; a new company, incorporated in July 2026 in an attempt to mask their true identity: the Center for Climate Reporting (CCR). The methods of its founder, Lawrence Carter, have previously been rebuked by members of the United States Congress for videos [that] appear to be substantially edited, creating an incomplete record of the conversation."
An Electoral Commission spokesperson said: "The law requires political parties to report all permissible donations they accept with a value over Â£11,180 and all impermissible donations over Â£500.
"Information about any potential attempt to evade the controls on donations is for the police to consider."
A spokesman for the Metropolitan Police told the BBC: "We're aware of media reporting on Thursday, 3 September involving political party donations and an alleged breach of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000 relating to polling. We will assess this matter and any information provided to us."
It is understood the force has not begun an investigation.
Jukes has been approached for comment.
![Thin, red banner promoting the Politics Essential newsletter with text saying, âTop political analysis in your inbox every dayâ. There is also an image of the Houses of Parliament.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/6133/live/2bce6ee0-0b00-11f0-97d3-37df2b293ed1.png)
summary: Undercover filming broadcast by Channel 4 captured a senior aide to Nigel Farage suggesting a method to circumvent UK electoral law to secure a £500,000 foreign donation for Reform UK. The footage showed Dan Jukes proposing that a UK-based son make the donation using funds provided by his non-permissible American father. Reform UK has denied any wrongdoing, dismissed the broadcast as a hoax by climate activists, and launched internal investigations into the staff involved, while the Metropolitan Police are assessing the matter.
key_points: Undercover reporters posed as a potential foreign donor and his UK-registered son to meet with Reform UK officials.
Senior aide Dan Jukes was filmed suggesting that the UK-based son could register the £500,000 donation while receiving the funds from his American father.
Nigel Farage was later recorded thanking the individuals and stating 'it's all above board' during a lunch meeting.
Reform UK denied wrongdoing, claiming they were targeted in a hoax by foreign-funded climate change activists.
The Metropolitan Police are assessing the media reports and information regarding potential breaches of electoral law.

title: Reform officials ‘plotted to break law on foreign donations’ in undercover film
author: Rowena Mason
content:
Nigel Farage is facing fresh criticism on the eve of the Reform UK party conference after some of his team were filmed appearing to plot to avoid electoral laws on foreign donations in an undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News.
A group of investigative journalists called Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party.
The polling was not attributed to Reform, and was reported in the Telegraph and the Times without those newspapers knowing that it was commissioned by the party and paid for by the US donor. The benefit in kind was also not reported to the Electoral Commission.
In footage of another meeting, a senior adviser to Farage, Dan Jukes, appeared to suggest to the fake UK-based supporter that his US-based father could make a substantial donation by channelling it through the son.
When the possible structure was explained to Farage, footage of a meeting between him and the fake donors shows him saying: “Thankyou both.”
The investigation will reopen intense scrutiny of Reform’s approach to donations and its finances, which are already the subject of a standards inquiry and police investigation.
Reform said it had been “the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded, climate change activists posing as would-be party donors” and the party denied any wrongdoing.
In Channel 4 News’ investigation, broadcast on Thursday night, footage shows the fake UK-based supporter also had conversations with Reform UK’s head of policy, James Orr, who talked about commissioning polling that would be paid for by the US-based father.
![Footage from the Channel 4 News and Verbatim undercover investigation into Reform finances.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/f9137dd4078cd07a4438200e8868571917088bde/287_0_2326_1598/master/2326.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In the film, Orr can be heard saying of the arrangement that Farage “doesn’t know, won’t know” and it was the kind of thing he would “rather not know”. At one point the footage shows him saying it was “totally legit” and with “nothing untoward about it at all”.
Farage was subsequently caught on camera in a meeting with the fake US donor in Clacton where he appears to be celebrating the success of the poll, saying it was “amazing” and provided “bang for buck”, adding: “It worked. Boom.”
Jukes, a close aide to Farage, was also filmed meeting the fake donor and at a Reform UK reception appearing to introduce the undercover operative in one conversation as “key donor for off the book project”.
In footage of a meeting with the fake US donor, he is heard describing the polling as “clandestine” and “hugely important”.
The polling, conducted by JL Partners, made headlines before the local elections in May. The foreign source of funding and its links to Reform were not publicly disclosed, and the Telegraph said it had now suspended the articles about the polling, while the Times said it was not aware of the relationship with Reform.
After Channel 4 News’ broadcast, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said the “scandal goes right to the top of Reform UK”. She added: “Nigel Farage needs to urgently prove today that his top team haven’t broken the law and secretly plotted to undermine our democracy.”
Ed Davey, the leader of the Liberal Democrats, called on the police and the Electoral Commission to investigate.
A Reform spokesperson said: “Reform UK has a robust vetting process for prospective donors approved by the Electoral Commission. The hoaxers are ‘Verbatim Investigations’; a new company, incorporated in July 2026 in an attempt to mask their true identity: the Centre for Climate Reporting.”
The party claimed the group’s methods had previously been “rebuked by members of the United States Congress” for “videos [that] appear to be substantially edited, creating an incomplete record of the conversation”.
The investigation is likely to create a serious problem for Farage as he attempts to turn the page on Reform’s summer of funding scandals, with his party conference speech scheduled for Friday.
In the speech, he will boast of record donations compared with the other parties, including £4m from a crypto billionaire pardoned by Donald Trump in the last quarter.
The Reform UK leader will tell the annual Birmingham gathering that the party is “much stronger than we were last year”, saying that it has the highest number of members and has brought in the most donations.
Farage will also seek to look to the future by claiming he would declare a “national emergency” in order to pass legislation day and night if made prime minister, insisting he believes Reform UK will win the next election.
The party outperformed Labour and the Conservatives with donations of more than £5m in the second quarter of this year, new figures from the Electoral Commission show.
However, it remains reliant on a handful of mega-donors who have been based abroad and could be caught by the government’s new £100,000 annual cap on overseas funders which requires donors to have been a UK resident for 12 months.
The biggest donation in the last few months was the £4m from Ben Delo, a crypto entrepreneur who has been based in Hong Kong in recent years but in April said he was moving back to the UK.
Delo, who was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money-laundering controls in his cryptocurrency business, before being pardoned by Trump, has previously given Reform £4m.
Party sources said it was “very confident” that none of Delo’s latest £4m would need to be returned due to the cap when the legislation is passed.
The government has said donors would have to have been on the UK electoral register for at least 12 months and meet a residency test showing that they are “genuinely resident at a UK address”.
Any gifts over the £100,000 cap from an overseas-based donor would have to be handed back once the new legislation is passed if deemed to be impermissible under the new law.
Reform’s confidence in the donation would suggest Delo has been on the UK domestic electoral register and believes he can meet residency test when the donations were made in April and May. Delo did not respond to a request for comment.
Christopher Harborne, the Thailand-based billionaire who has given the party £15m and £5m to Farage personally, did not give any cash after the cap was introduced in March.
The £5m gift to Farage from before the last election is under investigation by the standards commissioner, and Reform has slid in the polls since the amount was first revealed by the Guardian.
summary: An undercover investigation by Channel 4 News and the Centre for Climate Reporting caught Reform UK officials allegedly plotting to bypass electoral laws regarding foreign donations. Journalists posing as a wealthy US donor and his UK-based son funded £30,000 of untriangulated polling for Reform without reporting it to the Electoral Commission. Reform denied any wrongdoing, stating they were targeted in a hoax by climate activists.
key_points: Undercover journalists posing as a wealthy US donor and his son funded £30,000 of polling that benefited Reform UK.
Senior Reform officials, including Dan Jukes and James Orr, were filmed discussing ways to conceal the foreign funding source and bypass electoral laws.
Nigel Farage was captured on camera thanking the fake donors and celebrating the success of the clandestine polling.
Reform UK denied wrongdoing, claiming they were the target of a hoax orchestrated by foreign-funded climate change activists.
Political opponents, including Labour and Liberal Democrat leaders, have called for investigations into the scandal.

title: Kemi Badenoch accuses Andy Burnham of kicking defence spending into the long grass
author: Jennifer McKiernan
content:
![Badenoch is pictured from below the podium where she is giving a speech, at London Scottish House in Westminster, with a royal blue background and a Union flag to her left. She wears her braided hair tied back in a low ponytail, with a navy jacket and a turquoise top.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/866e/live/265146b0-a7a1-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch giving a speech on defence
- Published
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused the prime minister of "kicking defence spending into the long grass" as she set out Tory plans to push the figure to 3% of GDP by 2030.
Badenoch said a Conservative government would fund the commitment, worth Â£10bn a year, through measures including reimposing the two-child benefit cap, reforming housing benefit and ending VAT exemptions for Motability cars.
Pointing to the threat from countries like Russia and Iran, Badenoch told a press conference: "Conflict is coming, we must act now."
So far Andy Burnham's government has only committed to setting out a plan in the spring to meet the Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035.
Speaking at an event in central London, Badenoch said: "Andy Burnham is kicking defence spending into the long grass.
"Our enemies are not going to sit around and wait for Labour to find the money to fight them."
Burnham has pointed to his choice of Chancellor, John Healey, who quit as defence secretary in June over the last government's failure to commit to a 3% increase, as proof of his commitment to defence investment.
However, Badenoch said the prime minister should call a general election if he is not willing to find the money now, adding that Healey's decision to quit over defence spending appeared to have changed since he became chancellor.
"He resigned because Britain was not on track to reach 3% by 2030 and I praised him at the time for that decision," she said.
"Now that he is chancellor he does not seem to believe that any more and I am concerned he has been bought off with a promotion."
Badenoch repeated existing Conservative plans to fund an increase in defence spending, including by reimposing the two-child benefit cap.
The cap, which was scrapped by Labour in April, meant parents could only claim universal credit or tax credits for their first two children.
She said the final part of her party's plans to reach the 3% spending figure on defence had now been completed.
The Tories said this would include saving at least Â£4bn through reforms to housing benefit and removing the VAT exemption for Motability vehicles, saving Â£1bn.
"Alongside savings from the disastrous Chagos deal and re-purposing money from the British Business Bank into defence, we will be able to hit that 3% target," Badenoch said.
Housing benefit made up about 12% of the government's welfare bill this year, with Â£37.3bn forecast to be spent.
The Motability scheme, operated by a private company overseen by a charity, has historically given disabled people in receipt of eligible welfare benefits a 20% VAT discount on cars.
Last year, Rachel Reeves made the first changes to the Motability scheme in 50 years, removing about 50,000 premium cars like BMWs and Mercedes from the scheme and reinstating 20% VAT for most new cars, along with higher mileage charges.
Challenged over whether she was increasing child poverty to fund defence by reimposing the two-child benefit cap, Badenoch denied this.
"It is not going to increase child poverty. What increases child poverty is children's parents not having work or being paid low wages. We want to grow our economy," she told the BBC.
"Right now there are some people making choices not to have children because they can't afford it and paying for other people to have more children. That is not fair."
Responding to Badenoch's speech, a Labour Party spokesperson said: "These unserious plans are hardly surprising from the same Tory Party that hollowed out our Armed Forces, shrinking the British Army to its smallest size since the Napoleonic era.
"Andy Burnham has made it clear that his Labour government is determined to give our Armed Forces the investment needed to keep us safe.
"In just two years, Labour has delivered the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War, with funding already higher than at any point during 14 years of Conservative government."
It comes after Badenoch pressed Burnham over the issue during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, when she urged him to cut welfare spending and invest the money in defence.
Burnham also came under friendly fire from Labour MP Tan Dhesi at PMQs, who called on the prime minister to urgently commit to setting out a path to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.
"Defence is definitely one area where vibes alone just isn't going to be enough," he said.
Burnham has insisted his government is committed to fully funding its defence plans, saying it will set out a pathway to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 in the spring.
![Thin, red banner promoting the Politics Essential newsletter with text saying, âGet the latest political analysis and big moments, delivered straight to your inbox every weekdayâ. There is also an image of the Houses of Parliament.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/6fad/live/133a6af0-dc98-11ef-bc01-8f2c83dad217.png)
Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to read top political analysis, gain insight from across the UK and stay up to speed with the big moments. It'll be delivered straight to your inbox every weekday.
summary: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of delaying defence spending, setting out Tory plans to reach 3% of GDP by 2030. The proposals would be funded through measures such as reimposing the two-child benefit cap, reforming housing benefit, and ending VAT exemptions for Motability cars. In response, Labour defended its record, stating it has delivered the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War and plans to outline a pathway to 3.5% of GDP by 2035.
key_points: Kemi Badenoch criticized the government for delaying a commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030.
Conservative funding plans include reimposing the two-child benefit cap, reforming housing benefit, and ending VAT exemptions for Motability cars.
The Labour government committed to setting out a pathway to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 in the spring.
Labour defended its defence record, arguing that funding is already higher than at any point during 14 years of the previous Conservative government.

title: Andy Burnham praises UK-EU ties in meeting with Emmanuel Macron
author: Ewan Somerville; Nick Eardley
content:
Watch: Andy Burnham and Emmanuel Macron shake hands outside No 10
- Published
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has praised the UK-EU relationship as he held talks with French President Emmanuel Macron about issues such as small boat crossings in the English Channel and defence.
The pair shook hands and posed for photographs alongside their wives outside 10 Downing Street on Thursday morning.
They discussed "shared challenges" including the rise of "mega dinghies" crossing the Channel illegally, which the Conservatives say shows the UK government has failed to "smash the gangs".
Burnham said it was "so fitting" that Macron was his first overseas visitor in Downing Street since becoming PM in July, describing him as "our nearest neighbour and close friend Emmanuel".
![Emmanuel Macron and Andy Burnham sit on chairs in Downing Street smiling and in conversation with their respective flags behind them.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/ab6f/live/2a95d360-a78f-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Macron and Burnham held talks on a range of issues
"It shows what collaboration can achieve, just as we are also showing on Ukraine, on small boats, and also on strengthening the UK-EU relationship," Burnham added.
Macron said: "This is a very strong relationship. For me it is extremely important, and I'm here with willingness and a commitment to get closer."
The French leader's visit to the UK was primarily to mark the Bayeux Tapestry's loan to the British Museum. He met King Charles at the museum on Wednesday, ahead of the medieval tapestry going on public display next week.
In bilateral talks on Thursday, Burnham and Macron discussed not only small boats but also the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, as well as defence and EU co-operation.
The arrival of the first foreign leader under the Burnham premiership is an important symbolic moment - it shows the relationship with Paris is an important priority.
But it also reflects an obvious reality - to further reduce small boats crossings, working with France will be essential.
France and the UK have been working extremely closely on Ukraine and Iran, trying to jointly influence the White House.
And Paris will be an important player as the UK seeks even stronger economic ties with Europe under the new No 10 administration.
The "mega dinghies" crossing the Channel illegally - first seen earlier in August with a 15-metre long vessel carrying a record 230 migrants towards the UK - are arguably the most pressing challenge facing the pair.
It follows a summer when the overall number of small boat arrivals in the UK fell to a seven-year low.
Downing Street says 45 extra police officers are being deployed to French beaches in a "surge team" to tackle larger dinghies with more people packed onto them.
Earlier on Tuesday, Home Office Minister Anna Turley said the officers were "just part of the armoury" of more than 1,000 officers on northern French beaches who are now doing "actual intervention" in the water.
She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that videos in recent weeks "show them going to the boats, slashing them, pushing people back, being bombarded with stones and bricks and coming under a lot of challenge to do that, so they are intervening".
In a post on X, external, in which he said he was "do[ing] politics differently", Burnham laid out the latest small boat, returns and asylum hotel figures, describing smuggling gangs as a "shared European challenge".
Asked about the extra police on French beaches, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch told the BBC she welcomed European collaboration "but the boats aren't stopping".
"We have spent hundreds of millions, if not billions, paying the French to man the borders," she said.
![Thin, red banner promoting the Politics Essential newsletter with text saying, âTop political analysis in your inbox every dayâ. There is also an image of the Houses of Parliament.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/6133/live/2bce6ee0-0b00-11f0-97d3-37df2b293ed1.png)
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham met with French President Emmanuel Macron at 10 Downing Street to discuss bilateral relations, defense, and shared challenges including small boat crossings in the English Channel. Macron's visit also marked the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum. Both leaders emphasized the importance of UK-EU collaboration and a stronger partnership.
key_points: Prime Minister Andy Burnham hosted French President Emmanuel Macron at 10 Downing Street for talks on defense, Ukraine, the Middle East, and small boat crossings.
Macron's trip to the UK primarily marked the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum, where he also met King Charles.
The leaders discussed the rise of illegal 'mega dinghies' crossing the English Channel, prompting the deployment of 45 extra police officers to French beaches.
Burnham praised the UK-EU relationship, while Macron expressed a strong commitment to getting closer to the UK.

title: Green party leader Zack Polanski seeks to stand in byelection for Keir Starmer seat
author: Alexandra Topping
content:
Zack Polanski will seek to stand as a candidate in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, he has announced.
The leader of the Green party in England and Wales told the Camden New Journal on Thursday he would “stand up for people struggling to pay their bills” if he was elected as the representative for the area, which became vacant when Keir Starmer announced he was standing down as an MP.
In an effort to stave off accusations he was parachuting himself into the seat, Polanski said he had lived and worked in “this community” over many years. “I know it well and I love it. It represents so many of the things that make London so special. I am so excited by the prospect of representing this place in parliament,” he said.
Local Green party members will have the final say on the selected candidate, but the Guardian understands that they are supportive of Polanski running, and that there is no clear local activist with significant support expected to oppose him.
![Polanski with smiling supporters with placards](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/9da6f35e1e5f1eb96b729815a914485f2247d55e/0_0_5000_3265/master/5000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The Green leader, who has led the party to record election results in Camden – the local authority that covers the constituency – and across the country, already represents the area as a city-wide member of the London Assembly. “Holborn and St Pancras has everything that’s the best of our country and so much potential – but for too long now it’s been held back by governments who have failed to make the changes to improve people’s lives.”
Polanski said he was confident that the Greens could win the seat. Holborn and St Pancras has traditionally been viewed as a Labour stronghold, but the Greens have gained ground there over the last year.
“We know that the Greens can win here, and by electing me, voters will have someone who will always fight their corner – never scared of big donors or the party whip,” said Polanski. “Too often Labour has stood up for corporations and big money. I will stand up for people struggling to pay their bills.”
after newsletter promotion
Adding that the byelection was a chance for the community to “make history” by electing London’s first Green MP, Polanski emphasised that the contest would be a two-dog fight between Labour and the Greens.
“We know that people are struggling – that the things we used to afford are increasingly out of reach – and this is a chance to send a very clear message that we won’t sit by as we get poorer and extreme wealth is concentrated at the very top,” he said.
The Greens are likely to pose the greatest threat in the byelection to Labour, which has held the central London constituency continuously since the seat was created in 1983, winning at least 40% of the vote at every election.
Only two Labour MPs have ever represented Holborn and St Pancras: the former health secretary Frank Dobson, from 1983 to 2015, then Starmer.
At the most recent general election in 2024, Starmer held the seat with 48.9% of the vote, ahead of the independent candidate Andrew Feinstein in second place on 18.9% and the Greens in third on 10.4%.
The Conservatives came fourth on 7.2%, Reform finished fifth on 6.1% and the Liberal Democrats were sixth on 5.8%.
The popularity of the independent and Green candidates at the 2024 contest, finishing second and third respectively, may have been partly owing to former Labour voters protesting against Starmer’s refusal to take a stronger position on Israel’s actions in Gaza in its war with Hamas.
summary: Green party leader Zack Polanski has announced his candidacy for the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, triggered by Keir Starmer stepping down as an MP. Polanski defended against accusations of parachuting into the seat, emphasizing his long-term residency and work in the community. While the constituency has historically been a Labour stronghold, the Greens aim to challenge them in what Polanski frames as a two-horse race to elect London's first Green MP.
key_points: Zack Polanski is seeking the Green party nomination for the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.
The seat became vacant after Keir Starmer announced he was stepping down as an MP.
Local Green party members have the final say on the candidate selection, though they are reported to be supportive of Polanski.
Holborn and St Pancras has been continuously held by Labour since its creation in 1983.
At the 2024 general election, Starmer won the seat with 48.9% of the vote, with the Green party finishing in third place.

title: French launch mega-dinghy police taskforce
author: Charles Hymas
content:
![People smugglers are using 15m-long dinghies to transport migrants across the Channel](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/02/TELEMMGLPICT000498008183_17883797367900_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![People smugglers are using 15m-long dinghies to transport migrants across the Channel](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/02/TELEMMGLPICT000498008183_17883797367900_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
France is setting up a special police unit to combat people smugglers using mega-dinghies to transport migrants across the Channel.
