On the eve of Andy Burnham’s first bilateral meeting with Emmanuel Macron, the French president, on Thursday, the two governments announced that a “surge” team of 45 officers would be deployed to the beaches west of Calais.
Officers supported by drones and aerial intelligence will be tasked with targeting beaches where mega-dinghies are launched, and disrupting boat and equipment supply lines before they reach the coast.
The 45-strong unit is in addition to the 1,050 French officers committed to stopping the boats. It was announced on Wednesday that the force was at full strength with the addition of a 75-officer unit focused on curbing crossings in northern France.
The move comes after 260 migrants crossed the Channel on a 15m mega-dinghy, breaking the record for a single boat of 165 migrants.
At least 30 migrants were thrown off the boat into the sea during its passage because it was so overcrowded, according to French officials.
While the number of boat crossings during the summer months has dropped to its lowest level since 2019, smugglers have started loading more people on to fewer, larger vessels, partly because of the success of law enforcement in disrupting their supply chains for boats and equipment.
As well as turning to larger boats, the people-smuggling gangs have also started launching their taxi boats further east and west along the French, Belgian and Dutch coasts to avoid interception by a new seaborne police unit and the increased number of officers on the beaches.
Before the talks, Mr Burnham said the two countries needed to “stay one step ahead” of the criminals’ evolving tactics as he pledged not to be “complacent” after a 45 per cent fall in the number of small-boat arrivals this year compared with 2025.
![A police officer uses a knife to slash a dinghy after it was abandoned by migrants trying to cross the English Channel on a beach in Gravelines, France](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/02/TELEMMGLPICT000432122415_17883798439781_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwWyaKjL1CatlwZEbgNRqSgg.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Mr Burnham said: “The progress we have seen this summer shows what can be achieved when the UK and France work together.
“But I am clear that we cannot be complacent. Smuggling gangs are constantly adapting their tactics, and the UK and France need to respond quickly and stay one step ahead of the criminals facilitating the dangerous crossings.
“The small boats crisis is a shared European challenge, and no country can solve it alone. Working with France and our international partners, we will restore order and control to our borders and prevent smugglers exploiting vulnerable migrants.”
Shabana Mahmood, the Home Secretary, signed a new £662m three-year deal with France increasing the overall number of French officers by 25 per cent to 1,050. It includes expanding from 18 to 30 officers a specialist French intelligence and judicial team seeking to root out and prosecute smuggling networks.
Some £160m of the money is earmarked for “innovative” tactics such as the new unit conducting interceptions at sea. It is this money which is being used to fund the mega-dinghy unit.
Ms Mahmood said: “We are boosting officer numbers to record highs to crack down on small boat launches and the gangs behind them.
“This work is bearing fruit. Over 48,000 crossing attempts have been prevented, small boat crossing numbers are down and removals of those here illegally are at record levels.
“But we are not complacent and we must be relentless. We will continue efforts on all fronts to tackle these illegal and dangerous crossings.”
![A girl is carried on a man's shoulders as migrants wade into the sea to try and board a dinghy to cross the English Channel](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/02/TELEMMGLPICT000436796442_17883798079080_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwWyaKjL1CatlwZEbgNRqSgg.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: “Since the election 95 per cent of illegal immigrants crossing the Channel have been allowed to stay – so no wonder they keep coming. Almost 20,000 illegal immigrants so far this year is still a disaster.
“I went to France recently and saw 10 armed French Gendarmes Nationale – who UK taxpayers fund – standing around doing nothing while 100 illegal immigrants embarked in knee deep water. I spoke to a Gendarme who said that they had orders not to intervene. The £660 million we pay should be withheld until the French prevent all embarkations in shallow waters.
“We now have a mega-dingy crisis with 150 illegal immigrants per dingy crossing every time the sea is calm. All we have from the government are press releases and gimmicks. They haven’t smashed the gangs and the ‘one in, one out’ deal has seen only 3 per cent of arrivals returned. It’s a joke.”
‘I do want a closer relationship’
As well as migration, Mr Burnham and Mr Macron will discuss the Ukraine and Iran wars and how they affect Europe’s security and economy, No 10 said.
The Prime Minister will push for greater co-operation with Europe, Downing Street said, as he looks set to continue his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer’s, policy of a “reset” of UK-EU relations.
During Wednesday’s Prime Minister’s Questions, Mr Burnham reiterated that Britain’s decade of low growth “has been partly a result of Brexit”.
“I do want a closer relationship – I will build on the work of my predecessor,” he told MPs, before a UK-EU summit later in the year.
Mr Macron is the first European leader to visit the UK since Mr Burnham took office in July.
The pair joined the King and the Queen to visit the Bayeux Tapestry at London’s British Museum on Wednesday.
summary: France is deploying a special surge team of 45 police officers to target beaches west of Calais and disrupt supply lines used by people smugglers operating mega-dinghies. The new unit is funded by a £662 million, three-year deal with the UK that increases the total number of French officers committed to stopping Channel crossings to 1,050. The measure comes in response to smugglers using larger vessels, including a 15-meter mega-dinghy that carried 260 migrants, as gangs adapt their tactics to evade law enforcement.
key_points: France is deploying a 45-officer surge team supported by drones and aerial intelligence to target mega-dinghy launches west of Calais.
The initiative is part of a £662m three-year deal that increases French security personnel tackling Channel crossings to 1,050 officers.
Smugglers have increasingly turned to larger vessels and alternate launch locations along French, Belgian, and Dutch coasts to avoid interception.
The tactical shift follows a record-breaking crossing where a single 15-meter mega-dinghy transported 260 migrants, during which at least 30 people were thrown into the sea due to overcrowding.

title: Bayeux tapestry loan symbolises ‘entente amicale’ between France and UK, says King Charles
author: Caroline Davies
content:
The loan of the Bayeux tapestry was “the best possible symbol” of the “entente amicale” between France and the UK, King Charles said, as he visited the famous embroidered masterpiece at the British Museum in London.
Though the tapestry recounts a conflict, “here it is today, nearly 1,000 years later, as a precious symbol of trust, at a time when trust seems sadly to be in short supply between nations,” he said.
The “70 metres of memory and artistry” were a reminder “that our two nations have been bound together for almost a millennium”, added Charles, speaking at the new exhibition and accompanied by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and UK prime minister, Andy Burnham.
In a speech partly delivered in French, he said: “We have defended our values together in times of peril; we continue to do so today across the world.”
He continued: “May this tapestry – and the treasures that will travel in return – stand as symbols not only of our shared past, but our shared future: a future woven, as it should be, by Britain and France together.”
Macron, also speaking in French and English, said that the return of the tapestry “had required a little patience” , since he first spoke of it in 2018.
“Since the first British request dates back to 1931, I choose to regard eight years as something of a speed record,” he said.
He added that, with the tapestry in Britain, his hopes were that the two countries could “forge a bond as close as the threads of this thousand-year-old embroidery”.
The tapestry – the woven record of the Norman conquest – has returned to the UK for the first time in almost 1,000 years, and is on loan until September 2027 as part of a special trilateral agreement between the UK, France and the museum.
Charles’s reference to entente amicale followed his use of the phrase to rebrand the famous “entente cordiale” between the two nations in his banquet speech at Windsor Castle when he hosted the Macrons in July last year.
During Wednesday’s visit, he expressed his “deepest appreciation” to Macron and the French people “for the trust you have placed in the United Kingdom by agreeing to this unprecedented loan”.
He said: “It once depicted warriors crossing the Channel; yet today it forms part of a cultural exchange that will see some of the British Museum’s own precious artefacts travel to France in return, in a spirit of friendship.”
Thanking all those who made the loan possible, he added: “Anyone studying the tapestry’s scenes in detail will notice that, even in the 11th century, historic events rarely happened without extensive discussion, careful planning and a great deal of organisation beforehand.”
The party, which also included Queen Camilla, France’s first lady, Brigitte Macron, and Burnham’s wife, Marie-France van Heel, stopped at key moments along the 11th-century artwork to hear from curators about historic events such as the coronation of Harold Godwinson and the much-disputed depiction of his death by an arrow to the eye at the Battle of Hastings in 1066.
At his first prime minister’s questions earlier on Wednesday, Burnham said: “The loaning of the tapestry is a great example of French-British cooperation, the same cooperation that has helped us reduce summer small boat crossings to a seven-year low.”
The Labour leader also said the Bayeux Around Britain programme, which will see the digital exhibition displayed in museums, galleries and castles in all four nations, would “give communities across the UK the opportunity to learn about one of the defining stories of our past”.
In exchange, Britain will loan the Sutton Hoo treasures – an assemblage of gold and other historic objects dating from the 7th century AD – and a selection of Lewis chess pieces and other masterpieces owned by the trustees of the British Museum to museums in France.
summary: King Charles and French President Emmanuel Macron celebrated the historic loan of the Bayeux tapestry to the British Museum as a powerful symbol of the "entente amicale" and enduring trust between the UK and France. The 11th-century masterpiece, recounting the Norman conquest, has returned to Britain for the first time in nearly 1,000 years as part of a cultural exchange. In return, the British Museum is loaning precious artifacts, including Sutton Hoo treasures and Lewis chess pieces, to museums in France.
key_points: The Bayeux tapestry is on display at the British Museum until September 2027 in an unprecedented loan between the UK and France.
King Charles stated the loan symbolizes trust and a shared future between the two nations.
President Emmanuel Macron joked that the eight-year turnaround since his 2018 proposal was a speed record, given the first British request was in 1931.
As part of the cultural exchange, Britain will send Sutton Hoo treasures and Lewis chess pieces to France.
The digital Bayeux Around Britain programme will display the exhibition in all four UK nations.

title: Jury discharged in trial of teacher accused of sex with pupil
author: Fiona Lamdin; Leigh Boobyer
content:
![A woman with long blonde hair is holding a mobile phone to her ear, while looking down at the floor. She is wearing sunglasses and a beige top as she walks.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/c1d2/live/33c66bf0-a5ed-11f1-8348-fb0cb1cd9761.jpg)
Bronwen James has denied having a sexual relationship with the pupil

The jury in the trial of a PE teacher accused of having sex with a 16-year-old pupil has been discharged.

The 30-year-old PE teacher has denied all charges.
The initial jury was discharged on the opening day of the trial.
The case has been adjourned until Thursday for a new jury to be sworn in.

title: Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron join King Charles and Queen Camilla in private viewing of famed Bayeux Tapestry | CNN
author: Lianne Kolirin
content:
Britain’s King Charles III and Queen Camilla were joined by the French president and first lady at the British Museum in London on Wednesday for a private tour of the Bayeux Tapestry — a world-famous artwork depicting a fateful battle between the two nations.
Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron are on a two-day visit to the United Kingdom, in a bid to foster closer ties between the two European countries. Their trip began with a visit to see the 11th-century embroidery — currently on loan to Britain from France — which arrived in the UK in July after an absence of more than 900 years.
Also joining the two couples on the tour of the blockbuster exhibition, which opens to the public next week, were the recently appointed British prime minister, Andy Burnham, and his wife, Marie-France van Heel. In the role since July 20, it is the first time that Burnham has met the French leader.
Stretching to 70 meters long (230 feet), the Bayeux Tapestry is not actually a tapestry at all but an embroidery of dyed wool stitched onto a bleached linen background.
![The Bayeux Tapestry, on exhibit at the British Museum in London on Wednesday.](https://media.cnn.com/api/v1/images/stellar/prod/gettyimages-2292621941.jpg?c=original&q=w_860,c_fill)
Created 960 years ago, it depicts the events leading up to the Battle of Hastings in 1066, which saw William of Normandy seize the throne from Harold Godwinson, the last Anglo-Saxon king of England, marking one of the great turning points in English history.
“The Bayeux Tapestry tells a story familiar to most people in this country … a moment that changed the course of these islands forever,” Charles said in a speech at the British Museum.
“I can’t help but feel its protagonists, on both sides of the (English) Channel, would look with satisfaction on the Franco-British gathering here today, and be pleased that our two great nations, which share such fundamental values, have prospered together,” he added.
The loan of the work to the British Museum follows a historic agreement reached between the two countries after years of negotiation, and exhaustive planning to transport it safely from its permanent home in Normandy, northern France.
“The return of the Bayeux Tapestry to England is a landmark moment in the history of our two nations, and I want people everywhere in the country to be able to enjoy it,” Burnham said in a statement, according to PA Media.
Tickets for the first stage of the exhibition sold out as soon as they went on sale earlier this year, with the British Museum recording its single biggest day of ticket sales in its history — more than £2.4 million ($3.2 million) in sales in the first 24 hours.
The VIPs were met at the museum by its director, Nicholas Cullinan, and George Osborne, a former British finance minister who is now the museum’s chair. They were then led along the length of the tapestry, as curators pointed out the key moments depicted within it.
After the tour, the dignitaries gathered in the museum’s glass-topped Great Court.
summary: King Charles III and Queen Camilla hosted French President Emmanuel Macron and First Lady Brigitte Macron at the British Museum for a private viewing of the Bayeux Tapestry. The 11th-century embroidery depicts the events leading to the 1066 Battle of Hastings and is on loan to the UK from France after more than 900 years. The VIP tour also included British Prime Minister Andy Burnham during his first meeting with the French leader.
key_points: Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron visited the UK on a two-day trip to foster closer ties between the two nations.
The Bayeux Tapestry is a 70-meter-long embroidery currently on loan to the British Museum from France.
The 960-year-old artwork depicts the events of the 1066 Battle of Hastings.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham met the French president for the first time during the museum tour.

title: Andy Burnham faces an impossible job. At least he’s got a secret weapon – Kemi Badenoch
author: John Crace
content:
Call it the gentlest of all reality checks. A quantum realignment in expectations. The faintest reminder to both Andy Burnham and Labour backbenchers that international bond markets are impervious to Manchester charm and positivity. Despite a summer of feelgood announcements from the government, there is no escaping the fact that the country is still up shit creek. It’s going to be a tough ride ahead. Nothing will come pain-free.
Still, a new prime minister has to learn to take the wins – however small – as they come along. In the wider scheme of things, a good prime minister’s questions means next to nothing: it’s nothing more than politics as performance. Yet it can set the tone and buy a prime minister some goodwill from MPs and the media. Plus, it’s a weekly event so you may as well be good at it.
Burnham can be very pleased with his first outing, even if it didn’t go totally as billed. We had been promised a more consensual politics. An end to point scoring. That lasted all of five minutes. After that, it was business as usual. Partly because that’s the way PMQs has always been set up, but mainly because Andy just couldn’t help himself.
It would have taken a will of iron to resist. Not least because Kemi Badenoch made it so easy for him. Not for the first time, Labour’s secret weapon is the Tory leader. She just can’t help herself from speaking without thinking, getting lost in her own sense of brilliance and failing to spot the traps she is setting for herself. Still, at least no one can call Kemi boring. Though it is quite hard to see why so many Tories seem to drink her Kool-Aid.
You could tell that Burnham was very nervous at the start. Understandably so. Twitchy. Not totally in command. PMQs is always an ordeal and never more so for a leader on whom so many Labour hopes have been pinned. Some of them Burnham has even pinned on himself.
“It’s good to be back at the dispatch box,” he began, before listing some of the Labour government’s achievements. Like the number of small boat crossings being at their lowest for years. The Tories barely looked up. It was almost as if they had never been that bothered about illegal immigration, and they certainly weren’t about to give Labour any credit. Opposition parties hate it when something goes well. There’s nothing that suits them better than a country in crisis. They never seem to realise that one day they might be called upon to sort it out.
![Kemi Badenoch speaking during prime minister's questions in the House of Commons. She is seen in profile and looks animated with one hand raised, pointing one finger in front of her.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/beb7d79b50dfe7266b46beeec01185f268378ec7/1185_548_1815_1452/master/1815.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Kemi’s opening gambit was flirtatious. Going out of her way to congratulate Andy on his stamina. Burnham merely nodded. A lot of people had said that to him. Then Kemi decided she had had enough sweet-talk. That was Burnham’s problem. Always promising the earth. Never daring to say no to anyone. Too desperate to be loved to be a good leader. So could he mention anything he had ever cut?
First the smile, then the reply. “Tax,” Burnham said. This was effectively game over for PMQs. Kemi had imagined a Keir Starmer-like evasion. A prime minister caught out. She had never dreamed of this. Andy spelled it out. He had removed VAT on electricity bills. He had cut business rates for pubs and hospitality venues. He didn’t choose to point out these cuts had been paid for by cutting a budget for digital ID that had never existed. Best to keep it simple.
Next Kemi turned to the bond markets. She seemed to think they had it in for Labour. Burnham kept it pleasant and polite. It was like this. The international bond markets didn’t have a special grudge against him. This wasn’t personal. They hadn’t been waiting for Tuesday’s statement, itching to put interest rates up.
This was a global problem. Other countries were also facing rising borrowing costs. And if Kemi really wanted to know where the blame lay, she could take a look at her own party’s 14 years of stagnant growth. It was the Tories who had trashed the economy. He was merely trying to pick up the pieces. He could also have blamed the Iran war and the spike in oil prices. A war for which Kemi had been initially enthusiastic. Her judgment is seldom the best.
Now Kemi sounded almost hurt. As if a promise had been broken. Burnham had said there would be no more point scoring, and here he was openly point scoring. I know, I know, said Andy unapologetically. He just couldn’t help himself. It was just too tempting. It made him feel good about himself to hear the laughs and support of his own backbenchers. PMQs wasn’t all about him. It was a team sport.
So while he was about it, Burnham had plenty more points to score. Kemi has yet to realise just how vulnerable she has made herself by appointing Andrew Griffith as shadow chancellor. The man who co-authored Liz Truss’s mini-budget and was one of its most outspoken defenders.
For Labour this is an open goal and they are going to be kicking the ball into the net as often as possible. Kemi may be a woman who doesn’t believe in history. Who thinks each day is a surprising new beginning. But the country is still a long way from forgiving the Tory party for the lasting damage caused by 49 days of Tory chaos. So the self-harm is going to continue for a while.
After failing to rule out further tax rises and spending commitments, Burnham went back to his happy place. Good vibes, hope and positivity. All of which are enough to make this a comfortable first PMQs. But he will be more than aware that this is a half-hour bubble and that life will only get tougher outside it.
Though Andy appears to be a sucker for work. He spent the rest of the session offering meetings to virtually every MP. Soon his whole life will be one long meeting. Or a meeting to find out why a meeting was not necessary. Meetings to rule out further meetings. Still, I am sure he will enjoy his meeting with Samantha Niblett, whose stated mission has been to have a summer of sex. And to tell as many people as possible about it.
Not everything went Burnham’s way. A disgruntled Tan Dhesi, the Labour chair of the defence select committee, was extremely grumpy about the 3% promise. Or possibly not being asked to be a minister. Still, Andy looked happy enough when the speaker called time. The first PMQs was over and he was 1-0 up. Not that anyone was keeping the score. Much.
summary: Andy Burnham navigated his first Prime Minister's Questions, which quickly abandoned promises of consensual politics in favor of standard point-scoring. Despite initial nervousness, Burnham effectively countered Tory leader Kemi Badenoch, highlighting tax cuts and blaming past Conservative economic mismanagement for ongoing global market pressures. While the session provided a successful start for Burnham, he remains aware that significant national challenges lie ahead outside the parliamentary bubble.
key_points: Andy Burnham had a successful first outing at Prime Minister's Questions despite initial nervousness.
Kemi Badenoch struggled during the session, making tactical errors that allowed Burnham to easily counter her arguments.
Burnham highlighted government actions such as removing VAT on electricity bills and cutting business rates.
Burnham deflected criticisms regarding bond markets by pointing to the economic damage caused by 14 years of Conservative governance.

title: King Charles, Macron and Burnham to get preview of Bayeux Tapestry at British Museum
author: Sean Coughlan
content:
![Bayeux Tapestry showing an embroidered image of William, Duke of Normandy](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/0af0/live/5f19e850-a6b9-11f1-ae1e-219da1d6451a.jpg)
The Bayeux Tapestry is going to be open to the public in London from next week
- Published
King Charles, French President Emmanuel Macron and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham are to preview one of the blockbuster cultural events of the year, when they get to view the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum.
The visit on Wednesday comes ahead of the medieval tapestry going on public display in London from 10 September.
The 70m (230ft) tapestry, originally embroidered in England but kept for centuries in France, tells the story of the Norman Conquest and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.
President Macron said the loan of the national treasure until July 2027 was a "powerful symbol" of the close ties between the UK and France.
![King Charles and President Macron in a carriage at the state visit to the UK in July 2025](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1376/cpsprodpb/05ca/live/ae682490-a6b8-11f1-ae1e-219da1d6451a.jpg)
The loan of the tapestry was announced at last year's French state visit to the UK
King Charles and Queen Camilla, Andy Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel, and Emmanuel Macron and Brigitte Macron will be shown key scenes in the tapestry, including the Coronation of King Harold and his death in battle.
School children from the UK and France will attend the event, with the King and the French president expected to make speeches marking the historic loan.
Sending the tapestry to the British Museum had been announced by Macron during the French state visit to the UK in July 2025, as an emblem of the strong partnership between the countries.
There had been some worries that moving the fragile tapestry could risk causing damage, but French government sources said ahead of the royal preview: "The display conditions at the British Museum are ideal."
The French authorities welcomed the way that visitors in London would see the tapestry lying flat, rather than upright, with this believed to be better for the conservation of the fibres, sewn more than 900 years ago.
It is believed that the final scenes of the tapestry have been lost or destroyed, as it has not always had such careful owners. In the 18th Century, during the French Revolution, it was rescued from being cut up to make covers for soldiers' carts.
At a state banquet hosted by King Charles in Windsor, Macron had said the missing end of the tapestry was a symbol that "in the great mural of Franco-British history, the end is yet to be written - it is up to us to do it".
![A boat from the Norman invasion depicted in the Bayeux Tapestry](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/992d/live/b516b1c0-a6b9-11f1-ae1e-219da1d6451a.jpg)
The tapestry tells the story of the Norman invasion of England in 1066
This trip to the British Museum will be the first official joint engagement carried out together by King Charles and Andy Burnham since he became prime minister in July.
Burnham said the tapestry exhibition would be a chance to celebrate the "shared heritage" between the UK and France.
"The return of the Bayeux Tapestry to England is a landmark moment in the history of our two nations," he said.
French government sources said the occasion will also be an opportunity for President Macron to get to know Burnham.
Support for Ukraine, the conflict in the Middle East, and relations with the European Union will be among the topics for the two leaders, say French sources.
Small boats crossing the Channel are likely to be discussed, as well as those Norman versions embroidered on the tapestry.
The Bayeux Tapestry records a much earlier chapter in Anglo-French relations, when King William of Normandy fought King Harold for the throne of England.
Using dyed wool stitched onto linen, it shows the competing claims to the throne, the Normans sailing across the Channel and the decisive Battle of Hastings, in which Harold was killed, allowing William the Conqueror to become monarch.
The tapestry, believed to have been embroidered by English women for the new Norman rulers in the 1070s, includes 58 separate scenes, with 627 human figures, 737 animals, 37 ships and 23 trees, with a Latin narration accompanying the images.
As part of this cultural diplomatic exchange, the UK is lending France one of the British Museum's prize exhibits - treasures from the Anglo-Saxon Sutton Hoo burial.
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said: "Britain and France have a unique shared history and nothing symbolises it more than the Bayeux Tapestry.
She said "a generation of British children will remember it for the rest of their lives".
There was strong demand for tickets to see the tapestry, with the exhibition already sold out until the end of 2026.
The next tickets, covering visits between January and March 2027, will be available from the British Museum from 21 October.
![Your Voice banner image. Your Voice is written in white against a purple background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/d048/live/80825d90-55a8-11f1-b682-cf91850925ea.png)
![Thin, purple banner promoting the Royal Watch newsletter with text saying, âInsider stories and expert analysis in your inbox every weekâ. There is also a graphic of a fleur-de-lis in white.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/ef34/live/a99f61b0-109d-11f0-b234-07dc7691c360.png)
summary: King Charles, French President Emmanuel Macron, and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham are previewing the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum ahead of its public display starting September 10. The 70-meter medieval tapestry, which depicts the 1066 Norman Conquest, is on loan from France until July 2027 as a symbol of Franco-British partnership. In exchange, the UK is lending France treasures from the Anglo-Saxon Sutton Hoo burial.
key_points: King Charles, Emmanuel Macron, and Andy Burnham are previewing the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum before it opens to the public on September 10.
The 70-meter medieval tapestry details the 1066 Norman Conquest and is on loan from France until July 2027.
Exhibition tickets are already sold out through the end of 2026, with the next batch for early 2027 releasing in October.
As part of the cultural exchange, the UK is lending France treasures from the Sutton Hoo burial.

title: Five people charged over Wincobank newborn baby death
author: Alex Moss
content:
![Two police officers stand guard outside the entrance to a house. Visible in the photo is some police tape and a bouquet of flowers.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/de1b/live/b3bb1cd0-a61e-11f1-bb6f-e5db02d232fa.jpg)
A post-mortem examination revealed the baby died as a result of stab wounds
- Published
Two men and two women have been charged with murder after a baby girl was found stabbed to death at a house in Sheffield.
The newborn was found at the property on Holywell Heights in the Wincobank area on Sunday morning, after police were called to reports of concern for her safety.
South Yorkshire Police said two men, aged 19 and 38, and two women, aged 20 and 37, had been charged with murder, causing or allowing the death of a child and perverting the course of justice by taking steps to conceal the killing of an infant.
A fifth person, a 15-year-old girl, has also been charged with perverting the course of justice.
Police said all five had been remanded in custody and were due to appear at Sheffield Magistrates' Court later.
They are:
- Peter Horvath, aged 19, of Holywell Heights, Sheffield
- Andrea Skopova, aged 20, formerly of Robey Street, Sheffield
- Nina Horvathova, aged 37, of Holywell Heights, Sheffield
- Peter Horvath, aged 38, of Holywell Heights, Sheffield
- The 15-year-old girl, who cannot be named for legal reasons
Two women, aged 26 and 37, who were arrested on suspicion of murder remain on bail, police added.
Det Ch Insp Tom Woodward said: "This is a significant step in our investigation into the tragic circumstances that resulted in the death of this baby girl.
"I would like to thank our communities, who I know will have been deeply impacted by this traumatic incident, for supporting us as we work through this intricate investigation.
"We would ask the public to avoid speculating and posting information online about this case while the legal process takes it course.
"Protecting the integrity of the criminal justice process is crucial to us securing justice for this little girl."
Police said officers would continue to be in and around the Holywell Heights area carrying out inquiries.
summary: Five people have been charged following the death of a newborn baby girl who was found stabbed at a house in the Wincobank area of Sheffield. A post-mortem examination confirmed the infant died from stab wounds after police responded to a concern for safety call on Sunday morning. Four of the suspects face charges of murder, causing or allowing the death of a child, and perverting the course of justice, while a fifth person has been charged with perverting the course of justice.
key_points: A newborn baby girl was found stabbed to death at a property on Holywell Heights in Sheffield.
Two men and two women have been charged with murder, causing or allowing the death of a child, and perverting the course of justice.
A 15-year-old girl has been charged with perverting the course of justice.
All five charged individuals have been remanded in custody to appear at Sheffield Magistrates' Court.
Two other women remain on bail after being arrested on suspicion of murder.

title: Burnham blames Brexit and Thatcher for ‘wrong turns’ in first Commons speech as PM
author: Pippa Crerar; Jessica Elgot
content:
Andy Burnham has blamed Brexit and Margaret Thatcher for a decade of low growth in the UK, arguing that Britain needs to be brutally honest about having taken “a series of wrong turns” in the last 40 years.
In his first Commons appearance since he took over as prime minister about six weeks ago, Burnham told MPs he wanted to build a new sense of optimism so “we can make this next decade better than the last”.
The British people wanted “much more substantial change” on the big issues facing the country, he said. “That is what I will bring. Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be. Things are not working as they should.”
The UK economy has taken a 6% hit from the effects of Brexit, according to economists’ analysis of internal Bank of England data on thousands of British companies since the referendum a decade ago.
Shortly before Burnham’s Commons address, Keir Starmer, his predecessor, announced he would stand down as an MP, saying he wanted to focus on international affairs, triggering a tricky first byelection test for Burnham in a seat where the Greens fancy their chances.
The cabinet was told on Tuesday that the government will have three key priorities: cutting costs of essentials like childcare and mortgages; the regeneration of communities; and greater public control of water, housing and energy.
Burnham’s deputy, Louise Haigh, will lead task forces on each of those issues, the Guardian understands. He told his ministers they must be “relentless” in fulfilling his priorities.
His plans are set against a tough economic backdrop. The chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s fiscal rules could be halved at his first budget if the current global bond sell-off persists, and economists warn mortgage rates could go up this autumn.
In his Commons statement, the prime minister also:
- 
  Hinted that he would commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, saying he had appointed John Healey as his chancellor “precisely because” of his position on military spending.
- 
  Signalled he is open to renationalising the water industry – saying he is looking at “all possible solutions”, as the sector is a “leaking monument” to the failures of privatisation.
- 
  Opened the door to looking again at electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto. “I do believe there needs to be a mandate to make that change. There are different views in this house, but I believe we will need to get a consensus at the next election. And if there is that consensus, then a change can be made in the next parliament.”
- 
  Announced he would attend the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey and continue pursuing green energy – but that he would be “pragmatic” on supply, amid expectations he will approve the Jackdaw gasfield. “The mistake is saying it’s got to be one or the other for political purposes. The truth is, it’s going to have to be both.”
Flanked by Healey and Haigh, Burnham suggested to MPs the Brexit vote had been a response to “a series of wrong turns” made by Britain in the 1980s onwards, that were then compounded by leaving the EU.
The prime minister, whose Makerfield constituency voted for Brexit, has previously argued it would be a mistake to rerun the referendum – but has said that he wants the UK to rejoin in his lifetime. He suggested the next UK-EU reset summit could take place in November.
“Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country de-industrialised. Austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this,” he said during a three-hour stint in the Commons.
“And then Brexit compounded the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration. Change begins with honesty … Unless we are blunt about what went wrong, we won’t turn things around.
“Far from taking back control, the combination of these policies took control out of the hands of communities up and down Britain for 40 years. Too many places have been drifting.”
He added: “The government I lead will be relentless in giving people and places what they were promised 10 years ago: ownership and control, and from that control over their destiny comes change and growth.”
after newsletter promotion
![Kemi Badenoch in the Commons](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a03d9697f54d9228690071350f8e15b4ef7495ac/0_0_6225_4983/master/6225.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, accused the prime minister of “living in the past” over his attacks on Thatcher – who was in power from 1979 to 1990 – and four decades of neoliberalism.
“The year is 2026 but the prime minister said everything has gone wrong since the 1980s, still complaining about Margaret Thatcher. He is talking about a woman who became prime minister before I was born. He is living in the past and he wants to take us back to the 1970s.”
In the statement, Burnham paid tribute to Starmer, saying he had created a platform for Britain to be fixed, “and we will use it well”. Just hours earlier, his predecessor announced he would be standing down as MP for Holborn and St Pancras, despite saying in July he planned to stay on until the next election.
“It has been a huge honour and privilege to represent the best constituency in the country,” he said. “I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs, including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world.”
Starmer’s seat, long seen as a safe Labour hold, is likely to be targeted by the Greens, potentially for party leader Zack Polanski, who is a London Assembly member. “Zack has always made it clear he would like to be a London MP. London has been his home for over 20 years,” a Green spokesperson said.
Just as the Makerfield byelection was seen as a proof of concept for whether Burnham could beat Reform, so the north London seat will test his progressive credentials. Labour will choose its candidate to replace Starmer next Wednesday under an accelerated selection timetable.
Burnham’s first taskforce will be charged with finding bold solutions to tackling “everyday rip-offs”. The cost of living taskforce will look at parking charges, subscription traps and cowboy builders, as well as long-term fixed pressures like mortgages, food costs and childcare.
The second will assess the affordability and practicalities of the state taking over failing essential services. Burnham believes that greater state control of essential services is the surest way to economic growth, avoiding the potential for ineffective profiteering by privatised services.
Government sources said that Haigh, the first secretary of state, wanted to look beyond sectors such as transport and explore serious opportunities for greater state control in areas like energy and housing – if it would bring down ordinary people’s costs.
The third taskforce will explore more radical ideas to revive crumbling high streets and impoverished districts, such as potential legislative options on houses in multiple occupation, as well as devolving powers to mayors and councils to help them regenerate local high streets.
summary: In his first Commons speech as prime minister, Andy Burnham blamed Brexit and the policies of Margaret Thatcher for a decade of low growth and structural decline in the UK. He outlined a government agenda focused on cutting everyday costs, community regeneration, and increasing public control over essential services like water and energy. The address came shortly after his predecessor, Keir Starmer, announced he would step down as an MP to focus on international affairs, triggering an upcoming byelection.
key_points: Prime Minister Andy Burnham argued that a series of wrong turns starting in the 1980s, compounded by Brexit, caused a decade of low economic growth.
The government's three key priorities include cutting the cost of essentials, regenerating communities, and increasing public control over water, housing, and energy.
Burnham hinted at a potential commitment to spend 3% of GDP on defense by 2030 and signaled openness to renationalizing the water industry.
Former prime minister Keir Starmer announced he is stepping down as an MP to focus on international affairs.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch criticized Burnham's speech, accusing him of living in the past and unfairly attacking Margaret Thatcher.

title: Andy Burnham promises more devolution and public control of essential services
author: Kate Whannel
content:
Watch: Key moments from Burnham's first Commons speech as PM
- Published
Andy Burnham has promised to set out plans for "stronger public control" of essential services as he addressed the House of Commons for the first time since taking power.
The prime minister said "a series of wrong turns" since the 1980s had seen economic power in the UK privatised and pointed to the water industry as "a leaking monument to that approach - a country run in the private rather than public interest".
He reiterated his belief that political power had been centralised and announced he would be making devolution powers available to more areas in England.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of offering "more government control, more taxes and more politicians".
"His diagnosis is completely wrong, his theory of growth is completely wrong, he thinks that if government spends more money, we will all get richer - that is not how this works," she said.
Badenoch also warned the prime minister that his new job would be "very different" to his previous Greater Manchester mayoral role where he "did not have to make difficult trade-offs".
Burnham became prime minister on 20 July shortly after Parliament closed for the summer recess.
Tuesday marked the first day of the new parliamentary session and provided his first opportunity to address MPs and take questions.
He told the House of Commons that "Britain is not where we would wish it to be", but promised to "build a new sense of optimism around the country".
Following his 10 years away from Parliament, Burnham said he was returning with a "clear diagnosis" of what had gone wrong in the country.
"From the 1980s, this country took a series of wrong turns," he said.
"Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country deindustrialised, austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this.
"And then Brexit compounded the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration."
In the months before becoming prime minister, Burnham stopped short of calling for full nationalisation but said he wanted to see greater public control of water and energy.
On Tuesday, he promised that a plan to achieve this would be produced "later in the year".
Pressed on his plans for the water sector by Conservative MP Alison Griffiths, Burnham said it was important to "look at all possible solutions".
"It's a very regrettable situation that the privatisation of water has left us in a position where we're going to find it very difficult to reverse," he added.
Burnham said his time as Greater Manchester mayor had given him "a clear theory of growth", namely that devolving powers to regions outside London would boost their economy.
He argued the approach had worked in Manchester and now he wanted "every single place across our regions and nations to be able to do the same, creating the conditions for good growth in every postcode".
Some MPs have raised concern that areas without mayors - and the new powers that have come with them - would suffer, leading to a two-tier system.
Efforts to secure a devolution deal in Cornwall have been stymied by the county's reluctance to form a group with Devon but also to having a mayor.
Burnham appeared to have accepted the county's concerns, telling the House of Commons his government would work with Cornwall Council and its six MPs on a devolution deal "with or without an elected mayor".
He added that he would be extending "the same offer to all parts of England without devolved power".
He also said he was interested in exploring "a local model of devolution" in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
Shortly before Burnham's speech to Parliament, Sir Keir Starmer said in a surprise announcement that he would be stepping down as an MP, less than two months after he quit as prime minister.
Burnham began his speech by paying tribute to his predecessor telling the House of Commons that Sir Keir had "given this country a lifetime of public service" and created a "platform to change this country for the better".
In his wide-ranging statement, which lasted three-and-half-hours, Burnham gave an indication of his approach on several other issues including welfare.
He suggested that providing more council homes and thereby bringing down rent for more people would be the "Labour way" of reducing the benefits bill.
The prime minister also committed to introducing legislation that would allow homeowners to move more easily from the leasehold system to a commonhold form of ownership.
Asked by Badenoch about defence spending, Burnham said he had specifically chosen John Healey to be his chancellor because of his "commitment to defence".
Healey resigned as defence secretary earlier this year, accusing then-prime minister Sir Keir of failing to commit the resources needed to keep the country safe.
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey used his question to argue that too much power in the UK was in "the wrong hands" and called for "fundamental change" of the political system.
Burnham said he would look at the voting system but would not introduce any changes before the next general election.
Both Reform UK's Richard Tice and the Green Party's Ellie Chowns asked whether the government would approve new drilling licences at the Rosebank oil field and the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.
Tice urged the PM to allow more drilling saying it was "madness to import gas from overseas when we have our own gas in the North Sea" while Chowns opposed such a move arguing that the "climate damage they would create hugely outweighs any possible benefit".
Burnham promised to take a "pragmatic approach" and said he wanted the transition to renewable energy to be done "as effectively and affordably as possible".
![Thin, red banner promoting the Politics Essential newsletter with text saying, âTop political analysis in your inbox every dayâ. There is also an image of the Houses of Parliament.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/6133/live/2bce6ee0-0b00-11f0-97d3-37df2b293ed1.png)
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham addressed the House of Commons for the first time since taking power, promising plans for stronger public control of essential services like water and energy later in the year. He also announced that devolution powers would be made available to more areas across England, including regions without elected mayors. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch criticized the agenda as offering more government control, taxes, and politicians.
key_points: Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced plans to introduce stronger public control of essential services.
Devolution powers are set to be extended to more areas in England, including those without elected mayors.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch criticized Burnham's approach, arguing it relies on increased government control and spending.
Burnham paid tribute to his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, following Starmer's announcement that he is stepping down as an MP.

title: ‘I think he’s sensible’: constituents on Keir Starmer stepping down as MP
author: Helena Horton
content:
In Keir Starmer’s north London constituency, full of pretty pubs and elegant townhouses, few tears were being shed at the news of his departure as its MP.
One man nursing a pint outside a pub in Kentish Town simply remarked “good” when informed his MP had quit. He added: “I thought he was very nice before he became prime minister; I met him a few times. But he messed the country up and screwed over pensioners.”
Annie, a 30-year-old doctor having a coffee and pastry on a bench near the tube station, said: “I think everyone here wanted him to leave. He’s had a rough time of it, sure, but we have all had enough of him.”
Dominic Ford, a 75-year-old pensioner reading a book outside the Parakeet pub, was more sympathetic. “I think he’s sensible. It would have been tough for him to sit behind the new prime minister,” he said. “He’s a very nice, honest guy, and he was very visible around here. We used to see him going to the Arsenal with his son. He was a good local MP, and very honest. I felt very sorry for him when he resigned as prime minister.”
On a quiet street among rows of pastel-coloured terrace houses is the Pineapple, Starmer’s favourite pub. It is out of the way of the high street, and the former prime minister is frequently seen there drinking a pint.
He may have become tired of his pub visits being documented in various newspapers, because when the Guardian visited and asked regulars what they thought about him stepping down, the bar staff firmly said that questions about Starmer were not allowed. Perhaps this commitment to discretion is why he has referred to the pub as his “church” and “the best pub in land”.
![Laura Hyland stands on the pavement of a street in Kentish Town](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/3253373b2b5adddc6c4fd859ce944031620bb7a9/0_0_8063_5376/master/8063.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Starmer announced his departure as prime minister in June after several unpopular choices including making Peter Mandelson, a friend of Jeffrey Epstein, ambassador to the US. On Tuesday, Starmer told the Camden New Journal he wanted to focus on international affairs and “pass the baton to a successor”.
Starmer had previously said he would seek to serve out his term as a backbench MP, and his decision to quit will spark a byelection. The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, is understood to be considering a run for the seat.
Laura Hyland, a 67-year-old artist, said she was pleased Starmer was stepping down and that she welcomed the prospect of a byelection. “He gave very little support for Palestine, and I hope Andy Burnham will be more supportive. Arresting people for holding signs saying ‘I support Palestine Action’ was disgraceful.”
Anita, 52, was doing her shopping on the high street. She also welcomed Starmer standing down, and said: “I can’t stand him. He was completely useless and I am glad he stood down.”
after newsletter promotion
![Lewis Galloway standing by padlocked sheds](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5744146baa8490593af61830efbcae002d3061f7/0_0_7574_5051/master/7574.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The former prime ministers Rishi Sunak and Theresa May both committed to serving out a term as an MP for their constituencies after losing a general election.
Sunak is still representing his North Yorkshire constituency, now Richmond and Northallerton, two years after Starmer taunted him about whether he would be moving to California to work in tech. Lewis Galloway, 43, who works in marketing, said he would have liked to see the same from Starmer.
“It’s a shame that he’s standing down,” he said. “There was something nice about Theresa May and Rishi Sunak when they stood down and still worked for their constituents from the backbenches. It is a real shame to lose him from this form of public service so prematurely.”
summary: Constituents in Keir Starmer's north London seat expressed mixed reactions to his decision to step down as their MP following his resignation as prime minister in June. While many residents welcomed his departure due to unpopular policies and actions during his tenure, some expressed sympathy and praised his local visibility. His exit will trigger a byelection, with potential interest from other political figures.
key_points: Keir Starmer stepped down as prime minister in June after unpopular decisions, including appointing Peter Mandelson as US ambassador.
His resignation as an MP will trigger a byelection in his north local constituency.
Local residents had mixed views, with some criticizing his policies on pensioners and Palestine, while others praised him as a good local MP.
Staff at Starmer's favorite local pub declined to comment on his departure.
Unlike predecessors Rishi Sunak and Theresa May, who served as backbench MPs after losing office, Starmer chose to quit his parliamentary seat entirely.

title: Live updates: Burnham pledges devolution deals and 'stronger public control' of services in first address to MPs
author: Live Reporting Edited by Manish Pandey; Imogen James
content:
![](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/128/cpsprodpb//vivo/live/images/2022/10/4/4c103344-c221-4117-8552-c919a61b6dc4.jpg.webp) Iain Watson
Political correspondent
![Andy Burnham next to West Streeting (right)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/vivo/live/images/2026/9/1/d0fe2d2d-807f-4b1a-b3aa-4f5e524b39a8.jpg.webp) Image source, UK Parliament
The Conservatives smell blood on defence spending.
While Andy Burnham has committed to fully funding the defence investment plan he inherited, he has been far more coy when it comes to committing to spending 3% of national income on defence by 2030.
He said there will be a date for 3% in next yearâs spending review but has avoided saying explicitly this date for this will indeed be 2030.
To ease the pressure in his first statement as PM in Parliament, he turned to the man sitting next to him â Chancellor John Healey, who resigned as defence secretary (thus helping push Keir Starmer out of the door of Downing Street) over a failure of the last administration to commit to that target.
Andy Burnham said with some flourish he appointed "this Chancellor" because of his commitments.
Itâs not clear if this is nodding and winking assent to the defence uplift, or if it is unduly raising expectations.
summary: In his first address to MPs, Prime Minister Andy Burnham committed to fully funding his inherited defence investment plan but avoided explicitly confirming a 2030 target for spending 3% of national income on defence. He stated that a date for the 3% target will be set in next year's spending review. To deflect pressure, Burnham highlighted his appointment of Chancellor John Healey, who had previously resigned as defence secretary over the prior administration's failure to commit to the defense spending target.
key_points: Andy Burnham committed to fully funding the inherited defence investment plan.
He avoided explicitly committing to a 2030 target for spending 3% of national income on defence.
A specific date for reaching the 3% defence spending target will be announced in next year's spending review.
Burnham pointed to Chancellor John Healey, who previously resigned over defence spending commitments, to ease political pressure.

title: Man in court after Grangetown fire in which woman and niece died
author: Fiona Trott
content:
Man in court charged with murder after fire deaths
![Supplied A composite image of Natalie McDonald and Valentina Foster. McDonald is wearing a white wedding dress with a tiara perched on her head. She has long dark hair and is holding a bouquet of white roses with four blue ones dotted within it. Valentina wears an electric blue dress with white flowers on the neckline and waist. She has long light brown hair with a blue and white headband. She is holding a small white basket with white and blue roses and she wears white gloves.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/0d9a/live/086fd350-a5c6-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png.webp) Supplied
A 23-year-old man has appeared in court charged with murdering a woman and her seven-year-old niece who died in a house fire.
Natalie McDonald, 34, died in the blaze in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of 26 August, along with Valentina Foster.
Jaden Wright appeared at Teesside Magistrates' Court charged with two counts of murder as well as multiple grievous bodily harm offences.
Wright, of no fixed address, was remanded in custody during the hearing that lasted less than two minutes, and is next due to appear at Teesside Crown Court on Thursday.
He is also accused of two counts of grievous bodily harm with intent and two charges of attempted grievous bodily harm with intent.
These charges relate to the six people in the house at the time of the blaze.
No pleas were entered during the hearing on Tuesday morning.
summary: A 23-year-old man has appeared in court charged with the murders of a woman and her seven-year-old niece following a house fire in Grangetown. Natalie McDonald and Valentina Foster died in the blaze in the early hours of 26 August. The suspect, Jaden Wright, was remanded in custody after a brief court hearing on Tuesday and faces additional charges related to other individuals inside the home during the fire.
key_points: Jaden Wright appeared at Teesside Magistrates' Court charged with two counts of murder.
The charges follow a house fire in Grangetown on 26 August that caused the deaths of Natalie McDonald and Valentina Foster.
Wright is also accused of two counts of grievous bodily harm with intent and two charges of attempted grievous bodily harm with intent.
The additional charges relate to six people who were in the house at the time of the blaze.
The defendant was remanded in custody and is scheduled to appear at Teesside Crown Court on Thursday.

title: Man dies after entering canal in Notting Hill Carnival police chase
author: Megan Howe; Niva Yadav
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![Dazzling costumes and street style: The best outfits from Notting Hill Carnival](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/01/5/28/GettyImages-2292358336.jpeg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75) ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) A young man has died after entering a canal close to Notting Hill Carnival while being pursued by police. A short time later he entered the water near Meanwhile Gardens, police said. Officers and members of the public pulled him from the water and administered CPR. He was taken to a central London hospital, where he was pronounced dead at 4.43pm. Enquiries are ongoing to inform his family. ![

Police at Notting Hill Carnival

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/01/5/28/GettyImages-2292358336.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) As of 8.30pm, there had been 315 arrests on Monday, bringing the total number of arrests over the two-day operation to 560. Police said the number is likely to rise slightly while later arrests are processed, with a confirmatory update to be provided in the morning. Commenting on the death, Commander Smart said: “This is a tragic incident and our thoughts are with the loved ones of the man who has lost his life. “Any death following contact with the police is passed to the Independent Office for Police Conduct so the circumstances can be fully investigated. I would encourage everyone to avoid speculation while this work takes place. “I acknowledge the efforts of the officers and members of the public who entered the canal to rescue this man. I know they will be devastated that his life couldn’t ultimately be saved.” ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/01/06/01M1CSZEZ0Z7GN47BK1FGC635A.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Read More A sea of colour swept through Notting Hill on Monday, with performers dressed in bejewelled bikini-style costumes, towering feathered backpieces and elaborate headdresses adorned with sequins and beads. Masqueraders danced their way along the parade route to the thunder of drums, while sound systems kept crowds moving throughout the day. Monday also brought a huge Latin American presence to the streets, with samba schools and Brazilian bloco bands joining the celebrations alongside the Caribbean sounds and traditions at the heart of Carnival. Percussion groups and drum queens helped get the party started as performers and revellers transformed the streets into one giant dance floor. Police said Shawn was last seen just before 5pm on Wedlake Street, near Kensal Road. He is described as black, 3ft 8in, and was wearing black shorts, a black top and a hat. ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/31/21/01M1C6MYY6B7X6R9ME6YJ3A9P1.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Commander Charmain Brenyah said: “We are becoming increasingly concerned for Shawn’s welfare due to his young age. “Notting Hill Carnival is an extremely large and busy event, and officers are carrying out extensive inquiries to find Shawn and reunite him with his family as quickly as possible. “We are asking anyone who has seen Shawn, or who has any information about where he may be, to contact police immediately.” Of the arrests made on Monday, 48 followed identifications using live facial recognition. Use of the technology allowed officers to stop 43 registered sex offenders to ensure they were complying with licence conditions. Three were arrested for breaching those conditions, in addition to three arrested for breaches on Sunday. Stop and search was used extensively, with 62 weapons seized across both days, including a handgun during the afternoon on Monday. There were two assaults with knives – one stabbing and one slashing – neither of which resulted in life-threatening injuries. ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/31/21/01M1C6JNRJ8W64AASQ9N6JSVMV.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) The annual carnival is Europe’s biggest street party and billed by organisers as “the greatest community-led event on the planet”. One carnival-goer, named Michael, said: “Carnival is actually an important part of the culture of London, it’s honestly where everyone can come and have fun. “No matter who you are, no matter your disability, no matter your race, no matter any background, you can come here and have fun and you’re going to meet people here that are going to make you feel welcome.” On social media, Carnival-goers celebrated the “camaraderie, advocacy, and profound history” of the event. Footage shared online showed one first-time attendee getting into the spirit of Carnival, dancing through the streets and blowing a whistle as a dancehall version of Angie Stone’s 2001 hit Wish I Didn’t Miss You played in the background. ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/31/21/01M1C6KV2QJED04G8GDJ4957DJ.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Elsewhere, regular attendees reflected on what Carnival means to them. For many, they said, it is more than just a giant street party, it is a melting pot of cultures and a celebration of diversity, community and inclusion. Councillor Elizabeth Campbell, leader of Kensington and Chelsea Council, said: “It’s been so much fun being out celebrating Notting Hill Carnival’s 60th anniversary with everyone who has come together to enjoy this incredible event. “The costumes, the music and the atmosphere are fantastic, and it’s a real reminder of what makes carnival so special. “I want to pay tribute to our officers, the organisers and partners who have worked so closely together to make this milestone celebration happen. “I hope everyone has a fantastic, safe and happy carnival.” Born out of resistance to racism and racial injustice, Notting Hill Carnival has grown into one of the world’s biggest street festivals while continuing to champion Caribbean culture and London’s minority communities. ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/31/21/01M1C6NCH19QAVFQ8S9GMKAVQN.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) At 3pm, a 72-second moment of reflection was observed for the 72-people who were killed in the Grenfell Tower fire. Sunday’s Families and Children’s Day had brought a more relaxed atmosphere to the streets, with younger performers taking centre stage. Last week, the force said more than 7,000 officers would be deployed to west London over the bank holiday weekend. The carnival, which is celebrating its 60th anniversary this year, includes parades, live music, street food and sound stages. In 2025, the Met said it made 528 arrests across the two main days of the carnival, including 167 for drug offences, 50 for possession of an offensive weapon, 21 for sexual offences, four for violence with injury and 49 for other violence. In 2024, there were eight stabbings, including the murder of 32-year-old mother Cher Maximen, with the same number the previous year, and seven including a murder in 2022.
summary: A young man has died after entering a canal near the Notting Hill Carnival while being pursued by police. Officers and members of the public pulled him from the water and administered CPR before he was taken to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead. The incident has been referred to the Independent Office for Police Conduct for investigation.
key_points: A man died after entering a canal near Meanwhile Gardens during a police pursuit at the Notting Hill Carnival.
Police officers and members of the public attempted to save him with CPR before he was taken to a central London hospital.
The Independent Office for Police Conduct will investigate the circumstances surrounding the death following police contact.
Across the two-day carnival operation, police recorded a total of 560 arrests, including 315 made on Monday.

title: Man dies near Notting Hill Carnival after entering canal
author: Ella Kipling
content:
![Dozens of members of the Metropolitan Police walk in uniform through the Notting Hill Carnival](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/933/cpsprodpb/f27c/live/01776750-a582-11f1-ae94-15924a612dd1.jpg)
- Published
A man died near Notting Hill Carnival in London on Monday afternoon, the Metropolitan Police have confirmed.
Police officers had attempted to stop the man, believed to be in his 20s, as he approached the event. He fled on foot with officers in pursuit, and entered the water in the vicinity of Meanwhile Gardens a short time later, the force said.
Taken to hospital by ambulance the man was pronounced dead a short time later.
Cdr Claire Smart said: "This is a tragic incident and our thoughts are with the loved ones of the man who has lost his life."
The Met Police said officers had attempted to stop the man at about 15:19 BST near Harrow Road.
The man entered the water in the vicinity of Meanwhile Gardens, off Kensal Road.
Officers and members of the public went in after him and pulled him from the water, police said, and officers immediately started CPR.
Paramedics were called and continued treatment at the canal side before taking the man to a central London hospital. He was pronounced dead at 16:43.
The Met Police said on Monday night that urgent enquiries were ongoing to locate and inform his next of kin.
Smart, gold commander for the Notting Hill Festival, said: "Any death following contact with the police is passed to the Independent Office for Police Conduct so the circumstances can be fully investigated.
"I would encourage everyone to avoid speculation while this work takes place."
She added: "I acknowledge the efforts of the officers and members of the public who entered the canal to rescue this man. I know they will be devastated that his life couldn't ultimately be saved."
The Met Police said the two days of the festival had passed "largely without incident".
There were two assaults with knives - one stabbing and one slashing. Neither resulted in life-threatening injuries.
On Monday evening, police said there had been 315 arrests that day, bringing the total number of arrests to 560.
summary: A man in his 20s died after entering a canal in London on Monday afternoon while fleeing from police officers near the Notting Hill Carnival. Officers and members of the public pulled him from the water and performed CPR before he was taken to the hospital, where he was pronounced dead. The Independent Office for Police Conduct will investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident.
key_points: A man in his 20s died after entering a canal near the Notting Hill Carnival on Monday afternoon.
Police officers attempted to stop the man, who fled on foot before entering the water near Meanwhile Gardens.
Officers and members of the public rescued him from the water and attempted CPR before paramedics arrived.
The Independent Office for Police Conduct is investigating the incident due to prior police contact.
Police reported a total of 560 arrests across the two days of the festival.

title: Villagers fight back after suspected travellers bulldoze wildlife haven
author: Fiona Parker
content:
![Three police officers talk to a topless man at a site  in Sawbridgeworth, England](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/31/TELEMMGLPICT000500200648_17881901495930_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf_4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Three police officers talk to a topless man at a site  in Sawbridgeworth, England](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/31/TELEMMGLPICT000500200648_17881901495930_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf_4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
“We’ve never had anything like this in Sawbridgeworth,” Katie says, her Girlguiding badges shining on her uniform. “We’re sleepy Sawbridgeworth.”
The 44-year-old local Guide leader is one of hundreds of somewhat unconventional protesters defending a small plot of land in the Hertfordshire town.
On Friday morning, the patch of land in question, off Sheering Mill Lane, a single-track 20mph road, was a tranquil, verdant wildlife hotspot.
But over the bank holiday weekend, the suburban setting, which lies a little more than a mile from Durrington House, the Grade II-listed mansion owned by Sir Rod Stewart and his wife Penny Lancaster, was transformed into an impromptu building site. Workmen with heavy machinery dug up the land, erected fences and felled at least one tree.
And all without planning permission.
![Police monitor the site where suspected travellers have been building on August, 31, 2026 in Sawbridgeworth, England](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/31/TELEMMGLPICT000500200680_17881901309220_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Although the identity of the land’s new owners is unknown, suspicion has fallen on travellers.
Greg Rattey, a councillor and former mayor of Sawbridgeworth, spoke on Sunday of the dismay felt by residents at the “illegal settlement” he said had been “built by travellers”.
With concerns growing about wildlife, house prices and planning laws, Facebook groups have issued a call to action. The locals mean to stop the construction vehicles in their tracks.
“People have been here all night,” one local resident told The Telegraph. “You had people sleeping in benches, doing shifts, people out all night long.”
![A row of people sitting in a country lane at night](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/31/TELEMMGLPICT000500229392_17882056108200_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq-ENWgDtJ141nMZEcdxZvJptZTPKJKBzBi89lQrubmi8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Fortunately, the middle-class protesters of the town, which has a population of slightly more than 10,000, worked hard to keep morale high.
“There was Prosecco, barbecues, gazebos, tea and coffees,” the young man said. “It was brilliant.”
East Hertfordshire district council served a temporary stop notice shortly after 10.45am on Saturday before making an urgent application to the High Court for an injunction.
An amended injunction was granted and served at around 12.30am on Monday, which allowed police to arrest anyone bringing caravans on to the site and occupying the land for carrying out works.
![Copy of the amended injunction, served at 12.30am on Monday, which allows police to arrest anyone bringing caravans on to the site and occupying the land](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/31/TELEMMGLPICT000500200701_17881902142820_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf_4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
At 7am, however, workers continued to defy the injunction, with around 20 to 25 people only leaving the site at around 9.30am on Monday when police officers arrived.
By mid-morning, dozens of people of all ages remained on guard by the field, many dressed in fashionable outdoor wear to keep warm.
“We’re so angry, what has happened to our village, the way that gipsies or whoever just come in and invade the land,” said Nicola Lever, wearing a quilted gilet, her leather bag slung across her shoulder. “It’s just awful, I can’t explain how bad it was.”
The law-firm worker, who lives near the site, said she assumed people were “fishing” when she first noticed a tent erected on the land as she returned home on Friday night. But before long, multiple lorries were pulling up, carrying cement and other materials.
“I said to my husband, ‘What are all these lorries doing?’”, Ms Lever said. “And before long they had started drilling.”
![Local resident Nicola Lever](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/31/TELEMMGLPICT000500200634_17881902144434_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqFmvNuCJhb9YlvApoMTSpqv4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The mother of one, who has lived in Sawbridgeworth for 22 years, said some of the unwelcome visitors attempted to provoke “a reaction” from residents, with one even resorting to obscene hand gestures.
“Some people from a wildlife organisation even came down to try and save the foxes and badgers on Saturday,” she added.
Samantha Soames, who lives three miles away in Bishop’s Stortford, previously worked as a journalist and drove to Sheering Mill Lane on Saturday morning with her beagle Charlotte, when she heard what was happening. However, the sight of a large crack willow being felled quickly pushed her “over the edge”.
![Samantha Soames, who said that her 'blood boiled' when she saw that a tree had been felled](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/31/TELEMMGLPICT000500200695_17881902142931_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
“I went to Sawbridgeworth to cover what was happening as a journalist,” the 56-year-old said, “but I ended up turning into an activist myself. My blood just boiled and I just shouted a profanity when I saw that tree torn down.
“What’s to stop other nature reserves being destroyed in this way if this happens? Apart from anything else, it is a flood plain.”
The following day, Ms Soames said people on the site had started to accuse concerned residents, hundreds of whom had turned out in force, of being “racist” because they were Irish.
“A lot of us have Irish relatives,” she said. “We are not racist, but of course they were playing the race card. They are being discriminatory against nature by destroying living things.”
Katie, who did not wish to give her second name, said: “I’m down here for today because I’ve got a young daughter. As Guides, we promote our girls to be strong independent women and to fight for what we believe in.
“That’s why I’m here today, to fight for the fact that I’m concerned about the safety of our town.”
The mother of two also said “house prices” were a concern.
Another woman, who did not want to be named for fear of potential reprisals, said: “We have the great crested newt, we have water voles, we have bats and we’ve got birds. It’s not actually a nature reserve, but it’s a flood plain and it’s home to so much nature, so much wildlife. And so for this land to be decimated, it’s devastating.”
![An aerial shot of the land where workmen began to erect fences](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/31/TELEMMGLPICT000500200636_17881902155903_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
By Monday afternoon only one man was left on the site, stalking around the field topless, while drinking a can of beer. He refused to tell The Telegraph who he was, but it was understood he was authorised to remain on the land and had permission from the landowner.
A court hearing has been scheduled for Sept 15 in an attempt to settle the matter.
![Diggers at work behind fences erected on land in Sawbridgeworth](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/31/TELEMMGLPICT000500200647_17881902147562_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Meanwhile, residents are prepared to continue guarding the land for as long as it takes.
Katie said: “It does seem like the community is going to have to continue to fight. Fortunately for the community of Sawbridgeworth, we are strong.”
A Hertfordshire Constabulary spokesman said: “Police entered the site this morning and all those who had unauthorised access, left the site peacefully. This was following an amended High Court injunction, which was granted and served this morning.
“The High Court injunction meant that anyone found carrying out activities prohibited by the injunction – including bringing caravans on site and occupying the land for carrying out development – could be arrested by the police.
“No arrests were necessary.”
In a post on its website, East Hertfordshire district council said: “The High Court injunction meant that anyone found carrying out activities prohibited by the injunction – including bringing caravans on site and occupying the land for carrying out development – could be arrested by the police. No arrests were necessary.
“We will continue to work closely with Herts Police and our other partners to monitor the site and prevent any further unauthorised works.”
summary: Residents of Sawbridgeworth mounted round-the-clock protests after a wildlife habitat and flood plain was illegally developed over a bank holiday weekend.
