Heavy machinery was brought onto the land, trees were felled, and fences were erected without planning permission by suspected travellers. Following a temporary stop notice, an amended High Court injunction was served, leading unauthorized workers to leave the site peacefully.
key_points: Over a bank holiday weekend, a wildlife hotspot and flood plain in Sawbridgeworth was illegally transformed into a building site without planning permission.
Hundreds of local residents organized round-the-clock protests, blockading the area and maintaining morale with food and drinks.
East Hertfordshire district council secured a temporary stop notice and an urgent High Court injunction prohibiting unauthorized development and caravan placement.
Police officers arrived on Monday morning, prompting unauthorized workers to leave the site peacefully without any arrests being necessary.
A court hearing to address the matter has been scheduled for September 15.

title: Mel Stride and Priti Patel replaced in major Tory reshuffle
author: AndrÃ© Rhoden-Paul; Iain Watson
content:
![A composite image. Mel Stride on the left in a suit and tie. Dame Priti Patel wears white.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/4289/live/abc92950-a550-11f1-8689-6589354d0f8e.jpg)
- Published
Sir Mel Stride and Dame Priti Patel have left the shadow cabinet as part of a significant reshuffle of the Conservative top team by leader Kemi Badenoch.
Andrew Griffith will replace Sir Mel as shadow chancellor, while Tom Tugendhat will take the place of Dame Priti as shadow foreign secretary.
Badenoch is forming a new shadow cabinet before the party's conference in October.
With most polls putting the Conservatives in third place, lagging behind Labour and Reform UK, the Tory leader will be hoping a refreshed shadow cabinet will help boost to her party's popularity.
Claire Coutinho, previously the shadow energy secretary, after her maternity leave will replace Griffith as shadow business secretary and act as his deputy.
Badenoch said that as shadow chancellor, Sir Mel had helped the party rebuild economic credibility and become an effective opposition.
A senior Conservative source said: "Kemi is changing the way the Conservative Party approaches economic policy and creating a new economic leadership team for the next phase, focused on growth, higher living standards and fiscal credibility."
Sir Mel, who was appointed to the role following Badenoch's leadership election in 2024, described his time in post as a "great honour".
New shadow chancellor Griffith said the Tories will deliver "an economic revolution" with lower taxes, Britain drilling again to bring energy costs down, slashing red tape and Labour's Employment Rights Act.
"The Conservatives will always back the risk-takers and wealth creators who deliver growth, investment and jobs," he said.
A senior Conservative source described Griffith as a "no-nonsense, pro-growth shadow chancellor with real business experience".
Before he became MP for Arundel and South Downs in 2019, he served as a top executive at Sky and as chairman of Just Eat.
As a Treasury minister, Griffiths defended Liz Truss' 2022 mini-budget.
Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds said the new shadow chancellor backed Truss to be prime minister and highlighted his role during the mini budget which "left families paying the price".
"Same old Tories, same old economic policies," she added.
Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said: "Griffith helped deliver the Truss mini-budget that sent mortgages soaring and the economy into turmoil.
"It's clear Conservatives haven't learned a thing. His appointment to shadow chancellor shows they're happy to forfeit any claim to economic credibility in their race to the bottom with Reform UK."
Reform UK shadow chancellor Robert Jenrick said: "They haven't changed and still aren't sorry for the damage they inflicted on our country. The Tories just cannot be trusted to cut handouts to illegal migrants, end mad net zero subsidies or to slash the ballooning benefits bill."
Dame Priti, who had been shadow foreign secretary since 2024, will return to the backbenches and will take on a new international role strengthening the Tories relationship with sister parties and centre-right movements abroad.
![Claire Coutinho speaks during a party press conference in central London. In the background is a UK flag](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/1831/live/3d9ab880-a551-11f1-8689-6589354d0f8e.jpg)
Claire Coutinho will become shadow business secretary after maternity leave
Badenoch will also need to select a new shadow health secretary after Stuart Andrew confirmed he will be returning to the backbenches, and a new shadow housing secretary after Sir James Cleverly quit the front bench, announcing he wants to run for London mayor.
Her reshuffle is intended to bring solutions to a number of problems.
First, she wants to retire those members of her top team that have had a relatively low profile, or who have not been delivering sufficient blows to both Labour and Reform UK.
Badenoch paid a warm tribute to Sir Mel but some recent polls suggested that Reform UK were more trusted on the economy than the Conservatives.
And that is something Kemi Badenoch felt needed to change.
Second, while familiar faces like Dame Priti were useful to have in the top team as they brought high-level government experience, they might also remind voters of the party they decisively rejected in 2024.
There has been a changing of the old guard, and Badenoch is now focusing on who can take the Conservatives into the next election - faced as she is by a new Labour leader and cabinet.
Third, she wants to focus on issues where Labour is perceived to be vulnerable.
One such area is defence spending and national security.
So as shadow foreign secretary she appointed Tom Tugendhat - a former security minister and current army reservist who served in Afghanistan and Iraq. He will work as part of a team with the shadow defence secretary.
Some opinion polls rate the economy as the most important issue for voters, above asylum and immigration, and again the Tory leader believes the government is vulnerable here, with sluggish growth.
So she has announced a new Conservative economic unit headed by Griffith, with his extensive business experience.
Coutinho as his deputy is seen as a rising Conservative star who has performed well in her previous role shadowing the former energy secretary Ed Miliband in the Commons, and as a potential future chancellor if the Conservatives were ever to recover electorally.
But the Tory leader has also included the former Conservative chairman and City Minister Richard Fuller in the unit, concentrating on fiscal responsibility and tax.
He will be deployed as an attack dog if - as she believes he will â the chancellor raises taxes in the Budget.
But the role will also underline that the Conservative leader is serious about making her sums add up, in contrast to her characterisation of Reform UK's plans as ill-thought out.
The question now though is whether Badenoch will change her own approach to political leadership.
While some of her top team may be seen as lacklustre, how much opportunity did they get to shine?
She tends to make the big announcements and is ubiquitous on the media.
If the Conservatives are to convince voters they are once again a government in waiting then the public will have to see that there is breadth and depth in the team that is shadowing current ministers.
summary: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has replaced Mel Stride and Priti Patel in a major shadow cabinet reshuffle ahead of the party's October conference. Andrew Griffith takes over as shadow chancellor, while Tom Tugendhat replaces Patel as shadow foreign secretary. The reshuffle aims to refresh the party's top team, address low poll numbers, and target perceived vulnerabilities in the Labour government.
key_points: Sir Mel Stride and Dame Priti Patel have left the shadow cabinet in a major reshuffle by Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch.
Andrew Griffith replaces Stride as shadow chancellor, and Tom Tugendhat replaces Patel as shadow foreign secretary.
Claire Coutinho will return from maternity leave to become shadow business secretary and deputy to Griffith.
Stuart Andrew and Sir James Cleverly are also stepping down to the backbenches, with Cleverly planning to run for London mayor.
The reshuffle is intended to boost party popularity as the Conservatives currently trail Labour and Reform UK in the polls.

title: Early release scheme could still see dangerous criminals released, Conservatives warn
author: Freya Scott-Turner
content:
![The interior of a prison, it has cream walls and metal fences. A prison guard walks up the corridor.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/e1ac/live/ebda0960-a514-11f1-89d5-dd5482a9fcc2.jpg)
- Published
Dangerous criminals could still be freed under the prime minister's early release scheme, shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy has told the BBC.
"In order to prevent one group of dangerous criminals being released early, he's looking at releasing a different group of dangerous prisoners", Timothy said.
Timothy's comments followed Andy Burnham's announcement that the early prisoner release scheme would be further narrowed to exclude anyone convicted of manslaughter, following a campaign from the family of PC Andrew Harper to block the release of two men convicted of his manslaughter in 2019.
Burnham said extra prison space would be found in part by releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences, known as IPPs.
Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences were given to offenders between 2005 and 2012 who were deemed to pose a significant risk of causing serious harm to the public.
Once a minimum term has been served, the prisoner can be released only once the Parole Board is satisfied they no longer need to be confined for public safety, meaning many are being held indefinitely.
There were 2,271 people serving these sentences, according to Ministry of Justice (MoJ) data up to June of this year.
Of those, 856 have never been released because the Parole Board thought it was not safe to do so. Ending indefinite sentences will also require new legislation, meaning it could be years before space is freed up.
"By definition, the people who are still in prison on those sentences are dangerous, because they've all been considered by independent expert assessors who have concluded that they are not safe to release and they would be a danger to the public," Timothy told the BBC.
Timothy conceded that the prime minister was grappling with an overcrowding problem not of his making: "I'm fully open about the fact that one of the failures of the last Conservative government was that not enough prison places were built".
"The government's number one priority is to keep the public safe and in order to do that we need a functioning criminal justice system", Alex Davies-Jones, Minister for Victims, Violence Against Women and Girls & International Justice, told the BBC's Today programme.
The scheme is to ensure "there is always a prison space available for someone who needs it", she said.
Speaking on BBC Breakfast she said "release doesn't mean freedom" and there will be a presumption that those released will be on a GPS tag.
On 3 August, the prison population in England and Wales was 86,495, around 97% of useable capacity.
![Alt text:
 Line chart showing weekly prison population and prison capacity in England and Wales from January to August 2026. The prison population (blue shaded area and line) remains consistently between about 86,000 and 88,000 people, while prison capacity (red line) stays just under 90,000. The gap between population and capacity remains small throughout the period, illustrating that prisons are operating close to capacity. The chart is titled âPrisons remain close to capacityâ and cites the Ministry of Justice as the source.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/474f/live/9bfcb670-a2fa-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png)
This early release scheme was introduced under the Sentencing Act 2026. It was designed to address the overcrowding crisis in prisons in England and Wales - which are more than 97% full - by releasing large numbers of inmates earlier than had been previously planned.
The early release scheme is scheduled to start on 1 October.
As well as manslaughter, those sentenced for rape, serious child sex and grooming offences are also not be eligible for early release.
Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Sunday, Burnham acknowledged that his decision to narrow the early release scheme's scope and keep PC Harper's killers in prison would mean that "hundreds" more people would remain behind bars and additional space would need to be found.
But the prime minister said he had applied "common sense" on the treatment of IPPs, which he had "long-standing concerns" about.
"I was faced with a situation where people on those sentences who have more than served their time, not being released when others who've committed very serious crimes being released early," he said.
On Tuesday, Justice Secretary Alex Norris is expected update Parliament with further details on the changes to the early release scheme, including how many people will be affected.
summary: Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy has warned that the prime minister's early release scheme could still result in dangerous criminals being freed. The scheme is being adjusted to exclude individuals convicted of manslaughter, rape, and serious child sex offences following public campaigns. To find alternative prison space, the government is considering releasing inmates serving indefinite Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences, which critics argue still pose a public safety risk. The early release initiative, set to begin on October 1 under the Sentencing Act 2026, aims to alleviate severe prison overcrowding in England and Wales.
key_points: Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy warned that dangerous criminals could still be released under the government's early release scheme.
The early release criteria are being narrowed to exclude individuals convicted of manslaughter, rape, and serious child sex and grooming offences.
Alternative prison capacity is being sought by releasing some inmates serving indefinite Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences.
The early release scheme is scheduled to begin on October 1 to address prison populations operating at roughly 97% capacity.
Ending indefinite IPP sentences will require new legislation, meaning it could take years to free up that specific prison space.

title: Man killed by falling sign at Christian festival named as church pays tribute
author: Harry Cockburn
content:
A 41-year-old man who died after a large wooden sign fell at a Christian festival on Friday has been named as Robert Guanco, a pastor at a church in Eastbourne, East Sussex.
A tribute from his church on Sunday described him as a respected pastor who was a “loving husband” and “a devoted and caring father”.
Six other people were injured when the overhead sign fell at the Big Church festival (BCF) near Steyning in West Sussex, including four who were taken to hospital.
Festivalgoers said they rushed to lift the heavy sign, which read “Everything’s Unmissable”, after it was blown over in the wind.
Jesus Living Water church in Eastbourne named Guanco, describing him as “our beloved brother, friend and pastor”, in a GoFundMe to help his family, who it said faced “unimaginable loss” following his death.
It said: “Pastor Robert was a faithful servant of God, a loving husband to Isay, a devoted and caring father to Ellie, and a blessing to so many people whose lives he touched. His life, his faith, his love and his service to God will never be forgotten.”
It added: “He was also a good friend, mentor and a blessing to so many people whose lives he touched. His life reflected humility, faith, love, compassion and service. Through his ministry, kindness, prayers and encouragement, he touched many lives.
“His passing is deeply felt by everyone who had the privilege of knowing him.”
![Aerial view of the festival, as people stand in front of the stage](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/162bc1779242029c4aed9db9cf37228d506f97bc/0_0_5000_4000/master/5000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Organisers of the BCF, billed as the UK’s biggest Christian festival, said they were “heartbroken” by Guanco’s death and cancelled the rest of the event.
“We are devastated by the serious incident that took place at Big Church festival 2026, in which Pastor Robert Guanco tragically lost his life and others were injured,” they said in a statement.
“First and foremost, all of our thoughts are with those who have been affected, their families and friends, and everyone who witnessed what happened. Particularly with the family, friends and church of Pastor Guanco as they process the immense grief of his loss.”
They added: “We are working with the police, the Health and Safety Executive and others as they establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.”
The festival opened on Friday and had been due to run until Sunday. The event, which includes worship, music and various performances, first took place in 2009.
The archbishop of Canterbury, Dame Sarah Mullally, said she was “sad and shocked” by the incident. “I pray for his family, friends and loved ones as they grieve,” she said. “I pray for those receiving treatment and the healthcare workers looking after them.
“And I pray too for the other festivalgoers, staff and event organisers as they come to terms with these tragic events.”
Many people at the festival were first alerted to the tragedy when God TV announced that “due to unforeseen circumstances” the festival live stream had been paused.
Sussex police’s Det Ch Supt Richard McDonagh said: “Our thoughts remain with the family and friends of the man who died and all others who have been affected by this tragic incident.”
He urged anyone among the “thousands of people” at the festival on Friday who had information or video footage to come forward.
summary: Robert Guanco, a 41-year-old pastor from Eastbourne, has been named as the man killed after a large wooden sign blew over in the wind at the Big Church festival in West Sussex. The incident also injured six other people, four of whom were hospitalized, leading festival organizers to cancel the remainder of the event. His church and festival organizers have paid heartfelt tributes, while authorities work with the police and the Health and Safety Executive to investigate the circumstances.
key_points: Pastor Robert Guanco, 41, died after a large wooden sign reading 'Everything’s Unmissable' fell at the Big Church festival.
Six other individuals were injured in the incident, with four requiring hospital treatment.
Festival organizers cancelled the remainder of the event following the tragedy and are cooperating with police and safety officials.
Guanco's church in Eastbourne described him as a devoted husband, father, and faithful pastor.

title: Tugendhat to replace Patel in Tory reshuffle
author: Tony Diver
content:
![Tom Tugendhat](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/politics/2026/08/30/TELEMMGLPICT000500133354_17881201634090_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqA7N2CxnJWnYI3tCbVBgu9T0aesusvN1TE7a0ddd_esI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Tom Tugendhat](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/politics/2026/08/30/TELEMMGLPICT000500133354_17881201634090_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqA7N2CxnJWnYI3tCbVBgu9T0aesusvN1TE7a0ddd_esI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Dame Priti Patel is to be replaced as shadow foreign secretary by Tom Tugendhat in a shadow cabinet reshuffle, The Telegraph can reveal.
Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, will launch an overhaul of her top team as soon as this week, in a move designed to prepare her party for an early general election.
Mr Tugendhat, a former soldier and security minister, has sat on the back benches since he ran against Mrs Badenoch for the party leadership in 2024.
Alongside his new foreign affairs brief, he will be tasked with amplifying the Conservatives’ message on defence, which sources close to Mrs Badenoch said was “one of the central organising principles of her leadership”.
Dame Priti has faced criticism from her colleagues in recent months for her association with previous Tory administrations, including her work on migration as home secretary under Boris Johnson, who oversaw a dramatic rise in arrivals of non-European Union migrants in the UK.
She will take on the new role of international secretary of the Conservative Party, with responsibility for maintaining relationships with other Right-wing parties around the world and assessing the potential for Rwanda-style migration deals if the Tories return to power.
Mr Tugendhat confirmed his decision to return to the front bench over the weekend while on a visit to Taiwan, where he was meeting officials about the threat posed by China.
The Tonbridge MP, 53, is considered one of the fiercest China sceptics in Parliament and has campaigned against Beijing’s new London embassy, as well as its human rights abuses against Uyghur Muslims.
His return marks the latest step in Mrs Badenoch’s attempt to restore her party’s fortunes in the opinion polls, while distancing herself from Johnson-era ministers including Sir Grant Shapps, who was blocked from standing again as an MP at the next election.
![Kemi Badenoch](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/politics/2026/08/30/TELEMMGLPICT000500137622_17881218349230_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The reshuffle will also include the departure of Sir James Cleverly, currently shadow housing secretary, who has resigned to pursue the Tory candidacy at the next London mayoral election in 2028, and Helen Grant, who is stepping down after her successful treatment for breast cancer.
Claire Coutinho, the shadow energy secretary, will leave the shadow cabinet on maternity leave before the birth of her second child later this year.
A source close to Mrs Badenoch said: “Within Parliament, Tom has almost unrivalled credibility in foreign affairs as a former soldier, security minister and chair of the foreign affairs select committee.
“Kemi actually gave Tom the good news while he was in Taiwan, talking to the Taiwanese government about the threat of China – a mark of how he is respected across the world.
“Contrast that with Ed Miliband, who has spent his first months touring the world pushing his weird net zero agenda.”
Dame Priti said her departure from the front bench would allow her to spend more time campaigning on constituency issues and “strengthening our relationships with fellow conservatives and centre-Right parties around the world”.
She said: “At a time of profound global uncertainty, when our values and freedoms are under threat, conservatives must work more closely together.
“We should be learning from each other, sharing ideas and making the case for the values we believe in: freedom, free enterprise, lower taxes and individual responsibility.
“From the appointment of Mandelson as US ambassador and kowtowing to China, to abandoning our friends and allies in the Middle East, Labour has repeatedly failed to put British interests first. I wish my successor well in continuing to hold the Government to account.”
![Dame Priti Patel](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/politics/2026/08/30/TELEMMGLPICT000470911654_17881202832890_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqi2ctj82rCJy3QOqq5vOjvf4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The Telegraph understands that Dame Priti’s new position will involve developing relationships with potential partners for new third-country migration deals such as the Rwanda agreement she signed as home secretary in 2022. She will replace Lord Hannan in the role.
Mrs Badenoch said: “Priti has been exceptionally loyal, hard-working and supportive during a very difficult period for the party.
“She came into the shadow cabinet when we needed experienced people who could operate without a large infrastructure behind them.
“Priti has done a very important job. Now I am asking her to do another important job, as international secretary of the Conservative Party.
“This role will draw on her time as home secretary and shadow foreign secretary, her work internationally and her relationships around the world. I am immensely grateful to Priti for the work she has already done and will do in her new role.”
summary: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is launching a shadow cabinet reshuffle to prepare for an early general election. Tom Tugendhat will replace Dame Priti Patel as shadow foreign secretary, while Patel moves to the role of international secretary of the Conservative Party. The overhaul also accounts for departures due to maternity leave, health reasons, and Sir James Cleverly's pursuit of the London mayoral candidacy.
key_points: Tom Tugendhat is set to replace Dame Priti Patel as shadow foreign secretary in a Conservative shadow cabinet reshuffle.
Dame Priti Patel will take on the new role of international secretary, focusing on global Right-wing party relationships and potential migration deals.
Sir James Cleverly has resigned as shadow housing secretary to pursue the Tory candidacy for the 2028 London mayoral election.
Claire Coutinho is leaving the shadow cabinet for maternity leave, and Helen Grant is stepping down following cancer treatment.

title: Prisons ‘one major event from disaster’ after U-turn on early release scheme
author: Alexandra Topping
content:
PC Andrew Harper’s killers will remain behind bars after a critical intervention by Andy Burnham, but the move has led to warnings that overcrowded prisons will be left “one major event away from disaster”.
Announcing a U-turn on the early release scheme after weeks of intense pressure, Burnham said he understood “how strongly people feel about this issue”.
The prime minister’s intervention will prevent the early release of offenders guilty of all forms of manslaughter, as well as rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers.
The decision, which affects about 1,400 prisoners, was welcomed by police, victims’ groups and families, including qualified support from Harper’s mother, Debbie Adlam.
But critics said the change could undermine progressive prison reforms in England and Wales. They said the steps Burnham outlined to free up space would take longer to bring into force, putting the orderly management of prisons at risk.
Harper was 28 when he sustained fatal injuries while responding to a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire in August 2019. Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were passengers in the vehicle and both 17 at the time, were sentenced to 13 years in custody for manslaughter.
![Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e162c848ca4ab13f79a77d791fd2d07c1d0af11a/0_0_3560_2468/master/3560.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Speaking to the BBC, which first reported the government U-turn on Sunday, Burnham said he had “heard” Harper’s family.
“I heard, obviously, what Andrew Harper’s family were saying,” he said. “I mean, who couldn’t? Nobody would want a position to arise where those guilty of killing a police officer are let out early from prison.”
Adlam said she was glad and grateful for the change in the new law but felt “a mixed bag of emotions” and campaigning for the change had been traumatic.
“On the one hand we are glad, but we’ve been [put] through the mill and we are only back at where we were to start with,” she told BBC Breakfast. “We’re not making any headway or anything, we are just literally fighting to get back to where we were.”
Harper’s force, Thames Valley police, said the news would be “welcomed by many across policing and our communities”.
Jason Hogg, the chief constable of the force, said: “Today is not about politics. It is about remembering Andrew, recognising the profound impact his death continues to have on those who knew him, the communities he protected and those who serve in policing today.”
Burnham’s 11th-hour intervention will limit the number of places that can be freed up in the prison estate, which ministers have repeatedly warned is on the brink of collapse.
Before the early prison release scheme that had been due to start this week, the prime minister said spaces would be made available by deporting foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.
But critics warned neither measure would free up sufficient space in a system that is operating at 98% capacity in England and Wales.
Up to 6,000 prisoners were due to have their sentences cut short under the new law, but government figures suggest the number will now be about 4,600. With the first batch of prisoners due to be released early in October, prison governor representatives said staff would be put under intense pressure.
“The truth is I wanted to go even further,” said Burnham. “But I’ve pushed the system to the very limits of what’s possible without risking the prison system collapsing within months, putting the public at enormous risk.”
Nicole Jacobs, the domestic abuse commissioner for England and Wales, said Sunday’s announcement would not bring reassurance to domestic abuse victims.
“Victims and survivors will still be forced to take measures to protect themselves from dangerous abusers because the government and our criminal justice system cannot,” she said.
Sources accused the prime minister of making a “politically easy decision” and warned that multiple governments had failed to deport foreign convicts. Burnham admitted the number that could be returned was in the “hundreds”.
The prime minister’s pledge to “end the injustice” of indefinite jail terms (IPPs) in this parliament was hailed as “a day that thousands of families have spent years fighting for”.
But prison experts said it would be complicated, take time and would be unlikely to free up many places in the short term. IPPs were abolished more than a decade ago but still keep more than 2,000 people in England and Wales behind bars.
“The decision to release people on IPPs is extremely welcome, but the government must now deliver it,” said Andrea Coomber, the chief executive of the Howard League, a penal reform charity.
She said Sunday’s announcement left the prison estate “one major incident away from a disaster”.
“All it will take is something like a serious riot or public disturbance and any capacity will be gone,” she added. “It is just too close to the bone and the government will be left with very little room to manoeuvre.”
She said the move threatened to undermine changes to the Sentencing Act, which were brought forward after a review led by David Gauke, a former justice secretary, and were designed to improve rehabilitation rates as well as freeing up spaces for people coming into the system.
“The Sentencing Act changes were based on deep work over a year from the independent sentencing review, the government and civil servants, with parliamentary scrutiny of the legislation,” said Coomber. “Today’s announcement has undone some of that work.”
Pia Sinha, the chief executive of the Prison Reform Trust, said the government should address the number of people on remand awaiting trial, which account for 18% of those in prison.
“If prisons are full they become warehouses – you can’t deliver interventions, self-harm goes up and rehabilitation goes down,” she said.
“The Gauke reforms were not a magic bullet, but they were brave and they were an investment in the future. That progress must not be lost.”
Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary, accused Labour of avoiding parliamentary scrutiny of the changes. “The government must delay the scheme, bring forward emergency primary legislation and exclude the worst offenders properly,” he said.
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced a U-turn on an early prison release scheme, ensuring that killers of police officers, rapists, and child abusers will remain behind bars. The decision affects about 1,400 prisoners and was welcomed by police and victims' groups, but critics warned it leaves the overcrowded prison system operating near full capacity and vulnerable to major disruptions. To compensate for the reduced space, the government plans to deport foreign prisoners and release inmates serving indefinite sentences, though experts caution these measures will take time.
key_points: Andy Burnham reversed an early release scheme to keep violent offenders, including the killers of PC Andrew Harper, behind bars.
The change affects approximately 1,400 prisoners, reducing the total number of inmates slated for early release from 6,000 to about 4,600.
Police and victims' families welcomed the decision, while prison experts and critics warned it leaves the system operating at 98% capacity and dangerously close to disaster.
Alternative plans to free up prison space include deporting foreign criminals and releasing inmates serving indefinite sentences, though critics argue these steps will take too long to implement.

title: Notting Hill Carnival's 60th year celebrated on family day
author: Victoria Cook
content:
![A child with headdress smiles from the parade](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1440/cpsprodpb/9df5/live/48d2b160-a481-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.png)
Sunday at Notting Hill Carnival is family day, with children taking part in the parade through the streets
- Published
As I walk into the heart of the 60th Notting Hill Carnival, the sun is shining and bouncing off the sequins, gems and sparkles of the costumes and decorations surrounding me.
Flags from all over the Caribbean and Africa have been hung from the windows of the houses and are draped over the shoulders of people passing by.
Everyone is dressed for sunshine, despite the rain that was forecast. It seems the spirit of Carnival has seen off those dark clouds.
The Sunday parade hasn't started yet, but the music is already pumping, and plenty of people are dancing, already covered in paint from J'ouvert, the traditional early-morning celebration which kicks off Sunday's festivities.
![Mum and baby hug on the roadside in costumes for carnival](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1504/cpsprodpb/667e/live/e76d2050-a47a-11f1-bed8-470734b5b662.jpg)
Twinsy and her daughter Triny-Savannah travelled from Paris to be part of Carnival
Today is all about families and the children. And they have certainly got the memo. There are children everywhere, all ready for the fun of the day.
Toddling past me is surely one of Notting Hill Carnival's youngest visitors. Triny-Savannah is just 18 months old, and is here with her mum Twinsy, all the way from Paris.
"It means a lot to be here," Twinsy says. She explains that her parents used to bring her and her twin sister, and now she's carrying on the tradition with the next generation.
"It's the celebration of the abolition of slaves, so it's a big day of memories," Twinsy says.
Sitting on the pavement nearby I spot eight-year-old Alex and his mum, Tiana. I soon find out it's Alex's first Carnival.
He has the biggest smile on his face and a water pistol loaded with paint.
"I haven't been for a long time," Tiana, from Enfield, explains, "but when I was younger I used to come religiously every year and it's nice to come back with Alex."
I ask Alex how he feels about the whole morning, and he says: "I love it. It's really busy, but then it's also like we're all together at the same time, so that's great."
![Mum and son on the pavement](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/9d47/live/525edcb0-a47a-11f1-bed8-470734b5b662.jpg)
Tiana's son Alex was "loving" his first Notting Hill Carnival
Before the parade starts, I go in search of a snack and find a food stall tucked away from all the crowds.
The man being served ahead of me, Dave, bites into his snack and he's instantly in heaven.
"When I bite into this, I feel like I'm about to land in Trinidad and I'm looking out of the window at the beauty," he says, still with his eyes closed, imagining it.
He's eating "doubles", a street food snack of flatbreads filled with curried chickpeas.
The woman serving, Christina Bedau, asks if I want to try it. Of course I do. But, hold the extra spice please, as I'm useless with anything too hot.
Christina hands me her creation, and it looks great. When I taste it, I can see what Dave means, although, I think to make it a fair comparison, I should probably fly to Trinidad just to check he's being accurate.
Christina has been coming to Notting Hill Carnival with her food stall, Sweet Hand Cuisine, for the past seven years. She says she "has to come" because if she didn't, the regulars who come back every year would be "up in arms".
She estimates she'll sell at least 500 doubles this weekend.
![Me and stall holder with the food being served](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/2b9c/live/4608b8c0-a47d-11f1-bed8-470734b5b662.jpg)
My first time trying doubles - flatbreads filled with curried chickpeas
Now the parade is well under way, and the swell of sound is all around us in the form of booming sound systems passing by on huge trucks, as well as dancers and steelpan groups.
Sunday's event is a much smaller version than the huge parade that will be here tomorrow, but this is still very impressive, and beautiful.
![Two boys hold flags and smile at the camera](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/b3b4/live/a09b3e50-a47a-11f1-bed8-470734b5b662.jpg)
Jay and Rio were part of the children's parade and said it was "so much fun"
![Heather, wearing a red top, smiles at the camera in the sunshine](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/7230/live/59462d20-a47b-11f1-bed8-470734b5b662.jpg)
Heather has been to every Notting Hill Carnival since arriving in the UK in 1992
Heather is part of one of the passing floats, and tells me she is a steelpan player, although today she's "just partying" on her float.
"I arrived in this country in 1992 and I've been to every Carnival [since]," she says.
"This is about recharging and being immersed in my culture.
"We work hard and we want to play hard and just enjoy our culture," she explains before she disappears back into the crowd.
![Betty stands outside a house selling accessories](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/1451/live/9b9741f0-a47b-11f1-bed8-470734b5b662.jpg)
Betty set up her stall to sell fans from Ghana, as well as other accessories
I spot a stall selling beautiful fans, and stop to buy one for my daughter. It's handmade, from Ghana, and Betty, who sells it to me, says it's made of cotton.
I then try to show Betty how to take card payments on her phone. But, it's already getting busy, so she may just have to rely on those with cash.
![People in the parade playing drums](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1440/cpsprodpb/a75c/live/7f11c870-a48a-11f1-8395-fb1eae51ae18.jpg)
The parade makes its way around the streets of Notting Hill for most of the day
There will be around two million people visiting this part of west London for the carnival this weekend.
It is Europe's largest street festival and the second-largest carnival in the world, surpassed only by Rio de Janeiro's Carnival in Brazil.
It doesn't matter how many times I come to Carnival, I am always surprised at the complete transformation of this area. It's almost unrecognisable.
The floats travelling past me are full of life and music. I could take photos of this all day long.
![A family pose for a photo at the parade, dressed in yellow and green](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/f02d/live/74140dc0-a47b-11f1-bed8-470734b5b662.jpg)
Daniel, Asher, Hazel and Rachel came to represent St Vincent, where Rachel's family are from
The family next to me catch my eye, all kitted out in matching St Vincent's outfits.
Daniel's five-year-old son Asher has already got tired legs, so he's popped him on his shoulders. It could be a long day for Daniel's shoulders.
Daniel explains that his wife, Rachel, is from the Caribbean island and they have all just returned from their first family holiday there.
"It's great to represent St Vincent here," Daniel says. "This is a perfect kind of event," he adds.
I say goodbye to the family and realise the time. I have to head off to write about my day. I take another 50 photos, at least, on the walk back to Paddington station.
I spot a poster as I leave, which says: "Fund 60 more," and asks people to donate money, to keep Carnival going.
I wonder what Carnival will look like in another 60 years? Perhaps some of the children I met today will remember this big milestone for the festival, and tell their children about today, in another 60 years.
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: The 60th Notting Hill Carnival kicked off with its traditional family day, featuring children's parades, vibrant costumes, and music. Attendees of all ages gathered to celebrate Caribbean and African cultures, heritage, and community. The event highlights generational traditions, traditional street food, and lively street celebrations.
key_points: Sunday marked the family day of the 60th Notting Hill Carnival, focusing on children and family traditions.
The festival is Europe's largest street festival and the second-largest carnival globally.
Attendees enjoyed traditional elements such as J'ouvert paint celebrations, steelpan music, and Caribbean street food like doubles.
Many families traveled long distances or returned to the carnival to pass down cultural traditions to the next generation.

title: Man Utd pay tribute to 'proud Red' crash death officer
author: Simon Stone
content:
![Handout photo of PC Matthew Blades issued by Cleveland Police](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1152/cpsprodpb/b481/live/f2005a60-a47e-11f1-bed8-470734b5b662.jpg)
Manchester United described PC Matthew Blades as "a devoted family man and a police officer who dedicated his life to helping others"
- Published
The two sons of a police officer killed in a crash on Teesside will lead out the Manchester United team as mascots for Sunday's Premier League match against Ipswich at Old Trafford.
PC Matthew Blades, described as a "proud Red" by United, was a regular at Old Trafford. The club have paid tribute to him in Sunday's match programme. His widow will attend the game with their children.
PC Blades and his colleague PC Tom Clough died in a head-on collision between their police car and a vehicle going the wrong way on the A66 near Middlesbrough early on 22 August. Five people in the other vehicle also died.
United said they learned of the deaths of the two officers "with great sadness".
"Matthew was a proud Red, a devoted family man and a police officer who dedicated his life to helping others," said the club, in a tribute in the programme.
At Elland Road, match officials for Leeds United's Premier League fixture against Brentford on Sunday wore black armbands as referee Tony Harrington was a friend of PC Blades.
On Saturday, there was a minute's applause in memory of PC Blades and PC Clough before Middlesbrough's Championship encounter with West Brom at Riverside Stadium. Pictures of the two men were displayed on a screen.
People also gathered to pay tribute at Seaton Carew FC's game against FC Hartlepool. PC Blades had been a junior football coach at both teams.
Earlier this week, 17 people were arrested in connection with the investigation into the crash bringing the total number of arrests to 24.
The occupants of the other vehicle, a Passat - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17, also died.
![Pictures of the two officers. Both are smiling. PC Blades, left, has stubble and short fair hair. PC Clough also has stubble and short dark hair.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/68ab/live/93348dd0-9f24-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.png)
PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough were killed in a crash near Middlesbrough
summary: Manchester United has paid tribute to PC Matthew Blades, a dedicated officer and club supporter who died alongside colleague PC Tom Clough in a head-on collision on the A66. Blades's two sons will lead the Manchester United team out as mascots for their match against Ipswich, while his widow attends the game. Tributes have also been held across various football fixtures, and 24 people have been arrested in connection with the crash investigation.
key_points: PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough died in a head-on collision on the A66 near Middlesbrough on 22 August, along with five people in the other vehicle.
Blades's two sons will walk out as mascots for Manchester United's match against Ipswich, and the club paid tribute to him in the match programme.
Various football matches have held tributes, including a minute's applause at Middlesbrough and referee black armbands at Elland Road.
A total of 24 people have been arrested in connection with the investigation into the crash.

title: Pastor killed by falling sign at Christian festival identified
author: Telegraph Reporters
content:
![Robert Guanco was a pastor at Jesus the Living Water Church in Eastbourne](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/30/TELEMMGLPICT000500047656_17880808905340_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq6W68AnHFIe5Slx_dOzS0aBGKJ4zGadcKM6YdlB04J4Q.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Robert Guanco was a pastor at Jesus the Living Water Church in Eastbourne](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/30/TELEMMGLPICT000500047656_17880808905340_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq6W68AnHFIe5Slx_dOzS0aBGKJ4zGadcKM6YdlB04J4Q.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
A pastor who was killed by a falling sign at a Christian festival in West Sussex has been identified.
Jesus the Living Water Church in Eastbourne, East Sussex, paid tribute to Robert Guanco, 41, after he was killed by a large wooden sign at Big Church Festival (BCF) near Steyning on Friday afternoon.
Organisers of the BCF, described as Britain’s biggest Christian festival, said they were “devastated by the serious incident”, which also injured six others.
In a statement, the church described Guanco as a “faithful servant of God”, saying: “We are mourning, grieving, praying, and trusting in the Lord during this incredibly difficult time.
“There are many things we may never fully understand, and our hearts may struggle to make sense of what has happened. Yet, even in our deepest sorrow, we continue to trust in the sovereignty of God.”
The statement added: “His life, his faith, his love, and his service to God will never be forgotten.”
Guanco is survived by his wife Isay and daughter Ellie, Premier Christian News reported.
Witnesses said that festival-goers rushed to lift a heavy sign which read “Everything’s Unmissable” after it fell on visitors.
![The incident happened at Big Church Festival in West Sussex on Friday](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/30/TELEMMGLPICT000499844345_17880809599530_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqyuLFFzXshuGqnr8zPdDWXhbQKbwj1ZsnNMhuR7O6ySI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Fred Abbott, from Morden, south London, told the Daily Mail that a “strong gust of wind” toppled the sign as he and his family were nearby.
He said: “We were by Tom’s Stage in the Field of Fun, about 20 metres away from where this massive wooden sign was. We heard this massive crack and bang, and me and my friend ran over.
“There were around 30 to 50 people, including me and my friend, picking up this sign.”
Andy Ollerton was walking “just a few paces” behind “when a huge overhead sign came crashing down on the people in front of us”.
The theologian and author explained on Instagram: “We rushed with others to lift the sign off them and then administered first aid with others as best we could until the paramedics arrived but tragically, one of those people, we’ve now heard, lost his life. So, we’re absolutely reeling, devastated, as you can imagine, and in a bit of shock as well. I am sure many others who witnessed it were too.”
Mr Ollerton said many people would have questions about the incident, adding: “Why did this happen? Why did this happen at human level? What went wrong, but also why did God let this happen? I suppose is the deeper question that I’m sure you’re feeling too.”
Event cancelled
BCF took “decisive action in difficult circumstances” and the crowds stayed calm and respectful, he said.
Festival-goers were alerted to the tragedy when God TV announced that “due to unforeseen circumstances” the BCF livestream had been paused.
The rest of the event, which opened on Friday and had been due to run until Sunday, has been cancelled.
South East Coast Ambulance Service was called out just after 3.30pm and treated six people at the scene. A spokesman said: “Four of those patients were taken to local hospitals for further treatment, including two patients with more serious injuries and two patients with less serious injuries.
“Our thoughts are with the family of the man who sadly lost his life, and with everyone affected by this tragic incident.”
Dame Sarah Mullally, the Archbishop of Canterbury, said she was “sad and shocked” to hear about the incident.
She said: “I pray for his family, friends and loved ones as they grieve. I pray for those receiving treatment, and the healthcare workers looking after them. And I pray too for the other festival-goers, staff and event organisers as they come to terms with these tragic events. May the God of comfort and healing be with them all.”
ParentFuel, a Christian parent support organisation, said its members who attended the festival were “all devastated but safe”.
‘God is still good’
In a statement, it praised BCF for the way it handled the incident and said: “What happened was awful. It was a freak accident. But God is still good.” It added: “Life is so precious and so so short. This weekend brought that ever closer for us all.”
On Saturday, festival-goer Ralph Scrutton posted: “The mood across the campsite is understandably subdued and melancholy, with people slowly waking up, packing down, and getting ready to leave the site. There’s a real sense of quietness this morning, with people reflecting on the events of yesterday. Keep praying church, for all those involved.”
The deceased’s next of kin have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers, Sussex Police said.
The incident has been reported to the health and safety executive and local authority, the force added.
Det Ch Supt Richard McDonagh said: “I recognise the immense distress this will have caused people at the festival, and we are working with a number of partners as we seek to establish exactly what happened.
“We know there were thousands of people at the festival and we’re urging anyone with any information, or any relevant video footage, to please come forward.”
summary: Pastor Robert Guanco, 41, was killed and six others were injured after a large wooden sign was toppled by a strong gust of wind at the Big Church Festival in West Sussex. Festival attendees rushed to lift the heavy sign and administered first aid until paramedics arrived at the scene. Following the tragic incident, the remainder of the festival was cancelled, and organizers and church communities expressed their grief and offered tributes.
key_points: Pastor Robert Guanco of Jesus the Living Water Church in Eastbourne was identified as the person killed by the falling sign at the Big Church Festival.
Six other people were injured, with four transported to local hospitals, including two with more serious injuries.
Witnesses reported that a strong gust of wind caused the large wooden sign to topple over on Friday afternoon.
The rest of the Big Church Festival, which was scheduled to run until Sunday, was cancelled following the incident.
Sussex Police reported the incident to the health and safety executive and local authority while appealing for information and video footage.

title: PC Harper's killers to stay in jail as PM announces early release scheme changes
author: Jake Lapham
content:
Watch: PM confirms PC Harper's killers will remain in prison
- Published
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told the BBC that PC Andrew Harper's killers will remain behind bars as he announced changes to the early release scheme aimed at easing prison overcrowding.
In an exclusive interview with BBC Breakfast, Burnham said anyone convicted of unlawful killing, including all forms of manslaughter, will be excluded from the scheme, which would have made two of the officer's killers eligible for early release.
Burnham said extra prison space would be created by deporting foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.
It follows months of campaigning from PC Harper's family and former colleagues to block the release of his killers.
The 28-year-old was responding to a burglary in Berkshire in 2019 when he was dragged along a road by a vehicle as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft.
When it emerged that two of the killers, Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, could be released early, there were passionate calls for the government to intervene and block those convicted of manslaughter from early release.
"I heard obviously what Andrew Harper's family were saying, I mean who couldn't? Nobody would want a position to arise where those guilty of killing a police officer are let out early from prison," Burnham told the BBC.
He conceded the announcement will mean "hundreds" more people stay in prison, meaning additional space will need to be found in a system that is more than 97% full in England and Wales.
'I've applied common sense,' says Burnham on ending Imprisonment for Public Protection sentences
The prime minister said that will be achieved in-part through ending Imprisonment for Public Protection sentences, or IPPs.
These were available between 2005 and 2012, and were given to offenders who pose a significant risk of causing serious harm to the public.
Once a minimum term has been served, the prisoner can be released only once the Parole Board is satisfied they no longer need to be confined for public safety, meaning many are being held indefinitely.
Burnham said he had applied "common sense" on the treatment of IPPs, which he had "long-standing concerns" about.
"I was faced with a situation where people on those sentences who have more than served their time, not being released when others who've committed very serious crimes being released early," he told the BBC.
"The judgement I've made is the public, in my view, would prefer a situation where people who have served their time to be considered for release before those who haven't."
According to Ministry of Justice data, 2,271 people are serving IPP sentences as of June. Of those, 856 have never been released because the Parole Board thought it was not safe to do so.
Burnham conceded that of those offenders, there will be "individuals who will pose a risk to communities", and said a cross-party oversight group would be established.
The government will table legislation to terminate the sentences by the "end of this Parliament", he added.
Pressed on how many foreign prisoners could be returned, Burnham said it was "hundreds".
The government has said powers will be implemented early next year to deport some foreign criminals immediately after sentencing.
Those powers would block foreign prisoners from ever returning to the country while "keeping those in prison for the most serious crimes locked up for a substantial period before they are removed".
The government is not thought to have signed any additional prisoner returns agreements with other countries.
It is understood that work has also begun to create more cells in existing prisons by adapting space used for other purposes, but that is also expected to take months.
None of the measures announced by Burnham are likely to create much additional prison capacity by the time the first batch of prisoners are released early in October.
The prime minister is said to have taken a "political decision" to use some of the remaining capacity in the prison system to ensure the changes announced today could be implemented immediately.
In addition to those in jail for manslaughter, the prime minister said prisoners convicted of indecent assault offences and death by dangerous driving will also remain in prison.
Historic child sex offences and causing or allowing the death of a child will also be exempted from the early release scheme, while new "restriction zones" to better protect domestic violence survivors from perpetrators released early will be introduced.
Burnham said the additional changes announced on Sunday would result in "hundreds" more prisoners staying behind bars.
The justice secretary is expected to give a more precise figure for how many people will be affected when he gives a statement in Parliament on Tuesday.
Earlier this month, Burnham announced prisoners guilty of rape, serious child sex offences and grooming will be excluded from early release eligibility.
![Andy Burnham wears a dark suit sitting on a chair speaking with Roger Johnson who wears a dark suit. They are both sitting on red chairs.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/4808/live/433d7c20-a3bf-11f1-b13c-0d78069132fa.jpg)
Andy Burnham speaks with Roger Johnson in Downing Street
The Sentencing Act 2026 was designed to address the prisons overcrowding crisis, by releasing large numbers of inmates earlier than had been previously planned. The early release scheme is scheduled to start on 1 October.
But it was met with fierce opposition from some, including family and former colleagues of PC Harper.
Cole and Bowers were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter in 2020 and would previously have become eligible for release under the scheme after serving half of their sentences, down from two-thirds.
The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was given an "extended" sentence of 16 years for manslaughter and was therefore not eligible for release.
PC Harper's widow, Lissie Harper, had described the prospect of their sentences being reduced as "deplorable".
His mother Debbie Adlam told BBC Breakfast earlier this month she was in "turmoil" following conflicting reports about whether the killers would be released, describing the handling of the situation as a "hash".
Conservative shadow home secretary Chris Philp previously accused Burnham and Labour of "re-traumatising victims and their families with their constant U-turns".
![Andrew Harper is pictured - he is a man with short brown hair and a slight beard wearing a shirt and smiling at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/efc9/live/6272a1d0-859f-11f1-bc30-6908d27da04d.jpg)
Police officer Andrew Harper suffered fatal injuries while on duty in 2019
During his early days as prime minister, Burnham announced the changes brought in by the Sentencing Act would be paused while a review was carried out.
On 3 August, the government announced prisoners guilty of rape, serious child sex offences and grooming would be excluded from the new policy.
Prisoners serving sentences for murder would not be eligible for early release.
While Downing Street initially warned it would not be possible to exclude "one or two offenders" convicted of manslaughter, Burnham later said he was "confident" of being able to block PC Harper's killers from the scheme.
It marked a shift from a week earlier, when he said there was "nothing more" he could do without risking the collapse of the prison system.
The Sentencing Act made a number of key changes designed to mean fewer people were sent to prison, and to free many inmates earlier than planned.
The prison population in England and Wales on 24 August was 86,843, which is 97.6% of the total capacity.
Additional reporting by Jack Fenwick and Claire Keenan
  - Published22 July
 ![Andrew Harper is pictured - he is a man with short brown hair and a slight beard wearing a shirt and smiling at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/efc9/live/6272a1d0-859f-11f1-bc30-6908d27da04d.jpg)
- ![A man dressed smartly, with a neat beard, smiles for the camera in a black and white image](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/880b/live/f4745520-956b-11f1-8b14-5d44448d174a.jpg)
- ![Albert Bowers (left) and Jessie Cole (centre), smiling, appearing to laugh or mock the assembled media, as they leave Reading Magistrates Court following an appearance in relation to the death of PC Andrew Harper.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/70de/live/acb174c0-923c-11f1-af4d-5164294a85c7.jpg)
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced that the killers of PC Andrew Harper will remain in prison after updating the government's early release scheme to exclude all forms of manslaughter. To address prison overcrowding, the changes will be balanced by deporting foreign prisoners and moving to terminate indefinite Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences. The modifications also keep individuals convicted of offenses such as indecent assault and death by dangerous driving behind bars.
key_points: PC Andrew Harper's killers, Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, will remain in prison following changes to the early release scheme.
The updated scheme excludes anyone convicted of unlawful killing, including all forms of manslaughter, as well as those convicted of certain sexual and driving offenses.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced plans to ease prison overcrowding by deporting foreign prisoners and ending Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences.
The early release scheme is scheduled to begin on October 1 to help address a prison system running at over 97% capacity in England and Wales.

title: Notting Hill Carnival mas bands call for funding amid threat to future
author: Niva Yadav
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
For many revellers, Notting Hill Carnival is just a booze-soaked bank holiday street party. The three-day affair comes and goes for most Londoners, who pay homage to Caribbean culture one day and forget about it the next.
But for the mas bands and creatives at the heart of Carnival, preserving the heritage and culture is a year long labour of love - one that is now threatened by economic pressures and tighter regulations.
What is a mas band?
Mas comes from the word masquerade and the bands of people playing music and dancing during the parade are known as mas bands. Early mas was linked to African traditions and the costumes were based on parodies of the French planter class, for example, satirical spoofs like Dame Lorraine
The groups will return to the streets of Notting Hill this bank holiday weekend, as Carnival attracts up to two million people. A Carnival steel band competition is taking place on Saturday, before the children’s and adult’ days parades on Sunday and Monday.
Operating a mas band is a serious business. Colin Julien, co-founder of Caribbean Sessions mas band, is at the helm of a huge operation - balancing expenses across costumes, marketing, security, music, catering, and transport.
It’s not just about selling a costume. Mas bands must deliver an experience to their members that includes meals, live DJs and security on Carnival day.
“It has to be to a high standard so that people return, people can tell their friends and family that they had a great time with us - they got fed, watered, and they felt secure,” Mr Julien explains.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/28/13/11/Screenshot-2026-08-28-at-14-09-06.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/28/13/45/Screenshot-2026-08-28-at-14-10-38.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Vinny Vincenzo Ranks, one of the owners at Karnival Mania, feeds more than 900 masqueraders every year. Even from their mas camp - the location where costumes are built and distributed - there is rum punch flowing on tap for customers collecting their outfits.
Yet the economics of carnival can be brutal for mas camp leaders. Bands must fund their own private security teams for the parade and rely on costume sales to offset the operational costs.
“Nobody runs a mas band for profit,” Mr Julien says. He recalls a year when costume sales were dangerously low, putting their band at risk. Some owners have even been left bankrupt or are struggling to pay their mortgages even months after the music stops, Mr Ranks says.
Read More
“There’s a lot of bands that need help. We really need some help in this carnival community with some funding,” Mr Ranks says.
Mr and Mrs Julien, and Mr Ranks, are among the fortunate mas bands that receive some funding towards operational costs from Notting Hill Carnival Ltd. Some also manage to secure corporate sponsorships to help juggle costs.
“We are forever grateful Notting Hill Carnival provided us with funding and we utilised that funding straight away into four departments - volunteering, food, security and transport,” Mr Julien said, adding that they were also able to secure sponsorship from a drilling company after more than 100 attempts.
Not every mas band is so lucky. Several bands have been forced to close their doors for good, while others are hanging on by a thread.
Duka Mas Dominik announced on Instagram it had withdrawn from the festival “driven by unsustainable financial and operational pressures,” adding that the decision was a “painful” one.
The group cited “escalating costs, absence of key funding streams, costume orders below anticipated levels, and an increasingly onerous regulatory landscape” as reasons that forced the move.
Arawak is another band that was forced to withdraw from this year’s carnival, explaining it was “due to the restrictions placed on bands this year.” Though details remain vague, regulations placed on bands are important to follow and every band must complete a rigorous application process to be allowed to perform at Carnival.
For example, no more than a third of the band can wear t-shirts - with the majority required to be in full costume. Though the rule is meant to maintain high standards, it also puts bands under pressure to sell costumes.
It can be especially gruelling when band leaders are making many efforts to keep costs down.
Mr Julien says, “It’s difficult to charge a mum and dad a certain fee for their child to come and spend the day listening to music”, adding that their basic kids’ costume starts at £75.
But other costumes, like those made at Karnival Mania, can stretch to £4,000 for adults.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/28/13/23/Screenshot-2026-08-28-at-14-10-11.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
While many mas groups outsource manufacturing to China or other countries, Pauline Jay, co-founder of Funatik Mas, constructs everything by hand in the capital. Having played mas since the 1990s, she uses the camp to pass down the craft to the next generation.
For Ms Jay and her husband Martin, the mas camp provides a secure environment for young people - in many ways a substitute for the youth clubs of the past.
“There were all different ages in the mas camp, from babies all the way up to 70 year olds,” Ms Jay says. “I know our youth are a bit misguided at the moment. But our band is one of the bands that would like to embrace that generation and help them”
“It will give them some sort of belonging,” she adds.
Her daughter Rachelle is also a fierce advocate for using mas bands to help funnel the creativity of young people into a source for good. After growing up in the mas camp alongside her mother, she now designs costumes for the band.
In the Julien household, traditions are already being passed to the couple’s six-year-old twins Christian and Gabriel, who are learning to shape wire and foam, dance to soca tunes, and run a large-scale mas band operation.
“It’s important to pass on the knowledge in a palatable way” Mr Julien says. When he grew up, attending mas camp was a “non-negotiable”, but he wants his children to be “invested” in the future of Carnival out of passion.
Every bead, sequin and feather carries a meaning, with themes being an integral part of costume design. This year, the Juliens settled on the theme of Olympus in a nod to Greek mythology, creating outfits based on Poseidon, Hera, and Athena.
Mr Julien has already decided a theme for next year and by October, cogs will be turning to ensure the costume can be marketed in January. Inclusivity is also a key consideration for Caribbean Sessions and the band offers three options - skimpy, standard, and curvy - that “enables all the women to feel comfortable.”
“Representation really matters for us. We’ve got that at the forefront with everything that we do,” says Mrs Julien.
Over in Haringey, Pauline and Rachelle have crafted costumes based on “untold stories”, picking a diamond as their primary emblem, while Vinny’s band is creating costumes based on “celebration.”
Matthew Phillip, CEO at Notting Hill Carnival Ltd, says that efforts are being made to support younger designers and help smaller bands to showcase their word.
“A lot of funding in recent years has been focused on safety and security,” he explained, but plans are in place to ensure more funding is given to the artists at the heart of the event. Notting Hill Carnival Ltd is also looking to help bands secure more funding and that more resources continue to be available.
Yvette Reinfor of Notting Hill Walks has pushed for carnival arts to be taken seriously and has warned that reducing the cultural aspect of the festivities puts the carnival at risk.
“Without cultural relevance, it becomes nothing more than a street party,” says Ms Reinfor. “And a street party is easily ticketed, displaced, or dismissed. Bring the culture back, and it commands respect.”
But that is a mission which is easier said than done. Mas bands, steel bands, and sound systems all need resources if Carnival is to survive. As Mr Julien says, “We cannot be the future if we don’t have the financial support to stand on.”
summary: Mas bands at the heart of the Notting Hill Carnival are facing severe threats to their future due to rising economic pressures, escalating operational costs, and tighter regulations. While some bands receive limited funding and sponsorships, others have been forced to withdraw or close down entirely. Band leaders emphasize that financial support and resources are urgently needed to preserve the cultural heritage of the festival.
key_points: Notting Hill Carnival mas bands are struggling with high expenses for costumes, private security, catering, and transport.
Economic pressures, lack of funding, and strict regulations have forced some bands, such as Duka Mas Dominik and Arawak, to withdraw from the festival.
Band leaders and advocates warn that losing the cultural heritage of mas bands turns the event into a basic street party vulnerable to displacement.
Notting Hill Carnival Ltd's CEO stated that efforts and future plans are being made to increase support, resources, and funding for artists and smaller bands.

title: US issues new ultimatum to UK over Falklands
author: Harriette Boucher
content:
The US is said to have issued an ultimatum to Andy Burnham, threatening to withdraw its support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falkland Islands if it does not increase defence spending.
Pentagon officials are understood to be reviewing Nato allies’ commitment to their 5 per cent defence spending promise, with the UK set to get “special attention”, a senior US official told The Telegraph.
Donald Trump’s administration believes the UK did not go far enough with its defence investment plan in June and is now looking at ways to incentivise the prime minister to invest further.
“I would expect the UK to receive special attention because it has so much potential,” the US official told the publication. “We will therefore continue efforts to incentivise and enable the UK to step up in a major way.”
They said that changing America’s stance on the UK’s claim to the Falklands, which the US president has previously considered, was a possibility.
“I can say that they [conversations] are candid and nothing is being ruled out as far as options for encouraging the sort of burden-sharing that we seek,” the source said.
![John Healey and Andy Burnham have refused to announce an increase in defence spending to 3 per cent of national income by 2030](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/19/09/a025240343b092ca29bfdd7d3748e8c8Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3MjE1MDAy-2.85400226.jpg)
The Treasury confirmed on Friday that chancellor John Healey’s first budget will fail to set out when the UK will meet the target of allocating 3 per cent of GDP on defence.
Mr Healey resigned as defence secretary in June, saying former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer had been “unable, and the Treasury has been unwilling, to commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country at this time of rising threats”.
The official told The Telegraph that the UK’s defence investment plan was a “step in the right direction”, but said “a step in the right direction isn’t enough.
“Given the scale of challenges facing us and our allies, we need allies like the United Kingdom to step up in major, fundamental ways. Fortunately, some already are. We strongly encourage the UK to do likewise.”
America’s recent demand follows a threat in April, in which a leaked internal Pentagon email suggested that the US could review Britain’s claim to the Falklands as revenge for a lack of support in the Iran war.
![The Falkland Islands have previously voted overwhelmingly in favour of remaining a UK overseas territory (PA)](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/04/24/12/1958f4a1adf8b7f8b88e1c9610704fadY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzc3MTE1NTUy-2.67016635.jpg)
A shift in the US position on the islands has been considered by the Foreign Office, but has been treated as a “hypothetical scenario”.
The islands are administered by the UK but are still claimed by Argentina, whose president is an ally of Mr Trump.
Downing Street insisted the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands were “not in question” following its earlier threat, while Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said a potential US policy review was “absolute nonsense” and compared it to Mr Trump’s previous threat to annex Greenland.
Admiral Lord West of Spithead, the commanding officer of HMS Ardent, a frigate that was sunk in the Falklands conflict, previously dismissed the threats, telling The Independent that, militarily, losing US support for British sovereignty would have “no impact”.
“The recognition or otherwise by the US does not make the islands less secure,” the former Royal Navy commander-in-chief added.
The Independent has approached the White House and Downing Street for comment.
summary: The US administration has warned that it may withdraw support for British sovereignty over the Falkland Islands unless the UK increases its defence spending. Pentagon officials are reviewing Nato allies' spending commitments and are specifically targeting the UK after its recent defence investment plans fell short of expectations. While the US considers altering its stance to encourage greater burden-sharing, Downing Street and military experts have maintained that the islands' sovereignty is not in question and that losing US backing would have little military impact.
key_points: The US has threatened to withdraw support for British sovereignty over the Falkland Islands if the UK does not increase its defence spending.
The Trump administration believes the UK's recent defence investment plan did not go far enough.
The Treasury confirmed that the upcoming budget will not set a timeline for meeting the target of allocating 3 percent of GDP to defence.
Downing Street insisted that the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands is not in question.
Military experts have stated that losing US recognition regarding the islands would have no practical military impact.

title: Man dies in Burscough after train hits van on crossing
author: Marc Waddington
content:
![Image shows a train stopped on a railway line, with fields on either side. An official in a hi-vis jacket can be seen standing in front of it.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1440/cpsprodpb/d0c8/live/9ed21db0-a3e3-11f1-9dd8-8fbe4c583bb8.jpg)
British Transport Police said a man who was travelling in a van died in the incident
- Published
A man has died after a train hit a van on a railway line.
The incident happened on a crossing in Burscough, West Lancashire, just after 15:00 BST.
British Transport Police (BTP) said a man who was in the van died at the scene, and two passengers on the Wigan Wallgate-Southport train suffered minor injuries.
A BTP spokesman said: "Enquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances of what happened."
![Image shows a field in which police vehicles, an ambulance and a fire engine can be seen.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/4c4c/live/94ccbad0-a3d6-11f1-9323-c53d27c293d7.jpg)
A large emergency services presence is on the scene close to the railway line in Burscough
A large emergency services operation was launched, with police, fire and ambulance vehicles on the scene and in nearby farmland.
Passengers could be seen being helped down from the train by emergency services teams.
Operator Northern said there would be "major disruption", with "all lines blocked" by an "incident between Wigan Wallgate and Southport".
summary: A man travelling in a van has died after his vehicle was struck by a train on a crossing in Burscough, West Lancashire. Two passengers on the Wigan Wallgate-to-Southport train sustained minor injuries in the incident. British Transport Police and other emergency services responded to the scene, causing major disruptions and blocking all lines.
key_points: A man in a van died after a train hit his vehicle at a crossing in Burscough.
The incident occurred just after 15:00 BST on a railway line in West Lancashire.
Two passengers on the Wigan Wallgate-Southport train suffered minor injuries.
Emergency services launched a large operation at the scene, blocking all lines and causing major travel disruptions.

title: James Cleverly resigns from shadow cabinet to run for mayor of London
author: Sammy Gecsoyler
content:
James Cleverly has resigned from the shadow cabinet to run for mayor of London.
The Tory heavyweight, who was once home and foreign secretary and is shadow minister for housing, communities and local government, told the Sunday Times he will resign with immediate effect.
The MP for Braintree, who lost his bid to lead the Conservatives to Kemi Badenoch, is considered a more moderate voice in a party that has lurched to the right. On breaking the news to Badenoch, Cleverly told the Sunday Times: “She took it very well. Kemi has been very gracious.”
He added: “Our route to getting Kemi in No 10 has got to be through success in London,” he said. “It’s a business city, entrepreneurialism, arts, culture. I don’t buy the lazy idea that London is a Labour city. It represents the philosophical heart of the Conservative party.”
Cleverly’s resignation comes in advance of the Conservative party conference in October, where he is expected to make his case to party members.
According to the Sunday Times, sources close to Badenoch said she was “gutted” about the news but added that she “is delighted that someone of his calibre wants to put himself forward to be Conservative nominee for mayor of London”.
