Cleverly had kind words for Badenoch. “Frankly, Kemi is doing really well now. She’s getting great cut-through. It took longer than any of us would have liked, but she’s getting it,” he said.
Sadiq Khan is halfway through his third term as mayor. He has not stated whether he will run for a fourth term in the contest to be held in May 2028. Susan Hall was the Tory candidate in 2024 but lost to Khan, who was declared the winner with 43.8% of the vote.
If Khan does step down, the Labour MP for Brent Central and Brent South, Dawn Butler, is expected to throw her hat in the ring, having previously revealed her desire for the job.
Cleverly is the most senior Tory politician to run for mayor of London in recent times. Making his bid, he said Khan was “asleep at the wheel” and accused him of using the role as a stepping stone for a higher-profile position.
after newsletter promotion
“Sadiq has been trying to get out of that job for quite a while. He went in with the intention of doing what Boris [Johnson] did, using it as a high-profile platform to get him his next big job in government. There has been lots of posturing, very little delivery. Lots of picking rows with the president of America, less focus on bringing down street crime. It wouldn’t surprise me if he bows out for 2028. He’s lost the passion for the job.”
Days before Keir Starmer stood down as prime minister, he handed Khan a peerage, potentially opening the door to him joining Andy Burnham’s cabinet in future. However, while Burnham and Khan have worked closely together over the years and have a shared understanding of the challenges of devolution, it is understood Khan has told the former Manchester mayor that he has no wish to be a minister in his government.
summary: James Cleverly has resigned from the shadow cabinet with immediate effect to run for the Conservative nomination for mayor of London. The Tory MP and former home and foreign secretary made the announcement in the Sunday Times ahead of the Conservative party conference. He stated that winning in London is essential for the party's future success and criticized current mayor Sadiq Khan.
key_points: James Cleverly resigned from his shadow cabinet role to run for mayor of London.
Cleverly informed Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch of his decision, and sources close to her expressed support for his candidacy.
Cleverly criticized current Mayor Sadiq Khan, accusing him of lacking passion and using the role as a stepping stone.
The mayoral contest is scheduled to be held in May 2028.

title: Royal Navy warships and helicopter track Russian vessels in three-day operation
author: Jake Lapham
content:
![A grey Royal Navy warship is in the foreground with a grey Russian vessel in water in the background](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/a833/live/9b14df80-a39f-11f1-bb7c-3b1918839019.jpg)
HMS St Albans (bottom) monitors Russian vessel Admiral Levchenko.
- Published
Royal Navy warships and a helicopter spent three days tracking Russian Navy vessels and sanctioned cargo ships in an "intense" operation in the North Sea and English Channel.
HMS Duncan, HMS St Albans and HMS Severn used radars to monitor four vessels last week, while a Merlin helicopter provided surveillance from the sky.
"Since that successful operation, we have seen Russian shadow fleet vessels increasingly forced to change their routes, imposing significant cost and delays to their journeys," Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord and Chief of Naval Staff, said.
It comes as data shows Royal Navy activity to monitor Russian movements is up 25% so far this year compared to 2025.
During the August operation, the Royal Navy warships including a Type 45 destroyer and a Type 23 frigate, tracked Russian destroyer Admiral Levchenko as it escorted sanctioned cargo vessels General Skobelev and Sparta south through the North Sea and into the English Channel.
The Royal Navy said Russia was "forced" to respond with "costly military resources" including the frigate Neustrashimy.
A statement said a Nato ally then took over monitoring off the coast of France, without specifying the country.
The operation comes after Royal Marine Commandos boarded a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel in June.
Marines joined by National Crime Agency (NCA) officers, with the support of the RAF, intercepted and boarded the Smyrtos in a six-hour operation - the first of its kind by UK armed forces.
NCA officers arrested an Indian national, 38, on suspicion of sanctions offences under the Russia Regulations and he was taken into custody.
Watch: MoD footage shows commandos boarding and searching the tanker in June
The UK has sanctioned more than 500 vessels it says are part of Russia's so-called shadow fleet.
Oil and gas revenue as a percentage of the total Russian budget fell to just 23% in 2025, the lowest percentage share in the past 20 years, according to an analysis by the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies.
However the institute notes that was compensated by strong growth from other taxes, namely a hike in VAT and corporate profits tax.
Moscow has also benefited from a recent rise in oil prices following the Iran war, however the broader economy is slowing.
summary: Royal Navy warships and a helicopter conducted a three-day operation to track Russian Navy vessels and sanctioned cargo ships in the North Sea and English Channel. The operation forced Russian shadow fleet vessels to alter their routes and deploy costly military resources in response. This activity is part of a 25% increase in Royal Navy monitoring of Russian movements this year compared to 2025.
key_points: HMS Duncan, HMS St Albans, HMS Severn, and a Merlin helicopter monitored four Russian vessels last week.
The Russian destroyer Admiral Levchenko was tracked escorting sanctioned cargo vessels General Skobelev and Sparta.
Royal Navy activity monitoring Russian movements is up 25% so far this year compared to 2025.
The UK has sanctioned more than 500 vessels belonging to Russia's shadow fleet.
In June, Royal Marine Commandos and NCA officers boarded the Russian shadow fleet oil tanker Smyrtos in the English Channel.

title: Big Church Festival 'devastated' as man dies after sign falls
author: Jacob Panons
content:
What we know about the incident at the Big Church Festival
- Published
Organisers of a Christian festival say they are "devastated" after a sign fell at their event and injured seven people, with one man dying at the scene.
Sussex Police said it had been called to the Big Church Festival at Wiston Park, near Steyning in West Sussex, at about 15:38 BST on Friday.
It was later confirmed a 41-year-old man from Eastbourne in East Sussex had died.
A spokesperson for the festival said: "We are devastated by the serious incident that took place at Big Church Festival 2026 today, in which a sign fell, injuring at least seven people, one of whom tragically lost their life."
South East Coast Ambulance service said four of the six people injured were taken to local hospitals for further treatment, with two people having serious injuries.
The Big Church Festival, which describes itself as the UK's biggest Christian festival, was founded in 2009.
The festival began on Friday and was due to continue until Sunday, but a decision was made by organisers to cancel the remainder of the event after the incident.
"We are working with the emergency services, police and the Health and Safety Executive as they establish the circumstances surrounding today's incident," the organisers said.
"We are incredibly grateful to everyone who responded, and to our teams and community for the care they have shown one another."
'Emotional whiplash'
The Reverend James Di Castiglione, rector of the parish of Chanctonbury in which Big Church Festival takes place, says the incident has been a "huge shock to everyone locally".
"We are all experiencing emotional whiplash about what's happened really because Big Church Festival is such a time of joy and unity and love and celebration," he added.
Di Castiglione said at the event there was "just a sense of confusion and shock that was rippling across the site".
"[It is] just the worst lightning bolt of tragic news striking everybody's hearts," he said.
![Map of southern England showing the location of the Big Church Festival near Steyning in West Sussex, north of Worthing on the south coast. An inset map highlights the festival site in southeast England within the UK](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/2df1/live/0a8c09f0-a310-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png)
Christian parent support charity ParentFuel said its people at the festival were all safe.
"We cannot praise the BCF (Big Church Festival) team enough for the way things have been handled," they said on social media on Saturday morning.
"We are currently sat in the volunteer tent with a brew in hand, worship music being played and the warmth of chatter around us."
The charity said it was a "freak accident".
"Life is so precious and so, so short. This weekend brought that ever closer for us all," they added.
![An ariel view of a festival.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/efad/live/c7f987b0-a301-11f1-80b3-bf1a174ac193.jpg)
The festival was cancelled after the incident
Theo Saville, who was at the festival, said a "large wooden sign" had collapsed near the entrance to a tented area.
Sussex Police is urging anyone with information about the incident to contact them.
The Health and Safety Executive and local authority had also been informed, the force added.
The Big Church Festival, which describes itself as the UK's biggest Christian festival, was founded in 2009.
Follow BBC Sussex on Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Sussex on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk , external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.
summary: Organisers of the Big Church Festival in West Sussex expressed devastation after a sign fell and injured seven people, resulting in the tragic death of a 41-year-old man from Eastbourne. Emergency services responded to the incident on Friday afternoon, and four of the injured individuals were subsequently transported to local hospitals, with two sustaining serious injuries. Following the accident, organisers made the decision to cancel the remainder of the festival and are currently cooperating with Sussex Police and the Health and Safety Executive to investigate the circumstances.
key_points: A 41-year-old man died and seven people were injured after a sign fell at the Big Church Festival in West Sussex.
Four of the injured individuals were taken to local hospitals, with two sustaining serious injuries.
Organisers cancelled the remainder of the weekend event following the incident.
Authorities including Sussex Police and the Health and Safety Executive are investigating the circumstances surrounding the accident.

title: Police arrest seven more men in aftermath of deadly A66 crash
author: Press Association; Guardian staff reporter
content:
Seven more men have been arrested as part of an operation tackling alleged organised crime after the head-on crash on the A66 that resulted in seven deaths, Cleveland police have said.
Officers said four men, aged 21, 25, 35 and 40, were being held on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life after a vehicle crashed into a house in Steele Crescent, Middlesbrough.
They were also being questioned over alleged arson after a caravan was set alight in Atlee Road on Wednesday morning, and over a drug offence.
The force said the men were in a vehicle when they were stopped by police in Kingsley Road in Grangetown on Thursday night.
Class A drugs were seized, officers confirmed.
The three other men arrested were a 23-year-old man, on suspicion of threats to kill, a 42-year-old on suspicion of threats to kill and possession of criminal property, and a 30-year-old on suspicion of possession of criminal property.
All three have been released on conditional bail.
It brings the total number of people arrested since the crash to 24.
Earlier on Friday, detectives confirmed they were not linking a house fire that killed a seven-year-old girl and her aunt to the A66 crash, which left two police officers and five young men dead.
Hundreds of extra police officers have been drafted in to support officers after a series of incidents in the Middlesbrough and County Durham area.
Inquests have been formally opened into the deaths of the seven people in the crash in the early hours of 22 August. The two police officers who died were PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38.
The Teesside area coroner, Paul Appleton, said that there was a collision at South Bank between a police vehicle and a Volkswagen Passat.
He said the provisional cause of death for Blades was head and neck injuries and for Clough it was neck injuries.
Later, inquests were opened and adjourned into the deaths of the Passat occupants, named as Cole Worthy and Theo Rae, both 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-olds Michael Robert Cahill and Jakub Matusiak.
Police initially arrested 17 people after the crash, which followed a police pursuit, as part of an investigation into alleged organised crime.
Cleveland police assistant chief constable Wayne Fox said of the latest arrests: “This latest disruptive activity now brings the total number of arrests to 24 since the investigation commenced.
“Several suspects arrested throughout the course of this week have been charged with serious offences and a number of offenders have been recalled to prison.”
On Friday, Cleveland police said Kai Inico, who was arrested on Monday on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group, had been charged with possession with intent to supply a class B drug.
The force said four other people arrested on Monday had been bailed – a 16-year-old boy and 18-year-old man arrested on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group, a 55-year-old man arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender, and a 23-year-old man arrested on suspicion of threats to kill.
Earlier this week, two other people were charged with offences and appeared in court.
Meanwhile, two men have been arrested on suspicion of murder in connection with the fire which killed Natalie McDonald, 34, and seven-year-old Valentina Foster, as well as injuring four others, in Grangetown.
Matt Storey, the police and crime commissioner for Cleveland, said on Friday: “After what has been the most tragic week in its history, I want to extend my heartfelt thanks to local residents for the outpouring of love and support they have shown to Cleveland police.
“My thoughts remain with the family, friends and colleagues of PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough. They will be remembered as selfless, professional and courageous police officers, dedicated to serving their communities.”
summary: Cleveland police have arrested seven more men as part of an ongoing operation tackling alleged organised crime following a fatal A66 crash that killed seven people. The latest arrests bring the total number of people arrested since the crash to 24. Meanwhile, authorities confirmed they are not linking a separate fatal house fire in Grangetown to the A66 collision.
key_points: Seven more men were arrested by Cleveland police, bringing the total arrests since the A66 crash to 24.
Four of the men were held for suspected criminal damage, arson, and drug offenses after being stopped in Grangetown.
Three other men were arrested on suspicion of threats to kill and possession of criminal property and have been released on bail.
Inquests have formally opened for the seven victims of the A66 crash, which included two police officers and five young men.
Police stated that a separate house fire in Grangetown, which killed a woman and a seven-year-old girl, is not linked to the A66 crash.

title: Deadly Middlesbrough house fire and A66 crash not linked, say police
author: Bryony Gooch
content:
A house fire in Middlesbrough that killed two people and a crash on the nearby A66 last weekend, which left seven people dead, are not being treated as linked by police.
Emergency services responded on Wednesday to a house fire where a seven-year-old girl and her aunt lost their lives, just days after a head-on crash killed two police officers and five young men in an incident linked with organised crime activity.
Hundreds of extra police officers have been drafted in to support officers after a series of recent incidents in the Middlesbrough and County Durham area.
Assistant chief constable Dave Sutherland, who is the head of local policing at Cleveland Police, said: “Since the tragic incident last Saturday morning in which seven people, including two of our serving police officers, PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough, sadly lost their lives, officers and staff have remained working around the clock to continue to serve the public of Cleveland.
![Police officers at the scene on Birchington Avenue, Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, where Valentina Foster, aged seven, and Natalie McDonald, 34, died following a fire (Owen Humphreys/PA)](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/28/09/e1e78f2d76ddf903e1051e63fc4c7a24Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3OTkyMjI0-2.85667736.jpg)
“In the same week, we have also seen a tragic house fire on Wednesday in which two people lost their lives, which is also understandably impacting the force and our local communities. At this time, we are not linking this incident to the fatal collision on the A66.
“Our thoughts remain with all those affected by these incidents as we continue our investigations into what happened.”
Valentina Foster, aged seven, and Natalie McDonald, 34, have been identified as the victims of the house fire which took place around 5am on Wednesday morning. Two arrests have been made in connection with the murder investigation, police said on Wednesday afternoon.
Meanwhile, police arrested 17 people after the A66 crash, which followed a police pursuit, as part of investigations into alleged organised crime.
There have been two reports of cars being rammed into properties and a stabbing at a housing estate in Eston which have dominated headlines, as people look to Middlesbrough with concerns over the levels of crime.
![Pc Tom Clough, left, and Pc Matthew Blades were killed in the A66 crash last weekend (Cleveland Police/PA)](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/28/14/edfbdc464fbfd463088688f5d5432f85Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg4MDEwODU2-2.85666409.jpg)
The assistant chief constable continued: “Since these two horrific events, the reality of policing in Cleveland and the levels of violence suffered in our communities, has come under the spotlight on a national level.
“Brave officers face significant challenges day in day out, but I want to reassure the public that we will remain unwavering in our efforts to tackle criminals and protect our communities. Despite these challenges, calls for service to the force are being answered effectively, we are deploying to incidents, and investigating crime as we do every day.
“It’s important to acknowledge the support and additional resource we are receiving from a number of other forces in the northern region and beyond, and also from the National Crime Agency. This support not only means we can maintain our service to the public, but also continue to conduct patrols in the areas most affected and be a visible presence should anyone wish to speak to officers with any concerns.
![Jacob Matusiak, Theo Rae, Michael Robert Cahill, Makai Saddington and Cole Robert Worthy were all killed](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/23/14/19/A66-split.png)
“Lastly, I want to thank the general public. Our officers work closely with many corners of our communities on a daily basis to tackle issues in their local neighbourhoods, and whose support these past seven days has been overwhelming and very much appreciated. It has provided officers, staff and the families of the officers with great comfort.”
Following on from the police announcement, Anna Turley, Redcar MP, affirmed that not every incident police attend was linked to the investigation into organised crime.
She said: “I think it’s really important to get across the fact that these incidents are not all linked.
“It could feel that way at the moment because of the national spotlight on us, but unfortunately, we know we’ve had a high level of crime and in this area for a long time now, these are incidents, sadly, that we see all the time.
“It shouldn’t be this way, and it’s up to us to make sure that there isn’t a business as usual which sees that high level of crime and disorder going forward.
“But Cleveland Police have been at pains to say we shouldn’t think that these are all connected, and we shouldn’t be jumping to conclusions.”
summary: Cleveland Police have confirmed that a fatal house fire in Middlesbrough and a deadly head-on crash on the A66 are not being treated as linked. The house fire claimed the lives of a seven-year-old girl and her aunt, resulting in two murder arrests, while the A66 crash involved seven fatalities and led to 17 arrests in connection with organised crime. Both incidents have drawn national attention to levels of violence in the area, prompting support from additional police forces and the National Crime Agency.
key_points: Police stated that the house fire and the A66 crash are not connected.
The house fire resulted in the deaths of seven-year-old Valentina Foster and 34-year-old Natalie McDonald, with two people arrested in a murder investigation.
The A66 crash killed two police officers and five young men, leading to 17 arrests related to organised crime.
Hundreds of extra police officers and National Crime Agency support have been deployed to the area following recent incidents.
MP Anna Turley cautioned against jumping to conclusions, noting that the area has dealt with high levels of crime for a long time.

title: Serial rapist police officer passed vetting despite warnings
author: Mark Daly
content:
![Head-and-shoulders portrait of Alan Greer who has short, cropped hair. He is  wearing a blue top and is facing the camera against a light grey perforated background. The image is tightly cropped around the face and shoulders.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/229b/live/ddf40e50-85b5-11f1-926f-c90d1bcfbc84.jpg)
PC Alan Greer took his own life in May while under investigation
- Published
A police officer - who was later exposed as a violent serial rapist - passed vetting checks to join the force despite having two reports of criminal behaviour against women on his record, BBC Disclosure can reveal.
Alan Greer was investigated by police in 2002 and 2005 for making inappropriate phone calls to women, with one case resulting in a formal police caution.
He was accepted into Strathclyde Police in 2009, despite vetting staff being aware of his previous offending.
The revelation comes a month after Police Scotland told the BBC there had been no "missed opportunities over the years" to identify Greer's offending sooner.
In response to further questions from the BBC, Police Scotland moved to clarify its earlier comments.
It said it had "provided answers to questions relating to Alan Greer's offending during the course of his police career" and did not believe it had been answering questions about his police vetting record.
Red flags
Greer had been a police officer for 17 years when he took his own life in May, just days after a police raid on his home as part of an investigation into offences dating back to 2012.
Last month, the BBC revealed he had committed a series of attempted murders or serious sexual assaults, including raping a vulnerable woman just hours after meeting her on duty.
It has since emerged that Greer had contact with hundreds of sex workers throughout his police career, and violently assaulted many of them.
It is also understood he took inappropriate photographs of female colleagues while working in police officer safety training.
Police Scotland has so far identified 15 of Greer's victims, amid fears the true number is far greater.
Assistant Chief Constable Lynn Ratcliff told the BBC there was "nothing to suggest there had been any missed opportunities over the years"
When the BBC revealed the story last month, Assistant Chief Constable Lynn Ratcliff was asked if there had been any opportunities to stop Greer's offending earlier.
She said: "At this point, and we will keep it under review, there is nothing to suggest that there have been any missed opportunities over the years."
When pressed if there were no missed red flags, she said "At this stage, we've got no evidence to suggest that is the caseâ¦"
Asked if there were any vetting issues in relation to Greer, ACC Ratcliff said the vetting landscape is "markedly different" today, that Greer would not have passed current vetting checks, but she did not offer further details.
The assistant chief constable added that officers were now subject to annual integrity testing and routine re-vetting.
A BBC Disclosure investigation can now reveal:
- Greer was investigated in 2002 by Strathclyde Police for making inappropriate phone calls to a woman in Glasgow. The case was reported to the procurator fiscal but no action was taken
- The Metropolitan Police issued Greer with a formal police caution in 2005 after he was again caught making inappropriate phone calls, this time to a woman he knew in London
- Four years later in 2009, Strathclyde Police accepted Greer into the force despite being aware of at least the formal police caution issued by the Metropolitan Police
Police Scotland has now confirmed that Strathclyde's vetting unit in 2009 was aware of Greer's 2005 police caution when he was applying for the job.
A partial paper vetting record exists for Greer and the caution is referenced.
The force said it was unclear whether the 2002 offence formed part of the interview process, or was known by vetting staff.
Sources say this 2002 "adverse trace" would "absolutely" have been discoverable on Greer's record.
A Strathclyde Police Standard Operating Procedures handbook for 2006 states: "The force should not recruit people with cautions or convictions, which may call into question the integrity of the applicant or the force."
A police source told the BBC: "Two reported crimes related to women before he joined should have been raising all sorts of alarm bells.
"He was clearly a menace from the off and should never have been allowed near a uniform to abuse his position."
![Head-and-shoulders portrait of Craig Naylor in a dark suit and striped tie standing in front of an HMICS sign on an office wall.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/3dff/live/0d17b530-a210-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Craig Naylor led a review into Police Scotland vetting processes in 2023
Craig Naylor, chief inspector for HM Inspectorate of Constabulary in Scotland HMICS), led a review into Police Scotland vetting processes in 2023.
He said the vetting landscape in 2009, though not as strict as today, should still have meant Greer's past would preclude entry to the police.
He said: "My view is that he should never have got in at that point, and my view is that in the intervening period, I'm surprised that something didn't come up about that.
"When I've run vetting in the past, he would not have got in."
Asked by the BBC if these were missed opportunities to stop Greer joining the police, Naylor answered, "Yes".
A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "We have been completely open and transparent around information which can be shared in relation to the ongoing investigation into Alan Greer.
"During an interview with the BBC on 20 July 2026 we provided answers to questions relating to Alan Greer's offending during the course of his policing career, which spanned almost 17 years.
"The investigation has not established any information during his career which could have resulted in his criminal behaviour being identified at an earlier stage.
"The recruitment and vetting process carried out by Strathclyde Police prior to Alan Greer joining in 2009 will form part of an independent and external review by the National Police Chiefs' Council.
"Our absolute priority throughout this investigation is to support victims. As work continues to identify and support everyone affected by this case it is imperative that we do not disclose any information which could be detrimental to that support."
A timeline of how Alan Greer's crimes came to light
The BBC has obtained a confidential briefing document about the case, "Operation Submarine", prepared by the investigation's SIO (senior investigating officer).
The document is dated 12 June this year, about four weeks before the BBC contacted Police Scotland over its intention to run a story about the case.
It is described as a "high level overview" into Greer's "significant serious sexual offending".
Point 3 of the document is headlined "Identified Criminality" and details of the 2002 and 2005 investigations are listed.
It states: "Within the current vetting regime, he would not have been granted Recruitment Vetting."
The document was provided to the Scottish government and the Scottish Police Authority (SPA), the oversight body tasked with holding senior officers to account.
Yet during a public board meeting of the SPA on 30 July, a week after the BBC broke the initial story, none of the SPA board put the details of Greer's vetting issue to DCC Alan Spiers, who was there in place of Chief Constable Jo Farrell.
Board member Chris Creegan asked DCC Spiers which of Strathclyde's previous vetting arrangements were of "particular relevance to this case and Alan Greer's own history" but did not press for an answer and no details of Greer's vetting record were disclosed.
The SPA told the BBC that only the authority's chairman Alistair Hay and chief executive Chris Brown, who were both present at the meeting, received the briefing about Greer's vetting - and that it had not been shared with Creegan.
It said operational briefings were not "routinely shared" with board members.
A spokesperson for the SPA said: "Three authority members raised a number of initial questions to seek assurance about the approach being taken, the impact on public confidence - and the assertion that significant changes to vetting regulations would mean an individual such as Alan Greer, would not be able to join policing today."
![Panoramic view of a Glasgow city centre skyline featuring a mix of historic sandstone buildings and modern glass office blocks under a pale blue sky. Rooftops fill the foreground, while prominent church towers and civic buildings rise above the urban landscape in the distance.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/3809/live/d5881aa0-866d-11f1-93cb-95d7eb12ec49.jpg)
Greer joined Strathclyde Police to work as a uniformed response officer in Glasgow
An HMICS inquiry in 2023 identified significant gaps in Police Scotland's vetting processes, including a failure to re-vet legacy staff since the forces merged in 2013.
Greer was one of about 8,800 police officers and staff who had still not been re-vetted, more than a third of the total workforce.
HMICS also reviewed certain vetting categories from a sample of about 10% of total applications (about 5,500 over four years) and found at least 29 cases where the risk posed by applicants had been "incorrectly assessed" by vetting officers.
HMICS made 15 recommendations, including an urgent review of all the identified problem cases as well as introducing annual integrity testing for officers and routine re-vetting every 10 years.
Eleven of the recommendations, including the review of the problem cases, have been fully discharged, with work ongoing on the rest.
HMICS chief inspector Craig Naylor said: "It is a concern...there are still people who are not vetted three years on [from the review]."
Historic data wash
Following the review and in response to concern over high-profile vetting failures in England including the case of David Carrick, Police Scotland initiated a "historic data wash".
It was part of a vetting improvement plan "to identify any intelligence or allegations that needed further investigation".
The Anti-Corruption Unit (ACU) led the project, along with the force's vetting unit, and concluded: "No significant matters were uncovered that the force were not already aware of."
Police Scotland confirmed the data wash flagged nothing in relation to Greer.
Naylor told the BBC this was another missed opportunity to spot him sooner.
A police source told the BBC: "So the data wash was useless then? How can they say there were no missed opportunities to spot Greer sooner?
"The question is, how many more Alan Greers have they missed?"
Police Scotland added: "We have already stated publicly that the vetting landscape in 2026 is markedly different from that in 2009 and, under current arrangements, Alan Greer's application would not have progressed."
Production/additional reporting: Kevin Anderson and Carla Basu
For support and information on the issues raised in this article, visit BBC Action Line.
summary: PC Alan Greer, who took his own life in May while under investigation as a serial rapist, passed police vetting in 2009 despite having a history of inappropriate phone calls to women, including a 2005 formal police caution. Police Scotland initially stated there were no missed opportunities to identify his offending sooner, but internal documents and outside inspectors confirmed his past conduct should have barred him from the force. The National Police Chiefs' Council will conduct an independent review of Strathclyde Police's original recruitment and vetting process.
key_points: Alan Greer was investigated in 2002 and 2005 for making inappropriate phone calls to women, resulting in a formal police caution from the Metropolitan Police.
Strathclyde Police's vetting unit was aware of the 2005 caution when Greer applied and was accepted into the force in 2009.
Police Scotland stated that under current standards, Greer would not have passed vetting checks.
Police Scotland has identified 15 victims of Greer, whose career spanned nearly 17 years.
An independent and external review by the National Police Chiefs' Council will examine the original vetting process carried out by Strathclyde Police.

title: Sports Direct's Ashley attacks Burnham over 'populist' High Street revival plans
author: Archie Mitchell; Ben King
content:
![Businessman Mike Ashley wearing a white shirt, and green suit jacket, smiling at the camera as he walks with a man behind him](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/a954/live/16d5b030-a25c-11f1-a2c3-9b22da0a32fd.jpg)
- Published
Billionaire Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley has criticised recent cost of living and retail policies from Andy Burnham as "populist reactions".
In a letter to the prime minister, the entrepreneur accused him of "jumping on 'everyday fixes' or bandwagons", while "disastrous" business rates policies and increases to the cost of employing workers were causing businesses to struggle.
He also described a previous proposal of increasing business rates on large warehouses to help reduce them for pubs and clubs as "delusional".
A Downing Street spokesperson said Burnham would "build a new economy that backs British business, delivers growth in every postcode and ensures the essentials in life - like energy, water and housing - are affordable again."
Promises including cutting VAT from household electricity bills and reducing business rates for some firms is "just the start", they added.
Earlier this month, Burnham promised to revitalise Britain's "hollowed out" high streets by helping councils block new vaping and betting shops.
He also brought forward a plan to end subscription traps and ban shops using misleading recommended retail prices, which can make it seem like discounts are larger than they really are.
In Ashley's letter, seen by the BBC and first reported by the Financial Times,, external he hit out at announcements made since Burnham succeeded Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister.
The businessman called on Burnham to use his first Budget, scheduled for 27 October, to lower costs for employers and change the government's position on business rates.
Pubs, social clubs and live music venues will get a 20% business rates cut from April, while a review has been launched into how the tax, which high street firms have long called for reform to, is calculated.
"Shortsighted or populist reactions to underlying business challenges are not the answer," Ashley said in the letter.
Ashley has repeatedly called for a fundamental overhaul of the tax, including levelling the playing field between High Street retailers and online rivals.
"If your answer is to tax larger retailers even more, through hiking business rates on retailer owned or third-party warehouses whilst reducing rates for pubs and clubs, then that is simply delusional," he wrote.
Burnham previously said before he was prime minister that cuts for pubs, clubs and music venues could be paid for by higher levies on warehouses operated by online firms such as Amazon, and targeting the owners of empty high street properties.
Ashley built Frasers Group from a single Sports Direct store in Maidenhead in 1982 to a sprawling empire of dozens of brands employing 30,000 people.
The billionaire has frequently attracted controversy from investors and the media, with accusations over the years of building success by exploiting workers.
In 2016, Ashley admitted to MPs that workers at his Derbyshire warehouse had been paid below the minimum wage and a policy of fining staff for being late was unacceptable.
The business, still owned by Ashley but run by his son-in-law Michael Murray, this month bought luxury department store Harvey Nichols and promised a "significant restructuring" of the business.
Ashley also used his letter to ask Burnham how the prime minister intends to revive Harvey Nichols, which has faced financial challenges in recent years.
Referencing comments by Tory peer and former Marks & Spencer boss Lord Rose, who called the announcements "hot air", Ashley said "I agree with him".
"It is the disastrous business rates position (which I have raised many times over the years) and the dramatically increasing cost of employing people that are really causing business to struggle," Ashley said.
"You have the chance to make a difference or get it horribly wrong," he added.
Ashley said the High Street will be "further devastated" without major reforms, and warned Burnham's suggestion he will consider further business rates changes in the coming Budget are "too little, too late".
He also used the letter to attack Burnham's plans to clamp down on the use of recommended retail prices, saying instead the real issue is "price fixing in sporting goods and other markets" - where he cited the rising cost of official football merchandise.
summary: Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley has written a letter to Prime Minister Andy Burnham criticising his recent retail and cost of living proposals as populist bandwagons. Ashley argued that disastrous business rates and the rising cost of employing workers are the true causes of business struggles rather than the issues targeted by the government. He urged Burnham to use the upcoming October budget to lower employer costs and fundamentally reform business rates.
key_points: Mike Ashley described Andy Burnham's retail and cost of living policies as populist reactions and short-sighted bandwagons.
Ashley dismissed Burnham's proposal to increase business rates on large warehouses to help pubs and clubs as delusional.
The billionaire businessman called on the prime minister to lower employment costs and reform business rates in the 27 October Budget.
Ashley also questioned Burnham on how he intends to help revive the recently acquired luxury department store Harvey Nichols.

title: Flooding in Birmingham as heavy downpours hit UK
author: Telegraph Reporters
content:
![Cars were submerged after heavy rain in Birmingham](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/27/TELEMMGLPICT000499640759_17878082025140_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqtGQB12KHxxQCrwnTZkX0nwgWqwm85JEWpGVhFb46TTg.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Cars were submerged after heavy rain in Birmingham](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/27/TELEMMGLPICT000499640759_17878082025140_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqtGQB12KHxxQCrwnTZkX0nwgWqwm85JEWpGVhFb46TTg.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Heavy rain has caused “significant flooding” across parts of Birmingham.
Fire crews across the city said they were battling rising water levels alongside police and council teams.
Thunderstorms are expected to strike parts of England and Wales on Thursday, with the Environment Agency issuing 22 alerts across the Midlands and South East.
Forecasters have warned the storms threaten to cause power cuts and more flash flooding.
West Midlands Fire Service said seven crews were deployed to deal with flooding and used portable pumps to clear as much water as possible.
Firefighters also went door-to-door to support residents who needed assistance because of mobility challenges.
![Two cars have been flooded on Church Road in Birmingham,](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/27/TELEMMGLPICT000499640748_17878082351703_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
West Midlands Fire Service said: “Crews are being supported by West Midlands Police and Birmingham city council. Please avoid the area, where possible.”
The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for thunderstorms across the South East, South West and East of England. The alert is also in place for parts of the North West, West Midlands, Yorkshire and Wales.
The alert, expected to remain in place until 10pm, includes warnings of travel delays, power cuts and flash floods.
![People attempt to unblock drains after the heavy rainfall](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/27/TELEMMGLPICT000499640758_17878082349442_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqx9qSHbeosvxfwsJrZyLDI_4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
It follows an exceptionally dry summer that has left three-quarters of England and the whole of Wales under official drought conditions.
Scientists have warned that baked, dry soil will struggle to absorb the sudden deluge, creating surface-water run-off rather than relieving groundwater deficits.
Steve Willington, the chief forecaster at the Met Office, warned that slow-moving thundery rain would bring prolonged rainfall to several areas.
“There remains some uncertainty around where the heaviest rain will fall, so it is important to keep up to date with the latest forecast and warnings,” he said.
Craig Snell, a Met Office forecaster, warned that some areas, particularly on east-facing high ground, could see totals exceed 75mm in 12 hours.
“We could see some further thunderstorms move into the south east around Thursday evening,” he said.
![Emergency services responded to rising water levels after heavy rains and thunderstorms](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/27/TELEMMGLPICT000499648058_17878082348220_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqxf0udJPckKC_3Kw9fqS3Nf4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The forecaster warned residents to prepare for power cuts by gathering torches and batteries, a mobile phone power pack and other essential items.
It also urged people to avoid sheltering under or near trees, or other structures which may be struck by lightning.
Commuters have been told to prepare for spray-related road closures, hazardous driving conditions, and potential delays or cancellations across rail and bus networks because of localised flooding and lightning strikes.
![Homeowners and residents were seen wading through water to get to their homes](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/27/TELEMMGLPICT000499666262_17878081856100_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqtGQB12KHxxQCrwnTZkX0nwgWqwm85JEWpGVhFb46TTg.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Despite the downpours, Thursday is expected to remain warm with highs of 27C to 28C.
However, temperatures are expected to drop closer to the seasonal average during the bank holiday weekend, reaching 24C to 25C on Friday before cooling to around 22C to 23C through to Monday.
The sudden wet weather threatens to affect travel plans for those travelling over the long weekend.
Mr Snell said: “It’s not going to be a complete washout. If you’ve got outdoor plans over the weekend, keep a close eye as there will be rain moving in across most parts.”
summary: Heavy downpours have caused significant flooding across Birmingham, prompting emergency services to deploy crews and assist affected residents. The Met Office has issued yellow thunderstorm warnings across large parts of England and Wales, threatening flash floods, power cuts, and travel disruptions. Scientists note that the sudden deluge is struggling to be absorbed by baked, dry soil following an exceptionally dry summer.
key_points: Heavy rainfall caused significant flooding in Birmingham, with fire crews, police, and council teams responding to rising water levels.
The Met Office issued yellow thunderstorm warnings across parts of England and Wales, warning of flash floods, power cuts, and travel delays.
Three-quarters of England and all of Wales remain under official drought conditions following an exceptionally dry summer.
Baked, dry soil is struggling to absorb the sudden heavy rainfall, creating surface-water run-off.
Forecasters warned that some areas could see rainfall totals exceed 75mm in 12 hours.

title: Wes Streeting describes ‘unbelievable volume’ of homophobic abuse since becoming defence secretary
author: Peter Walker
content:
Wes Streeting has described receiving a mass of homophobic abuse since he was made defence secretary last month, while also saying his appointment had been welcomed by some in the Ministry of Defence (MoD) as a sign of change.
Until 2000, gay men and lesbian women were banned from serving in the UK military, with about 200-plus personnel thrown out of the forces each year due to their sexuality – an estimate, as proper records were not kept.
Streeting, who is the first out gay defence secretary, told the All Talk podcast hosted by Iain Dale: “I have experienced more online homophobia in the last three weeks than I have in my entire life.
“Unbelievable volume – because people cannot cope with the idea that a gay person might lead the armed forces of the United Kingdom.”
He went on: “And I have two things to say in response to that. One is, firstly, being the first openly gay defence secretary has been almost entirely unremarked upon in the media.
“And I think, ‘Great, here we are in the third decade of the 21st century and it doesn’t matter, brilliant.’ But of course, online it matters to a lot of people. And I am proud of the fact that in my lifetime we’ve gone from gay people not being able to serve in the military to a gay defence secretary.”
In 2024, Keir Starmer’s government set up the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme, under which personnel who were dismissed or discharged because of the ban in place from 1967 to 2000 can apply for payments of up to £70,000.
Some MPs have since expressed concern at what they say is the slow pace of processing claims, while two veterans have begun legal action to challenge the fact that personnel who were forced to resign, rather than being dismissed or discharged, receive lower payments.
after newsletter promotion
Streeting told the podcast: “In my first week, someone in the MoD said to me, ‘As a gay man, I’m really proud that we have our first gay defence secretary. It means a lot to us who remember the bad old days.’ So I was quite touched by that.
“As for the stuff online, I sort of think one of the wonderful things about today’s day and age is that we get to show just how strong we are. I see strength in all sorts of places in the LGBT community and people living normal, dull, suburban lives. It’s ordinary now being gay in Britain, which is brilliant.
![Pete Hegseth next to a US flag](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/252b700d1b26959a77230ab0f0bedebffd0383b8/0_0_3720_2478/master/3720.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“But I also look at service personnel, athletes now with some footballers coming out, we have got strength in numbers and we’ve got strength in confidence. It’s an opportunity for me to demonstrate strength in this role as well and to challenge the sort of stereotype that clearly persists in dark corners of the internet.”
Part of Streeting’s role involves liaising with Pete Hegseth, the US’s more stereotypically traditional defence secretary, who last month unveiled plans to test US service personnel for their levels of testosterone.
Like others in the Trump administration, Hegseth is a vehement opponent of equality and inclusion. Last year, he ordered the renaming of a US navy ship named in honour of Harvey Milk, the murdered navy veteran, gay rights activist and politician.
summary: Wes Streeting revealed that he has faced an unprecedented volume of online homophobic abuse since becoming the UK's first openly gay defence secretary last month. Despite the online backlash, he noted that his appointment has been welcomed by some Ministry of Defence personnel who remember when gay people were banned from serving in the military. Streeting also discussed his upcoming role in liaising with US defence secretary Pete Hegseth, a prominent opponent of equality and inclusion.
key_points: Wes Streeting is the first out gay defence secretary of the UK.
He reported experiencing more online homophobia in three weeks than in his entire life.
Gay men and lesbian women were officially banned from serving in the UK military until 2000.
Streeting's role involves liaising with US defence secretary Pete Hegseth, an opponent of diversity and inclusion initiatives.

title: Justice Secretary ‘confident’ Pc Harper’s killers will stay in jail
author: Charles Hymas
content:
![Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000235725564_17877523234193_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqBoAHBNnsOk47ZzuFbgUwCjnfe3GeCB6mIajkC9al4KA.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000235725564_17877523234193_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqBoAHBNnsOk47ZzuFbgUwCjnfe3GeCB6mIajkC9al4KA.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
The Justice Secretary is confident two of the killers of Pc Andrew Harper will be barred from early release from prison, police chiefs have been told.
Alex Norris will announce changes to the early release scheme next week that will exclude prisoners guilty of the type of manslaughter for which the pair were convicted in 2020.
Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole were jailed for 13 years for the manslaughter of Pc Harper, 28, who was dragged for more than a mile behind their car after he responded to reports of a theft near Sulhamstead, Berkshire.
The Telegraph revealed last month that they were among 6,000 criminals eligible for release either halfway through their sentence, rather than the usual two-thirds, or after serving one third rather than 40 per cent of their prison terms.
The early release scheme is a central plank of the Government’s efforts to avoid running out of prison space. After a backlash, Labour agreed to exempt 1,000 rapists and child groomers from the early release scheme, but not those convicted of manslaughter.
However, under pressure from police chiefs, front-line officers and a million-strong petition, Andy Burnham announced a further review by Mr Norris to find a way to exempt the two killers and “other individuals”.
Police chiefs have been told Mr Norris plans to introduce secondary legislation – a mechanism to change existing laws quickly – to enact the changes, which are likely to cover manslaughter, rape and child grooming.
They are expected to exempt “unlawful act” manslaughter, where a person causes the death of another while committing an illegal act.
![Pc Andrew Harper and his wife, Lissie](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000235724695_17877523226914_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq-vHkRz5MoGiG1Dt8YyGXDNkM9MM8VM3G1BxlGUO4L8Q.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Bowers and Cole were attempting to steal a quad bike, and fled when Pc Harper arrived to investigate. The driver, Henry Long, who was jailed for 16 years, is not eligible for early release.
It is understood the unlawful killing exemption could cover causing death by dangerous driving, but not voluntary manslaughter – an intentional killing with a partial defence such as sudden provocation – or gross negligence manslaughter, where death is caused by extreme carelessness.
Domestic abusers may still be eligible for early release, partly because there is no specific offence to cover them except coercive control. This is likely to prompt an angry backlash from domestic abuse campaigners and MPs.
Police chiefs have been assured there will be no changes to the remand of suspects into custody, or to the recall of offenders to jail for breaches of licence or further crimes.
There have been demands from some prison insiders to reduce the 17,000 prisoners on remand (nearly a fifth of the total) or the 12,000 offenders who have been recalled to jail.
The Sentencing Act 2026 increased the length of time prisoners recalled to jail had to spend in custody to 56 days, to give prisons more time to prepare their re-release in order to avoid further licence breaches or reoffending.
Police chiefs, including Sir Mark Rowley, the Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police, have complained that too many offenders are being freed on bail, allowing them to continue criminal behaviour, because of concerns about prison overcrowding.
The Justice Secretary wants to repurpose some young offenders’ institutions and parts of the women’s prison estate to free up space. It is thought unlikely that Mr Norris will announce any immediate decisions on such changes.
The Prime Minister has previously said he wants the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) to deport more foreign offenders, who number around 10,000 in jails in England and Wales, and review the 2,271 prisoners on indefinite Imprisonment for Public Protection sentences, many of whom were originally jailed for less serious offences.
![Pc Andrew Harper and his wife, Lissie](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000289448726_17877523235292_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwUNnX6VZ-e9B4QWD4BFDzTM.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Mr Burnham has been told in a letter signed by more than 100 organisations that the early release scheme “directly contradicts” Labour’s pledge to halve violence against women and girls (VAWG).
The letter said: “We note your party’s manifesto commitment to halving VAWG in the decade and believe the scheme – the first major development for victims under your premiership – will instead put the lives of women and children at risk.”
An MoJ spokesman said: “The death of Pc Andrew Harper was a horrific crime. Our thoughts are with his family and friends, and we share the anger from the police community that we are in this position.
“The Prime Minister has asked the Justice Secretary to work through further options to keep a greater number of the most serious offenders in prison, including the killers of Pc Harper.
“Thanks to tireless campaigning by Andrew’s family, Harper’s Law means that anyone convicted of killing an emergency worker whilst committing a crime now gets a mandatory life sentence.
“This Government has gone further by introducing a presumption that anyone convicted of murdering a police, prison or probation officer is handed a whole-life order.”
summary: The Justice Secretary is confident that two of the killers of Pc Andrew Harper will be barred from early release following a review prompted by police chiefs and public pressure. Alex Norris plans to introduce secondary legislation to exclude prisoners guilty of unlawful act manslaughter from the government's prison overcrowding early release scheme. Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole were originally jailed for 13 years for the 2020 manslaughter of Pc Harper, while the driver, Henry Long, is not eligible for early release.
key_points: Justice Secretary Alex Norris will announce changes to exclude certain manslaughter convicts from the early release scheme.
Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole were jailed for 13 years for the manslaughter of Pc Harper in 2020.
The early release scheme was implemented to help manage prison space shortages, but drew backlash for potentially releasing serious offenders.
New secondary legislation is expected to target unlawful act manslaughter, rape, and child grooming.

title: Fundraiser for police officers killed in A66 crash in Middlesbrough tops Â£1m
author: Jason Arunn Murugesu
content:
![Pictures of the two officers. Both are smiling. PC Blades, left, has stubble and short fair hair. PC Clough also has stubble and short dark hair.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/68ab/live/93348dd0-9f24-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.png)
PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough were killed in the crash near Middlesbrough on Saturday
- Published
A fundraiser for two police officers who were killed in a wrong-way crash has reached more than Â£1m.
PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough died during the early hours of Saturday when a Volkswagen Passat, going the wrong way on the A66 at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, hit their vehicle. The five young men in the Volkswagen also died.
Among the donations to the police officers' fundraiser, which was launched by the Cleveland Police Federation, was Â£4,000 from the Cleveland branch of the National Association of Retired Police Officers.
Its chair Grant Thorburn said the officers' deaths had "hit home hard" and that seeing the tributes and donations paid to them had been "humbling".
He said: "Once you're a police officer, you're always a police officer, so even after you retire, particularly in Cleveland, it's such a small, compact force, everyone knows everyone else."
The Police Federation's acting deputy national chair Paul Williams said there was "tremendous grief" among Cleveland officers.
"The policing family is deeply scarred by this incident," he said. "This just brings it home as to how vulnerable we actually are."
He said police officers were human beings who were your ordinary relatives, friends, parents, partners and colleagues.
The fundraiser will be split equally between the families of the two men to be used as they wish, according to the Cleveland Police Federation.
![PC Blades takes a selfie with a medal for completing a run in Middlesbrough.  He has neat stubble and is smiling, with a grey running cap on his head.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/702/cpsprodpb/e74b/live/5f3c9330-a071-11f1-a9ee-9bb6b032b6a3.jpg)
PC Matthew Blades had previously been an English teacher
The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) previously said that officers had been pursuing the Volkswagen Passat seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when the Passat turned on to the dual carriageway.
PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough had been in a vehicle looking for the Passat after its cloned registration plates triggered an automated number plate recognition camera, although they were not involved in the pursuit, the IOPC said.
PC Blades, a 37-year-old father of two, was described by his family as a "beloved husband" and the "most devoted father".
"He may have left this world committed to the duty he believed in, but his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave to his family," his wife said, adding he would be "forever our super hero".
Hear from those who have contributed to the fundraiser
PC Clough had served in the Army, with one man saying he was a "true friend, fantastic soldier and I have no doubt even better police officer".
His family said he had a "fantastic sense of humour" and would jump "into action whenever needed".
They added he had been their "hero", always "willing to help anyone for any reason".
![PC Clough in his police uniform including a thick black stab vest smiles as he holds a small yellow duckling.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/791/cpsprodpb/e67f/live/2a826d70-a073-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
PC Tom Clough had previously been a soldier
Tributes have also been made to the five young men who died in the Volkswagen Passat, but a community group has urged people not to graffiti buildings with messages.
Active Tees Valley made the appeal on Facebook after messages were spray-painted on the East Middlesbrough Events Centre - formerly the Middlebeck Social Club.
Messages on its walls included: "RIP The Boys", "Never Be Forgotten RIP The Lads", and the initials of those in the car with "Rest easy boys".
The Facebook post said: "We understand that people want to express their emotions and pay their respects, but damaging buildings that are being used to support local residents ultimately impacts the same community we are all trying to look after."
Police said 17 people, aged between 18 and 61, had been arrested across Teesside as part of an ongoing investigation into the lead-up to the crash.
They have been held on a range of offences, including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group.
Follow BBC Tees on X,, external Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Tees on BBC Sounds.
summary: A fundraiser established for PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough, who were killed in a wrong-way crash on the A66 near Middlesbrough, has surpassed £1m in donations. The officers died when a Volkswagen Passat traveling the wrong way hit their vehicle, resulting in the deaths of all five occupants in the car as well. The funds raised will be divided equally between the families of the two officers.
key_points: A fundraiser for PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough has raised over £1m.
The officers died when a Volkswagen Passat traveling the wrong way on the A66 struck their vehicle, killing the five young men inside the car as well.
The Cleveland Police Federation launched the fundraiser, which will be split equally between the families of the two officers.
Seventeen people have been arrested across Teesside for various offenses as part of the ongoing investigation.

title: Teenager, 15, arrested over fatal stabbing at Brent Civic Centre
author: Gem O'Reilly; Jess Warren
content:
![A police cordon is in place outside Brent Civic Centre.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/0a98/live/65dd42d0-a124-11f1-92eb-a9b3bbcf6f4a.jpg)
Emergency services were called to Brent Civic Centre on Tuesday afternoon
- Published
A 15-year-old boy has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a young man was found fatally stabbed in a building which houses Brent Council's headquarters and a library.
Emergency services were called at about 14:30 BST on Tuesday to Brent Civic Centre, near Wembley Stadium in north-west London, where the victim was pronounced dead at the scene.
Police said he had not yet been formally identified but he is believed to be 17-year-old David Wynter.
The boy was arrested on Tuesday, 25 August and is being held in police custody.
![Satellite map of Wembley in northwest London showing the area around Wembley Stadium and Brent Civic Centre. Wembley Stadium is labelled near the bottom centre, and Wembley Park Underground station is marked to the north. A red callout box labelled âStabbing at Brent Civic Centreâ points to a highlighted building just northwest of the stadium. An inset map of London in the top left shows Wembleyâs location within the city. Distance scales of 100 metres and 500 feet appear in the bottom right.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/1a3f/live/c04aae40-a09f-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png)
On Wednesday, one man who works in the area told BBC London the stabbing "felt normal".
"These things happen every single day here, in London and in the area. It's not a big surprise," he said.
"You see things like this happen all the time. You read the news and every single day there's something going on. If it's in Harrow, or Wembley, or Neasden, or Willesden or wherever, it doesn't come as a surprise."
However, one woman who lives in the area said the stabbing "came as a shock".
"I've never felt unsafe around here and it's a bit concerning," she said.
Student Demi said he felt "uneasy" after the stabbing.
"It's not really an unsafe area," he said. "It's a bit out of the ordinary.
"These things happen, unfortunately, but it's a bit strange to have it happen here."
Kate, another local resident, said: "Usually we feel very safe. We're fortunate living in this area because there are lots of security patrols and there are always people around.
"Stabbings are terrible tragedies, but it could happen anywhere, and I know there are areas of London that have to deal with that every day.
"I still feel safe. We're fortunate to live here with so much security; I wish that everyone lived in such an area."
![Police officer stationed outside Brent Civic Centre](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/e5dd/live/4e7fcc10-a0bc-11f1-b8cc-1bd2cc322bf4.jpg)
Police outside Brent Civic Centre, which is closed while an investigation is ongoing
Muhammed Butt, leader of Brent Council, said on Tuesday that the borough had been "shaken" by the "appalling and deeply tragic incident".
"Our thoughts are first and foremost with the victim, their family and loved ones, as well as the staff, residents and visitors who witnessed what happened," he said.
Butt said the Civic Centre would remain closed until further notice.
A Section 60 order is now in force across eight Brent wards, giving police enhanced stop and search powers.
It runs from 15:00 BST on Wednesday until 03:30 BST on Thursday.
Supt Chris Clarke, the Met's lead for emergency response policing in the area, said the force was urgently working to identify the victim and inform his next of kin.
"We recognise the concern this incident will cause within the local community and are committed to keeping residents informed as our inquiries progress," he said.
"In light of the incident, we have authorised additional stop-and-search powers to help prevent further violence, support our investigation, and keep people safe.
"There will be an increased police presence in and around the area in the coming hours while our officers continue their investigation."
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: A 15-year-old boy has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a young man, believed to be 17-year-old David Wynter, was fatally stabbed at Brent Civic Centre in north-west London. Emergency services responded to the scene on Tuesday afternoon, where the victim was pronounced dead. Brent Civic Centre has been closed until further notice, and police have enacted a Section 60 order providing enhanced stop-and-search powers across eight Brent wards.
key_points: A 15-year-old boy was arrested on suspicion of murder and is currently in police custody.
The victim is believed to be 17-year-old David Wynter, though formal identification is pending.
The fatal stabbing occurred on Tuesday afternoon at Brent Civic Centre, which houses Brent Council's headquarters and a library.
Brent Civic Centre remains closed until further notice while police investigations continue.
A Section 60 order granting police enhanced stop-and-search powers was put in place across eight Brent wards.

title: Police not ruling out links to A66 crash after two killed in Middlesbrough house fire
author: Mark Brown
content:
A murder investigation has been launched after two people were killed in a house fire in Middlesbrough, with police not ruling out links to organised crime or the fatal crash on the A66 that killed seven people including two police officers on Saturday.
The blaze in the early hours of Wednesday came as police continued to investigate the wider circumstances around the collision.
Cleveland police said officers were called at 5.23am to reports of a house fire in the Grangetown area of Middlesbrough. Two people died in the fire and a woman was in hospital in Newcastle in a critical condition, police said. A further three people sustained non-life-threatening injuries and were receiving treatment in hospital, a spokesperson added.
Supt Emily Harrison, Redcar and Cleveland’s local policing commander, said: “We are working to establish the circumstances of exactly what has happened, but we are keeping an open mind and cannot rule out any links to wider organised crime at this time.”
![A fire engine is parked in front of a white end of terrace house which has its roof burnt out and fire damage around a window. Union jack flags are flying from lamp-posts and railings in the street.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a02a60b1bddc7a5da9dd651fc596b7d215296e8e/0_1314_4060_3247/master/4060.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The blaze was about two miles from the scene of Saturday’s collision in which a Volkswagen Passat, travelling in the wrong direction, crashed head-on into a police vehicle on the A66. PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, were killed in the collision.
The five occupants of the Volkswagen Passat were also killed, and pronounced dead at the scene. They have been named as Cole Worthy and Theo Rae, both 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and Michael Robert Cahill and Jacob Matusiak, both 23.
Since then Cleveland police said they had “continued to disrupt those suspected of being involved in serious and organised crime”. That effort has resulted in 17 arrests.
Wayne Fox, the assistant chief constable responsible for the strategic leadership of the investigation, said: “This has been a fast-moving and complex investigation, with significant links to serious and organised criminal activity. The events of that tragic night will have a lasting and profound impact on the Cleveland area and the communities we seek to protect.
“We have a duty to respond to, and thoroughly investigate, the serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident, and to bring all those responsible to justice. Our robust response will continue in the weeks and months to come, as we continue to tackle those that seek to cause harm to our communities and tackle serious and organised crime.”
Cleveland fire brigade said it had sent six fire engines and an incident command unit to the scene of the Grangetown blaze. A spokesperson said road closures were in place in the surrounding area and asked members of the public to avoid the area where possible.
At the scene a 20-year-old neighbour described how people had tried to rescue the occupants of the house. Ellie, who declined to give her surname, said: “The entire house was scorching. I couldn’t get near the front of the house, it was that hot.”
She described holding the hand of a crying woman who had jumped from an upstairs window, staying with her until paramedics arrived, and said she believed a child was one of the casualties.
Another neighbour, who asked not to be named, said: “My daughter heard shouting and screaming … the dogs were barking. I don’t know the people who live there, we just say hello when we walk past.”
Adam Brook, a Redcar and Cleveland borough councillor for Grangetown, said the fire was “absolutely devastating”, but urged people not to speculate or “share unconfirmed information”. He said: “Many residents have been in touch with me throughout the morning, and I know there is understandably a great deal of concern. However, I would urge people not to speculate or share unconfirmed information.”
Police have previously said the five occupants of the Passat may have had links to “serious and organised criminal activity”. Four of the five had criminal convictions and were believed to be associated with another car that was seen ramming properties earlier that morning.
Inquests into the deaths of Blades and Clough are due to begin in Middlesbrough on Thursday morning, with inquests for the other five people killed scheduled to open later that afternoon.
summary: A murder investigation has been launched following a house fire in Middlesbrough that resulted in two deaths, several injuries, and a woman in critical condition. Cleveland police stated they are keeping an open mind and cannot rule out potential links between the fatal blaze and a recent A66 crash involving a vehicle traveling in the wrong direction that killed seven people. The investigation into the fire also intersects with ongoing efforts by police to tackle serious and organised crime in the area.
key_points: Two people were killed and multiple others were injured in an early morning house fire in the Grangetown area of Middlesbrough.
Cleveland police have launched a murder investigation and are not ruling out links to organized crime or a fatal A66 crash that killed seven people days earlier.
The A66 collision involved a Volkswagen Passat traveling in the wrong direction that crashed into a police vehicle, killing two police officers and five occupants of the Passat.
Police have made 17 arrests as part of a wider crackdown on serious and organised crime in the area following the recent tragedies.

title: Police chief who banned Maccabi fans investigated for gross misconduct
author: Charles Hymas
content:
![Craig Guildford is under investigation alongside three other officers and a member of staff](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000456797804_17877461271920_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqgsaO8O78rhmZrDxTlQBjdLdu0TL-Cg_AMOUqySXmFgU.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Craig Guildford is under investigation alongside three other officers and a member of staff](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000456797804_17877461271920_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqgsaO8O78rhmZrDxTlQBjdLdu0TL-Cg_AMOUqySXmFgU.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
A former West Midlands Police chief constable is being investigated for gross misconduct over his role in banning Maccabi Tel Aviv football fans from a match.
Craig Guildford is under investigation by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), alongside three officers and a staff member.
The announcement by the police watchdog came after the force was accused of fabricating and exaggerating evidence to justify a ban on the Israeli fans at a Europa League game against Aston Villa at Birmingham’s Villa Park.
Mr Guildford, the former head of England’s second biggest police force, stepped down from his post after an official inquiry found that “greatly exaggerated” intelligence was used to justify the ban.
The IOPC said on Wednesday that it had examined 600 pieces of evidence, including operational documents, reports, intelligence research, meeting minutes and correspondence, as well as witness statements.
It said the evidence indicated that Mr Guildford “may have had oversight” of an intelligence briefing that was found to contain “inaccuracies and misleading information”.
The briefing was found to have presented an “imbalanced view” of the risk that Israeli fans posed.
![Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from a Europa League game against Aston Villa](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000444778640_17877434405980_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwSX5rhseiWKOo9p9OQ-ymek.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
A senior serving officer is also under investigation for failing to ensure the accuracy of the briefing, while a staff member involved in researching and compiling intelligence is alleged to have sourced inaccurate information using AI.
Two other senior serving officers, who played important roles in the force’s planning for the match, are being investigated for potential misconduct.
Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, said: “It is encouraging to see the IOPC are investigating Craig Guildford for gross misconduct, but this scandal should have been dealt with by the Pcc Simon Foster months ago. The police should never allow themselves to be dictated to by Islamist anti-Semitic extremists, which is what happened here.
“West Midlands Police covered up threats of violence by elements of the local Muslim community towards Jewish football fans. The force then fabricated evidence to pretend the ban was instead because of the Maccabi fans’ own behaviour based on a previous game in Amsterdam. This is simply unacceptable.
“The police’s first duty is to protect those under threat of violence – West Midlands Police failed to do this and it’s right that those involved are thoroughly investigated.”
Mr Guildford retired with immediate effect on Jan 16, two days after a damning report that caused Shabana Mahmood, the Home Secretary, to say she had lost confidence in him.
The 52-year-old believed he could hang on until Simon Foster, the West Midlands police and crime commissioner, decided his fate, a decision that was not due for at least 10 days, with Ms Mahmood having no legal power to oust him.
But he was heavily criticised by Cabinet ministers. Downing Street made it clear that Sir Keir Starmer had also lost confidence in Mr Guildford and fellow chiefs told him that clinging to office risked damaging the police’s reputation.
It also became clear to Mr Guildford, who had a £220,000 annual salary and would retire on a full pension, that the row would cause months of distraction. One senior policing source described him as a “dead man walking” after the report.
summary: Former West Midlands Police chief constable Craig Guildford and four other individuals are facing an Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) investigation. The inquiry follows accusations that the force used exaggerated and inaccurate intelligence to justify banning Maccabi Tel Aviv fans from a match against Aston Villa. Guildford previously stepped down from his post after an official report found flaws in the evidence used to enact the ban.
key_points: Former West Midlands Police chief constable Craig Guildford is under investigation for gross misconduct by the IOPC.
The investigation concerns the banning of Maccabi Tel Aviv fans from a Europa League match against Aston Villa at Villa Park.
An official inquiry found that 'greatly exaggerated' and inaccurate intelligence was used to justify the fan ban.
Five individuals total, including Guildford, three other officers, and a staff member, are under investigation.
Guildford retired from his position shortly after a damning report caused government officials to lose confidence in him.

title: Harry and Meghan land in Britain
author: Hannah Furness
content:
![The Sussexes landed at Birmingham Airport at lunchtime on Wednesday](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000499589845_17877451933760_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq-cVLixJZjJiTSS6NRQsYH3wSCF1R0VweJ7DS2UnVMSQ.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![The Sussexes landed at Birmingham Airport at lunchtime on Wednesday](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000499589845_17877451933760_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq-cVLixJZjJiTSS6NRQsYH3wSCF1R0VweJ7DS2UnVMSQ.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have landed in Britain, ready to begin an “extended stay” with their children.
The Sussexes landed at Birmingham Airport at lunchtime on Wednesday.
Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, will start at a British school next week, at the start of the autumn term.
The family made a short visit to Britain in July for a summer holiday, with the Duchess sharing photographs of their time at Althorp on her Instagram page.
