![The Duchess posted on Instagram pictures of Prince Harry and the children at the Althorp estate](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000496219368_17877338450660_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqG5EXgvdXl1oBhJJqank9JMwZgCewa-xkrckcIXHk6m8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The Duke and Duchess are moving to Britain six years after they left the working Royal family. Their UK home is thought to be in the Cotswolds.
They plan to live as an “international” family, keeping their homes in California and Portugal.
A source told The Telegraph: “How long will they stay? I don’t know, but it will be for an extended period. Whether that’s six months, a year, two years… who knows.”
The couple are bringing their dogs Mia and Pula with them, but are keeping their chickens in Montecito rather than rehoming them, suggesting they plan to return.
The Duke and Duchess will not resume their pre-2020 roles as working members of the Royal family in Britain.
![Duke and Duchess](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000499564657_17877229551950_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwVVuduJKBIVmdsWxwOVYZQY.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
While their allies have signalled that the Sussexes hope to be “half-in, half-out”, in the model of their tour of Australia earlier this year, the King and Prince of Wales are said to be united in upholding the terms of the Sandringham summit.
Then, Elizabeth II ruled that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex could not adopt a part-time working role in the Royal family while also making money in the way they had proposed.
The King and Queen hosted the Duke and Duchess, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, for tea at Highgrove in July.
The meeting was said to have gone well, but details of what was said between father and son have not yet been revealed.
The Prince of Wales and the Duke of Sussex are no longer in personal contact.
![Prince William, Prince Harry, Duchess of Sussex, the King](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/26/TELEMMGLPICT000430339435_17877230872370_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq-PSyyIpYuv3hhTxnBm0pRlHmPOpeFd0SyQx9dn7kM_w.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Prince Harry is expected to embark on charity engagements including the WellChild awards in early September, while the Duchess is planning to continue her As Ever business.
The family is not yet known to have had formal changes to their security status, which has been decided on a case-by-case basis to date.
The Duke and Duchess married at St George’s Chapel, Windsor Castle, in May 2018.
In March 2019, Buckingham Palace announced they would set up their own household, breaking from the joint operation they had with the then Duke and Duchess of Cambridge.
In January 2020, the Duke and Duchess announced they intended to step back as “senior” members of the Royal family, become financially independent, still support Elizabeth II, but split their time between the UK and North America.
The late Queen ruled at the Sandringham summit, which was convened to resolve the crisis, that the couple could not be “half-in, half-out”.
By March 2020, they had set up a permanent home in California, officially stepped down as senior royals and stopped using their HRH styles.
Since their “farewell tour”, the Duchess has only returned to Britain with her husband for the late Queen’s funeral and a family holiday in July, when she did not join him in public.
summary: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have arrived in Britain at Birmingham Airport for an extended stay with their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. The children are set to start at a British school the following week as part of an arrangement that will keep the family in the UK for an undetermined period. Despite allies suggesting the couple hopes for a part-time royal role, the King and Prince of Wales remain united in upholding the late Queen's Sandringham summit terms preventing a 'half-in, half-out' arrangement.
key_points: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex landed at Birmingham Airport on Wednesday for an extended stay in Britain.
Their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, will begin attending a British school at the start of the autumn term.
The couple plans to live internationally while maintaining their homes in California and Portugal, and will not resume working royal roles.
The King and Prince of Wales are united in upholding the Sandringham summit terms, meaning the Sussexes cannot adopt a part-time working royal model.

title: Large parts of UK under thunderstorm and flood warnings today – full list of regions
author: Bryony Gooch
content:
Thunderstorm warnings have come into place across parts of the country as the Met Office warns of flooding and disruption.
Yellow warnings for storms are in place across the West and East Midlands, as well as the North West, South East, South West and east of England, and all of Wales.
The alerts came into force in England and Wales at 3am and will last until 10pm on Wednesday. Another thunderstorm warning will kick in at 6am on Thursday until 10pm.
![A thunderstorm warning is in place across England and Wales today](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/26/9/51/Screenshot-2026-08-26-at-10-10-06.png)
The Met Office warned there is a “small risk of flooding and disruption from thunderstorms” with the potential for power cuts after a summer of record-breaking dry conditions.
Five flood alerts are in place as the Environment Agency warned the following areas could experience a deluge on Wednesday:
- Loughborough urban watercourses and local tributaries to the River Soar
- River Leen, Day Brook and Tottle Brook in Nottinghamshire
- River Maun in Nottinghamshire
- River Trent Tributaries in Nottinghamshire
- Tributaries in Leicester City
A band of heavy showers and thunderstorms is expected to move northwards this morning, with the possibility an intense downpour of 20 to 30mm of rain could fall in less than an hour.
Some spots could see 40 to 50mm in two to three hours, leading to some surface water flooding, with the possibility of large hail and frequent lightning.
![Thunderstorms will return on Thursday](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/26/9/15/Screenshot-2026-08-26-at-10-31-50.png)
These showers and thunderstorms are expected to drift northwards and ease during the evening.
On Thursday, another band of thunderstorms and heavy rain is expected to move slowly across England and Wales. The Met Office said that 20 to 30mm of rainfall is expected to accumulate in three hours across the affected areas, and up to 50mm in 12 hours can be expected in places.
There is a small chance that some places may see more than 50mm in three hours and more than 75mm through 12 hours, especially over east-facing high ground. Lightning and hail of 1 to 2cm will also be hazardous, the forecaster warned, with some strong gusts presenting a hazard across the south of England early on Thursday morning.
![Heavy rain is expected across parts of the country](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/25/9/51/Screenshot-2026-08-25-at-10-02-22.png)
The Met Office warned of a slight chance that power cuts could occur, impacting homes and businesses which could be flooded quickly. Buildings could face damage from floodwater, lightning strikes or hail. Flooding and lightning could cause delays and cancellations to train and bus services.
The risk of spray and sudden flooding could also lead to road closures and difficult driving conditions.
Met Office chief forecaster Steve Willington attributed the unsettled weather to warmer and more humid air moving north across the UK.
He said: “As we move into Wednesday there is a growing risk of heavy rain and thunderstorms, with warm and humid air helping to trigger heavy showers and thunderstorms. Some places could see significant amounts of rain falling in a short period of time, bringing the potential for localised flooding, travel disruption and frequent lightning.
“On Thursday, slow-moving heavy and thundery rain may bring prolonged rainfall to some areas, increasing the risk of localised impacts. There remains some uncertainty around where the heaviest rain will fall, so it is important to keep up to date with the latest forecast and warnings."
The incoming downpour comes as England and Wales are expected to record one of the driest summers on record. Almost three-quarters of England is designated as under drought, as is the entirety of Wales.
Scientists previously warned that a heavy downpour could cause more harm than good following the dry and hot summer, as it could lead to flash flooding in parts of the country.
summary: The Met Office issued yellow thunderstorm and flood warnings across large parts of England and Wales following a record-breaking dry summer. Heavy downpours, potential power cuts, lightning, hail, and travel disruptions are expected as a band of storms moves northwards. Five flood alerts have been issued by the Environment Agency, primarily affecting areas in Nottinghamshire and Leicestershire.
key_points: Yellow thunderstorm warnings are in place for the West and East Midlands, North West, South East, South West, east of England, and all of Wales.
The initial alerts run until 10pm on Wednesday, with a subsequent warning active from 6am to 10pm on Thursday.
The Environment Agency issued five flood alerts for local watercourses and rivers in Nottinghamshire and Leicestershire.
The unsettled weather is attributed to warmer and more humid air moving north across the UK following a severely dry summer.
Forecasters warn of potential flash flooding, power cuts, lightning, large hail, and significant travel disruptions.

title: UK homes face winter energy squeeze as Ofgem reveals 4% price cap rise
author: Rich Booth
content:
Millions of households will face a squeeze from soaring energy bills this winter with prices set to hit a three-year high from October.
Regulator Ofgem increased the price cap to a three-year high on Wednesday, raising it by 4 per cent from October 1 for a typical household in England, Scotland and Wales.
Ofgem said the price cap will rise by £60 per year – or £5 per month – to £1,723 for the average household using both electricity and gas if this level was sustained for a year.
It serves as a major blow for the Labour government, as the energy secretary admitted the prime minister’s formerly announced help on energy bills will not cover the price hike.
Andy Burnham has vowed to continue to look for ways to get prices down in the long term, but faces criticism from political opponents and calls to do more to help households.
![Regulator Ofgem increased the price cap to a three-year high on Wednesday, raising it by 4 per cent from October 1 for a typical household in England, Scotland and Wales](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/26/07/01M0YC91X6JNMV6YZAJJPRA9Q9.jpg)
Speaking to reporters from a supermarket in London, the prime minister said: “It’s difficult for people and I recognise that.
“But it’s why, within days of taking office, I announced that we would remove VAT off electricity bills to give people that little bit of help.
“That kicks in from October. We know the price cap will have an impact, but it is what we can do right now.
“And we’ll continue to look as we go forward at how we get energy prices down in the long term, and that’s what we need to do too.”
Reacting to the energy price cap rise, Miatta Fahnbulleh said: “Families will be understandably concerned about the cost of energy bills this winter, which is being driven up by the Iran war.
“Energy is an everyday essential and it needs to be affordable for everyone, which is why we have cut VAT on electricity bills from October, to give families some breathing space.
![It serves as a major blow for the Labour government, as the energy secretary admitted the prime minister’s formerly announced help on energy bills will not cover the price hike](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/26/8/56/Energy-secretary-says-I-cant-control-wars-in-defending-Ofgem-4-price-cap-rise.png)
“This has limited the rise in the price cap and follows the £150 in costs we removed from bills earlier this year, and we will keep looking at what more we can do to protect families from unaffordable bills.”
But she admitted the prime minister’s energy measures won't cover price cap increase, telling Sky News: “It doesn't, but it helps.
“So it's £45 lower than it would have been had we not acted. But look, we know that there is more that we need to do.”
It comes after the Middle East conflict affected wholesale prices. The ongoing heatwaves across Europe have added further pressure by increasing gas demand for power generation to meet air conditioning and cooling demand.
Asked if she was frustrated about the impact of Donald Trump’s war on Iran had raised prices, Ms Fahnbulleh said: “ I am frustrated that global events are having an impact on households, businesses in this country.
“Of course I am, and you know when you're working to do things like increasing the amount of clean power to drive down bills, and then you've got shocks like that that then increase bills. That is massively difficult for families, but it's hugely frustrating for government as well.”
![Andy Burnham has vowed to continue to look for ways to get prices down in the long term, but faces criticism from political opponents and calls to do more to help households.](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/25/17/01KYM103X4AJ0CF410G67S5ZFG.jpg)
However, she denied the government’s drive to net zero had pushed up energy bills, and said: “Well, so it's simply not true, and when I talk about clean power, it is, yes, good for the environment - but it's absolutely critical to our strategy to delivering bills that are more affordable because it breaks that link to global fossil fuel markets.”
The increased October cap, which will remain in place for three months, will come into force as households start to increase their energy usage further by using their heating more regularly, adding to bills.
In a further blow for households, analysts Cornwall Insight released their latest forecast on Wednesday for a further 9% increase to the price cap in the New Year.
Neil Kenward, Ofgem’s director general for markets, said: “High international gas prices are continuing to drive energy costs in the UK.
“We welcome the government’s intervention to remove VAT from electricity bills, without which customers would have faced even higher costs this winter.
“Savings are available by choosing a fixed tariff, which are available at £100 or more below the October price cap, and many suppliers offer tariffs with cheaper electricity to smart meter customers for electricity consumed out of peak times.
“It’s also worth considering different payment methods, with prepayment customers paying the lowest price cap rates, and could save consumers an average of about £45 compared to direct debit.”
The Conservatives have accused Labour of failing to deliver on its promise to cut energy bills, with Claire Coutinho, shadow energy secretary, having said: “Labour promised to cut energy bills by £300, but they have gone up by nearly £400 instead.
“Our cheap power plan would cut energy bills for households and businesses by scrapping Government taxes and levies on bills, and it wouldn’t cost the taxpayer a penny. We have to put cheap energy first.”
The Resolution Foundation think-tank urged the government to take more action on energy bill.
“This underscores the need for the government to have targeted support with energy bills designed, costed and ready to switch on as soon as January, in order to protect households from another cost of living crunch,” Jonathan Marshall, Principal Economist at the Resolution Foundation said.
The energy price cap was introduced by the government in January 2019 and sets a maximum price that energy suppliers can charge consumers in England, Scotland and Wales for each kilowatt hour (kWh) of energy they use.
It aims to ensure that prices for customers on default energy tariffs are a fair reflection of the cost paid by suppliers for wholesale energy, and that the profit firms make is capped.
Ofgem sets its cap every three months as the average amount paid by the typical household.
summary: Ofgem has announced a 4 percent rise in the energy price cap for typical households in England, Scotland, and Wales starting October 1, bringing bills to a three-year high of £1,723 per year. The increase is driven by global factors including high international gas prices, the conflict involving Iran, and European heatwaves. While the government has introduced measures such as removing VAT from electricity bills, officials admitted this will not fully cover the price hike, and analysts forecast a further 9 percent increase in the New Year.
key_points: Ofgem raised the energy price cap by 4 percent, adding £60 per year to an average household bill starting October 1.
Global events, including the war on Iran and European heatwaves, drove up wholesale energy prices and contributed to the hike.
Government measures like removing VAT on electricity will reduce the impact slightly, but officials admitted it does not cover the full increase.
Cornwall Insight analysts forecast another 9 percent price cap increase in the New Year.
Political opponents have criticized the Labour government, while think-tanks call for targeted support to protect households from a winter cost-of-living crunch.

title: Burnham announces plan for 10,000 work experience placements for young people – UK politics live
author: Taz Ali; Julia Kollewe
content:
Burnham calls on businesses to offer work experience opportunities for young people
PA has reported some remarks by the prime minister on his visit to Sainsbury’s this morning, where he is announcing his work experience plan.
Andy Burnham said the UK needs more employers to step up and offer work experience opportunities for young people.
“This is a really positive development today,” he said.
He continued:
One of the biggest British brands out there, Sainsbury’s, coming forward and saying 10,000 placements for young people, work placements, apprenticeships. This is exactly what we need.
We need a national drive to challenge youth unemployment and give more opportunities for our young people, and I would ask other businesses to do the same.
We have a huge challenge – too many young people are out of work – but it can be fixed.
I think we need to fix the education system, which is what I’m doing as well, giving young people technical paths alongside the academic route.
But then we need employers to step forward and offer those work placements too.”
PA followed the prime minister around as he spoke to 14 to 16-year-olds on a summer careers programme and shoppers at Sainsbury’s in Nine Elms, south-west London.
One man at the self-checkouts told him he hailed from Manchester and “London isn’t for me”. Andy Burnham replied: “I’m adapting.”
Burnham told the teenagers about his first work experience, when his interest in languages meant he was placed at a travel agent in St Helens.
“The experience was, let’s say, hard,” he said, adding “it wasn’t wasted” as he realised that line of work was not for him.
“You won’t fall on your feet straight away,” he told the young people, noting “it takes a little while” to find the right career path.
Prime minister Andy Burnham speaks to members of staff and young people during his visit to Sainsbury's in Nine Elms, London. Photograph: Richard Pohle/The Times/PA
Burnham was joined by London mayor Sadiq Khan and work and pensions secretary Pat McFadden, after the government and supermarket chain announced a programme to help more young people in deprived areas into work
The prime minister has called on more businesses to offer work experience opportunities for young people to tackle youth unemployment. He said the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) is a “huge challenge” which employers need to help address.
Andy Burnham accompanied by mayor of London Sadiq Khan and work and pensions Secretary Pat McFadden during his visit to Sainsbury's . Photograph: Richard Pohle/The Times/PA
“I was a huge fan of what Dolly did around literacy around the world. I was culture secretary when her libraries were first coming through and the books that went into communities across Britain, you know, what a legacy to leave.
And it was so moving to hear about her dad and how that experience made her want to give back so much. So, yeah, she leaves that legacy as well as obviously great music that people will treasure for ever.”
Government to look at ways to bring energy bills down after price cap increase, says Burnham
Answering questions on the energy price cap, which will increase by 4% from October to a three-year high, Burnham said he acknowledged how “difficult” it will be for people to deal with rising energy bills, but that the government will look at ways to bring them down.
He told reporters:
It’s why, within days of taking office, I announced that we would remove VAT off electricity bills to give people that little bit of help.
That kicks in from October.
We know the price cap will have an impact, but it is what we can do right now.
And we’ll continue to look as we go forward at how we get energy prices down in the long term, and that’s what we need to do too.”
When asked by reporters whether Britons should be worried about possible Russian attacks on the UK, Burnham responded: “It’s a challenging situation when we look around the world right now.
“But from what we’re doing, people need to be sure of this: We’re doing what we’ve done since the start of this conflict, which is to provide that back up support to Ukraine to be able to defend themselves, because they do need to do that.”
He added: “I visited Ukraine to send a really clear message to the Ukrainian people that Britain isn’t changing course. We said we would support them. We are supporting them and that won’t change.”
Prime minister Andy Burnham and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on Monday. Photograph: Ukrainian Presidency/SIPA/Shutterstock
Burnham calls on businesses to offer work experience opportunities for young people
PA has reported some remarks by the prime minister on his visit to Sainsbury’s this morning, where he is announcing his work experience plan.
Andy Burnham said the UK needs more employers to step up and offer work experience opportunities for young people.
“This is a really positive development today,” he said.
He continued:
One of the biggest British brands out there, Sainsbury’s, coming forward and saying 10,000 placements for young people, work placements, apprenticeships. This is exactly what we need.
We need a national drive to challenge youth unemployment and give more opportunities for our young people, and I would ask other businesses to do the same.
We have a huge challenge – too many young people are out of work – but it can be fixed.
I think we need to fix the education system, which is what I’m doing as well, giving young people technical paths alongside the academic route.
But then we need employers to step forward and offer those work placements too.”
While we wait to hear from Andy Burnham, here is a report by my colleague Richard Partington from earlier this monthon the Neet crisis, an issue that has risen up the government’s agenda:
Government looking at 'fundamental reforms' to lower energy bills
Julia Kollewe
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy sectary, said the government will explore “what more we can do” to help those struggling with high bills, via “fundamental reforms” including investment in renewable energy.
Families will be understandably concerned about the cost of energy bills this winter, which is being driven up by the Iran war.
Energy is an everyday essential and it needs to be affordable for everyone, which is why we have cut VAT on electricity bills from October, to give families some breathing space.
This has limited the rise in the price cap and follows the £150 in costs we removed from bills earlier this year, and we will keep looking at what more we can do to protect families from unaffordable bills.
The government is looking at “fundamental reforms” to drive down energy bills for good, the energy secretary said.
Energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh arrives at 10 Downing Street for prime minister Andy Burnham’s first cabinet meeting on 21 July. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
Speaking to Sky News, Fahnbulleh said:
If you look at energy bills, if you look at how much of a family’s finances it is taking up, it is far too expensive.
So, whether that is short-term support that we’re providing to provide a bit of breathing space, which is what the government has done and will continue looking at that, or more fundamental reforms that we need to make to the energy market to drive down bills for good, we are absolutely determined to do that.
She argued renewable energy investment is “absolutely critical” to breaking the link between high gas costs and bills.
Fahbulleh also said she was “frustrated” global events had increased bills in the UK but would not be drawn on criticising Donald Trump for starting the war in Iran.
For the latest updates, follow our business live blog here:
Opening summary: Burnham to announce plan for 10,000 work experience placements for young people
Morning, and welcome to our UK politics blog. Prime minister Andy Burnham is nipping to the shops this morning to announce a plan to get teenagers working, as the government seeks to tackle the “youth unemployment crisis”.
Burnham will be in Sainsbury’s to welcome the supermarket’s plan to offer 10,000 work experience placements in deprived areas, focusing on communities with a high number of young people not in education, employment or training, otherwise called Neets.
Here are the deets: from October, Sainsbury’s will offer work experience and skills sessions for young people from the age of 14 in England, Wales and Scotland. Running for a year, it is hoped the plan will “help young people build confidence, gain experience and get a foot in the door,” Burnham said.
Prime minister Andy Burnham at No10 North in Manchester . Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian
“I encourage more businesses across the country to do the same,” he added. “Access to opportunity and work experience shouldn’t depend on who you know, it should be within reach for every young person wherever they live – and that’s what I’m determined to deliver.”
The prime minister is due to speak to the media from about 9am, but other headlines this morning may overshadow the press briefing.
Ofgem, the energy regulator for Great Britain, announced the energy price cap will increase by 4% from October, meaning millions of households will face the highest energy charges in three years this winter. The Guardian’s energy correspondent Jillian Ambrosereported the following:
Gas and electricity prices will rise by 4% from October under the new cap, months after climbing 13% at the start of July to take account of soaring global energy market prices caused by the war on Iran.
Ofgem, said the new rate for about 22m households was equivalent to £1,723 a year for a typical household’s gas and electricity use, compared with the rise to £1,663 for the July to September period.
As the bill rises in consecutive quarters the typical household will pay an extra £350 a year more than in 2024, when the Labour government came to power with a promise that it would cut bills by £300 a year by the end of the decade.
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham visited a Sainsbury's in London to announce a plan aimed at tackling youth unemployment by encouraging businesses to offer work experience. During the visit, Sainsbury's committed to providing 10,000 work placements and apprenticeships for young people in deprived areas. Additionally, officials addressed rising energy bills following a 4% increase in the energy price cap set for October, noting that the government is looking at short-term relief and long-term reforms.
key_points: Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced a work experience plan to tackle youth unemployment and help young people not in education, employment, or training (Neet).
Supermarket chain Sainsbury's agreed to provide 10,000 work placements and apprenticeships for young people starting in October.
The energy price cap is set to increase by 4% in October, reaching a three-year high.
The government stated it will look into ways to bring energy bills down in the long term, including removing VAT on electricity and exploring renewable energy investments.

title: Winter energy prices expected to rise to three year high
author: Kevin Peachey
content:
![Woman in floral dress with blonde hair pinned up adjusts heating system in her home](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/b19a/live/2109aba0-a091-11f1-b11c-1bea5fc925f5.jpg)
- Published
Energy bills for millions of households are expected to rise this winter to the highest level for three years, under a price cap to be announced by the industry regulator on Wednesday.
The cap will reflect the rise in the wholesale cost of gas, paid by suppliers and will hit bills just as the colder weather arrives in October until the end of December.
Analysts expect Ofgem to say prices will go up by 4% compared with the current cap, affecting those on variable tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales.
Firms say energy debt has jumped and, with high bills likely to persist, have called for more support for those struggling to pay. The government says VAT is being cut from electricity bills.
The price cap for about 33 million households is expected to rise, driven by volatility in international wholesale gas prices.
The average price of gas has been 61% higher over the past three months compared to late 2025, according to suppliers' trade body Energy UK.
Millions of people have moved on to fixed energy tariffs, some in response to the uncertainty created by the impact of the US-Israeli war with Iran.
Anyone on a fixed deal will not see the price they pay rise, until at least the end of the term of their tariff. About 40% of billpayers have fixed tariffs.
![A bar chart showing the energy price cap for a typical household on a price-capped, dual-fuel tariff paying by direct debit, from January 2022 to April 2026. The figure was Â£1,319 based on typical usage in October 2021. This rose to a high of Â£4,414 in January 2023, although the Energy Price Guarantee limited bills to Â£2,500 for a typical household between October 2022 and June 2023. Bills dropped to Â£1,685 in July 2024, before rising slightly to Â£1,846 in October, Â£1,869 in January 2025, Â£1,992 in April 2025, Â£1,854 in July 2025, Â£1,892 in October 2025, Â£1,758 in January 2026, Â£1,641 in April 2026. The cap in July is Â£1,663 under the new typical household consumption values.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/800/cpsprodpb/be66/live/922d0330-a074-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
The energy cap sets a maximum price for each unit of gas and electricity, not the total bill, so a household's final bill depends on what they use.
In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back owing to high prices of recent years while energy efficiency has improved.
Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year.
Cornwall Insight, the consultancy, has forecast that a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity, paid through direct debit, will pay Â£1,729 a year from October.
This is up from Â£1,663 between July and September and woild be the highest for three years.
Households are paying hundreds of pounds a year more on average than before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 started the energy crisis. Bills have gone up by about 70% compared with the pre-crisis norm, according to industry data.
That means unpaid bills and charges have shot up. Energy UK estimates total debt to have collectively risen to Â£6bn, with an expectation of it to increase to about Â£7bn by the end of the year.
The average billpayer in debt, without a payment plan, owed Â£3,500, it said.
The trade body has called for a flexible discounted tariff for those most in need, funded by taxation. That is supported by many debt charities.
"Without urgent intervention â namely a national social tariff and implementation of the long-awaited debt write off scheme from Ofgem â we expect this [debt] figure to rise in the coming months, and with that see an increase in the number of people coming to us for help with energy bills," said Emily Whitford, senior public policy advocate at StepChange.
The Trades Union Congress has called for a windfall tax on bank profits to be used to reduce energy bills.
The government is cutting VAT from electricity bills in October, which should knock about Â£50 off a typical annual bill, and some policy costs were cancelled or shifted in April, but ministers say there is more to do.
Suppliers offer a host of support schemes to anyone struggling to pay, or who is likely to find it difficult.
Energy UK has a list of these schemes, external. But it stresses that companies can often only help if you get in touch with your supplier to tell them you are unable to pay.
summary: Energy bills for millions of households across England, Scotland, and Wales are expected to reach a three-year high this winter due to rising wholesale gas prices. Ofgem's upcoming price cap is anticipated to increase by 4% for those on variable tariffs starting in October. In response to mounting energy debt, which Energy UK estimates could reach £7bn by the end of the year, industry groups and charities are calling for targeted financial support and social tariffs.
key_points: Ofgem is expected to announce a 4% increase in the energy price cap for variable tariffs, effective from October to December.
The rise is driven by volatility and increases in international wholesale gas prices.
About 40% of billpayers on fixed tariffs will not experience price increases until their current terms end.
Collective household energy debt has risen significantly, with industry groups calling for government intervention and social tariffs.

title: Man sentenced for attempting to murder woman at Leeds bus stop
author: Daisy Couture
content:
A man has been sentenced for attempting to murder a woman in Leeds.
Ibrahim Albashir, 34, of no fixed abode, was sentenced today (August 25) to 25 years in prison.
He was made the subject of a hospital order at Leeds Crown Court after pleading guilty to attempted murder.
Albashir will be detained in hospital for as long as necessary and will serve the remainder of his sentence in prison if discharged.
The court heard how the incident unfolded shortly after 9pm on March 17, when police were alerted to an attack on Otley Road.
A member of security staff at The Original Oak pub reported that a man had attacked a woman with a glass bottle at a nearby bus stop.
The security staff intervened, preventing further harm to the victim.
Emergency services found the 32-year-old woman with lacerations to her neck, chest, head, and hands.
She was promptly hospitalised for treatment.
Albashir was arrested at the scene and taken to hospital for a check-up before being placed in police custody.
Detective Inspector Richard James, of Leeds CID, said: "Albashir has approached a lone woman and subjected her to a ferocious, sustained attack which has only stopped thanks to the intervention of these security staff.
"Thankfully they heard the victim’s screams and rushed to her aid, potentially putting themselves in harm's way to protect her.
"They have not only detained Albashir but also treated the victim’s injuries until the attendance of paramedics.
"Without their actions, this could very easily have been a murder investigation.
"It is hard for anyone to imagine the traumatic experience that the victim has been subjected to.
"Albashir has been convicted of the offence he committed against her, and I hope that this helps her find some form of closure on this truly awful chapter of her life.
"We also understand the wider public concern that an incident such as this can cause.
"We will not tolerate violence against women and girls, and this investigation has been treated with the upmost seriousness since the outset.
"We gathered the evidence that has resulted in Albashir being charged with and admitting an offence of attempted murder.
"The court has found, following expert medical advice, that Albashir is suffering from a mental disorder and should be detained within a hospital setting so that he can receive appropriate treatment."
summary: Ibrahim Albashir, 34, was sentenced to 25 years in prison and given a hospital order at Leeds Crown Court after pleading guilty to the attempted murder of a woman. The attack occurred on March 17 at a bus stop on Otley Road, where Albashir used a glass bottle to inflict severe injuries before security staff intervened. The 32-year-old victim was hospitalized for her injuries, while Albashir was arrested at the scene.
key_points: Ibrahim Albashir was sentenced to 25 years in prison with a hospital order after pleading guilty to attempted murder.
The attack took place on March 17 at a bus stop on Otley Road, involving a glass bottle used against a 32-year-old woman.
Security staff from a nearby pub intervened, detained the attacker, and provided first aid to the victim, preventing further harm.
The victim sustained lacerations to her neck, chest, head, and hands, requiring hospital treatment.
Medical experts determined Albashir is suffering from a mental disorder, leading to his detention in a hospital setting for treatment.

title: How UK missile deal will change the future of Ukraine's war
author: Alex Dakers
content:
Andy Burnham’s agreement to provide Ukraine with blueprints to produce long-range missiles could make a “real impact” in the country’s war against Russia and increase the pressure on Vladimir Putin, experts have said.
Ahead of a visit to Ukraine on Monday, his first foreign trip as Prime Minister, Burnham announced that he would allow European defence firm MBDA to declassify information on UK components for the long-range Scalp missile, the French-produced version of the UK’s Storm Shadow.
Ukraine and France are looking to set up local assembly lines in Ukraine to produce the deep precision strike missiles, which use shared French and British technology.
Kyiv has for years been using the missiles, supplied by its allies in limited quantities, to strike targets in Russia, but is now expected to use its new capabilities against military targets, as well as building up its strikes on oil refineries, creating fuel shortages for Russians.
Shorts
‘Unconventional’ thinking
Luke Coffey, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute’s Centre on Europe and Eurasia, said the announcement reflects “unconventional” thinking by Ukraine’s allies to help the country develop its military capabilities.
He said that while much would depend on Ukraine’s production capacity, “it could have a real impact on the battlefield”.
Dr David Jordan, a defence studies lecturer at King’s College London (KCL), said that the move was “potentially very, very significant in several ways”.
Kyiv producing its own Scalp missiles would “dramatically increase the long-range strike capability that Ukraine can deliver from the air”, he said. “It’s not an invincible missile by any means, but it’s about numbers if you are saturating the defences, as the Ukrainians do.”
![](https://inews.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309391965.jpg?w=644)
Jordan said Ukraine would typically fire drones first – which would get shot down, decoy or spoof Russia’s surface-to-air missile fences – creating a pathway that a Storm Shadow missile could follow to its target.
“In terms of numbers, you want to be building in redundancy, meaning the more missiles you have available, the better it is,” said Jordan. “So, this will give the Ukrainians the ability to strike more targets without having to worry about essentially preserving resources received from allies as much.”
Dr Mark Galeotti, a historian, lecturer and author specialising in Russian crime and security, said Burnham’s announcement – following French President Emmanuel Macron’s unveiling of the plans for local Scalp manufacturing in Ukraine earlier this summer – signalled the “changing nature” of the Russia-Ukraine war.
“Once upon a time, it was about the West providing actual systems,” he said. “Now, increasingly, it’s Ukraine building its own systems and the West providing technology and know-how. This is a reflection of that change.
“But, at the same time, so much depends on how long it will take before this actually turns into systems that the Ukrainians can deploy.”
![An aircraft weapons display including Dual Mode Brimstone, Iris-T, and Shadow/Scalp missiles at the Farnborough International Airshow in Farnborough, UK, on Monday, July 20, 2026. The??airshow opens with Boeing, Airbus and leading aerospace and defense companies expected to announce aircraft orders, discuss military technology and navigate geopolitical pressures. Photographer: Jason Alden/Bloomberg via Getty Images](https://inews.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309369251.jpg?w=644)
Most experts agreed that it could be at least a year to 18 months before a Ukrainian-made Scalp missile will be used on the battlefield. But Coffey pointed out that it was “likely that the war will still be continuing in some form by then”, adding that the longer-term impact could translate into real military capability.
Mykola Bielieskov, a research fellow at the National Institute for Strategic Studies think-tank in Kyiv, predicted it could be two to three years before Ukraine could master production of the missile from scratch, but that the assembly of the weapons in the country could happen within a year.
Dr Marina Miron, a visiting researcher at KCL’s war studies department, said Ukraine would need to build up its infrastructure, technical knowledge, machinery, quality control and safety regulations.
But she said that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky “can certainly use all this … as a kind of PR”, after Ukraine marked its independence day on Monday. Zelensky needs a good news story: the UK announcement comes against the backdrop of ex-defence minister and would-be presidential hopeful Mykhailo Fedorov demanding the country hold elections to address what he called a “crisis of governance”.
Ukraine’s targets in Russia
Describing the missiles as a “valuable part” of Ukraine’s arsenal, Bielieskov told The i Paper: “The Storm Shadow/Scalp has been used by Ukraine since May 2023 against diverse targets [including] Black Sea Fleet ships, bridges, logistics bases, air defence assets and military industrial complex.”
He predicted that further Scalp missiles would be targeted at Russian forces’ assets and military industrial complex enterprises in the border regions.
Galeotti said that the key advantage was that “this would give the Ukrainians the capacity to actually penetrate the Russian air defences”, even after they are upgraded.
“It would be a bit of a waste to use Storm Shadows against things like oil refineries, essentially soft targets,” he said. “Storm Shadows are designed to go after high-value military targets where precision and capacity to basically penetrate defences really matters.
“I think what we are largely going to see is the Storm Shadows, or Scalps, would essentially be going after military targets, but the point is that frees up other systems, currently used against them, to go potentially after civilian targets.
![This photograph shows a Rafale jet fighter and a Storm Shadow (Scalp) missile with Ukraine's and France's national flags in the background before the arrival of Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky at the Villacoublay air base, in Velizy-Villacoublay, near Paris on November 17, 2025. Ukraine's President visits Paris on November 17, 2025, in a new bid to secure weaponry to defend his country against increasingly lethal Russian missile and drone attacks. His visit is part of a brief tour of his western allies. (Photo by Christophe Ena / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)](https://inews.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309369261.jpg?w=644)
“I think it’s more and better of the same, particularly because there is an expectation that the Russians are already adapting, proving much better at shooting down Ukrainian cruise missiles.”
Jordan said that while Ukraine was already targeting oil refineries with drones, “using Storm Shadows, it gives them extra capability and probably makes it more likely to get through to the target”.
He noted that these attacks were leading to ordinary Russians “queuing for hours for petrol that isn’t there”, saying that the more capacity Ukraine had to build long-range weapons, “the greater the pressure that they apply to the Russians”.
Coffey added: “I suspect a major focus will be on further isolating Crimea from the Russian Federation, as we have seen in recent months.
“I can’t imagine Russia responding in any significant new way, simply because it lacks the ability to do so … It’s not as if Russia is currently holding back capabilities that it could then use against Ukraine in retaliation.”
Creating an arms exports competitor
The move by the UK could also open the door to Ukraine becoming a global arms competitor. Galeotti noted that “the West is building up this extraordinarily large, powerful Ukrainian defence industrial complex. And after the war, that’s not going to just disappear, but they’re going to be looking for export markets”.
He said that the Ukrainians had “proven to be very innovative in their engineering”.
“It may well be that in five years’ time, we are going to see markets that are traditionally held by the British or the French or the Germans increasingly colonised by Ukrainian companies.”
Jordan agreed that we could reach the stage “where you can actually find the RAF buying missiles from the Ukrainians”.
“The Ukrainians are now major players in terms of drone warfare – probably the best at it in the world,” he said. “They integrate the attacks very effectively with missiles and aircraft.”
Coffey said Ukraine’s partners were increasingly recognising the potential of the Ukrainian defence industry. “Allowing Ukraine to produce missiles such as Scalp could, in the longer term, also benefit the UK by increasing the number of missiles available and expanding overall production capacity. The more missiles that can be produced, the greater the potential to bring down the unit cost.”
Ukraine, added Bielieskov, was now “critical” to the self-defence of the UK and Europe.
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced that the UK will provide Ukraine with blueprints and declassified information on UK components for the French-produced Scalp long-range missile, enabling Ukraine and France to set up local assembly lines. Experts suggest this unconventional move signals a shift toward Western allies providing technology and know-how rather than finished systems, potentially boosting Ukraine's long-range strike capabilities and battlefield impact. While local production could take anywhere from a year to three years to fully master, the increased missile supply is expected to put greater pressure on Russian military targets and infrastructure.
key_points: The UK agreed to share blueprints and declassified component information for the long-range Scalp missile to facilitate local assembly in Ukraine.
Experts estimate it will take between a year and three years for Ukraine to fully master production of the missile from scratch, though assembly could happen within a year.
The initiative reflects a changing dynamic where Western allies supply technology and know-how instead of finished military systems.
Increased missile production capacity is expected to help Ukraine penetrate Russian air defenses and strike high-value military targets and infrastructure.
Developing Ukraine's defense industrial complex could eventually transform the country into a global arms competitor and export market after the war.

title: Nigel Farage wants to scrap GDPR for the UK
author: Mizy Clifton
content:
LONDON — Reform UK on Tuesday night outlined plans to scrap the U.K.’s data protection regime as part of a broader package of measures designed to help small businesses.
The U.K. decided to incorporate an amended version of the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) privacy laws into British law post-Brexit. Reform UK says it would replace the U.K. version of GDPR with a “light-touch” privacy law modeled on New Zealand’s approach to data protection.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said small businesses have had to deal with “suffocating EU red tape” and the package, which includes abolishing GDPR, is a “bold, common-sense rescue plan.”
summary: Reform UK has proposed replacing the U.K.'s post-Brexit data protection regime, which is based on the EU's GDPR, with a lighter-touch privacy law modeled after New Zealand's. Party leader Nigel Farage announced the measure as part of a rescue plan aimed at relieving small businesses from suffocating EU red tape.
key_points: Reform UK outlined plans to scrap the U.K.'s data protection regime.
The current U.K. regime is an amended version of the EU's GDPR incorporated post-Brexit.
The proposed replacement would be a light-touch privacy law modeled on New Zealand's approach.
Nigel Farage described the package as a bold, common-sense rescue plan to help small businesses deal with red tape.

title: Civil defence planning accelerated over threat from Russia
author: Rozina Sabur
content:
![Fire fighters take part in a civil defence exercise in London, 2019](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/25/TELEMMGLPICT000499525855_17876806924800_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqGQR7TMwEvfaYG0TH6J-Ry06Usa8KZCn8ZaDf3fwLU6E.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Fire fighters take part in a civil defence exercise in London, 2019](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/25/TELEMMGLPICT000499525855_17876806924800_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqGQR7TMwEvfaYG0TH6J-Ry06Usa8KZCn8ZaDf3fwLU6E.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Civil defence planning for a major emergency has been accelerated amid fears Russia could strike a critical sector within “the next few years”.
Sources told The Telegraph that the Cabinet Office had been told to bring forward planning for the home defence programme, an initiative that aims to bring together civilian and military planning for crises.
The programme is led by COBR, a national emergency committee named after the Cabinet Office Briefing Rooms, and includes plans for the “war book”, the Government’s classified blueprint to transition the country for crisis and conflict.
Sources said that some elements of the plans for homeland defences had been brought forward from a previous deadline of 2035 to 2030.
They declined to say which element the deadline related to because of the sensitivities around the plans. But one source said: “We do need to accelerate preparedness in a range of threat areas, which means in the next few years, not the next decade.”
Last month, the Government published an updated national risk register listing 95 risks but omitting the most sensitive, classified ones.
Sir Keir Starmer, the former prime minister, warned earlier this year that Moscow could launch an attack “on Nato as soon as 2030”, echoing assessments by intelligence agencies and Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general.
‘Grey zone’ attacks
The move to accelerate civil defence planning came as a former senior Russian official warned on Tuesday of the prospect of a “semi-military” response against British drone factories supporting Ukraine.
Security and defence chiefs have warned for some time that Russia and other hostile states are scaling up so-called “grey zone” attacks between peace and war, including cyber attacks on critical infrastructure.
The Telegraph revealed on Sunday that Iran successfully shut down a British power station for four days in an unprecedented cyberattack.
The affected plant was relatively small and the outage did not impact the wider power grid. However, it demonstrated that hostile actors can access sensitive sites. An energy resilience strategy is expected to be published later this year.
Officials fear the public is not sufficiently attuned to the potential risks and plan to launch an information campaign on “national resilience” this autumn, with guidance on stockpiling food, water and candles.
One source said: “We need to be ready for threats to become more possible by 2030.”
As part of the preparations, Operation Albiston Shadow, the largest-ever national home defence exercise run by COBR, will be carried out in 2027.
Some former Cabinet Office officials have expressed frustration with the slow pace of preparations, claiming complacency had resulted in the “war book” last being updated in 2004.
A government spokesman said: “The Government has been running the home defence programme since 2024, ensuring the country is fully prepared to deal with a variety of threats. Safeguarding national security is the first priority of any government, and we routinely plan for a range of scenarios as a vital part of maintaining our preparedness.”
summary: Civil defence planning has been accelerated by the Cabinet Office due to fears of a potential Russian threat within the next few years. Deadlines for elements of the home defence programme have been moved forward to 2030, and a public information campaign is planned for the autumn to advise citizens on stockpiling essentials. Additionally, the government will conduct its largest-ever national home defence exercise, Operation Albiston Shadow, in 2027.
key_points: The Cabinet Office has accelerated home defence planning amid concerns of a potential Russian strike by 2030.
The initiative includes updating the classified 'war book' blueprint for crises and conflict, which was last updated in 2004.
An upcoming autumn information campaign will advise the public on stockpiling food, water, and candles.
Operation Albiston Shadow, the largest national home defence exercise led by COBR, is scheduled for 2027.

title: UK weather: Met Office warnings in force amid thunderstorm and flood risk
author: Ben Rich
content:
![A man holding an umbrella and another man sheltering under a newspaper, walking down a street in the rain, with a city scene in the background](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/f669/live/02a8a940-a07d-11f1-bfeb-dfb02ea642ef.jpg)
- Published
Downpours and thunderstorms will continue to bring the risk of flooding to parts of the UK on Wednesday.
A Met Office yellow warning for thunderstorms is valid from 03:00 until 22:00 BST, covering much of the Midlands, parts of northern, eastern and southern England, as well as the far east of Wales.
The rain could be heavy enough to bring flash flooding and travel disruption, with lightning and large hail posing additional hazards.
A further Met Office yellow warning has been issued for Thursday with more thunderstorms expected.
For some areas that have seen barely any rain so far this August, the next few days could bring the wettest weather in many weeks.
Where will Wednesday be wettest?
The Met Office yellow thunderstorm warning covers a large swathe of England and Wales.
A band of showers and thunderstorms will push northwards during Wednesday morning with sunny spells following from the south.
However, further scattered downpours and storms will spring up during the afternoon.
As many as 20-30mm (0.8-1.2in) of rain could fall in some locations within just an hour, and it is even possible that 40-50mm (1.6-2in) could accumulate over a few hours.
However, due to the hit-and-miss nature of showers, some places will miss the rain and weather apps may struggle to get the detail of the forecast correct.
![A weather map showing the yellow thunderstorm warning area for Wednesday, covering Stockport, Sheffield, Wrexham, Nottingham, Peterborough, Birmingham, Banbury, Ipswich, Gloucester, London and Basingstoke](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/8285/live/20468e40-a087-11f1-bfeb-dfb02ea642ef.jpg)
The wettest places could see 40-50mm of rain in just a few hours
Where the rain does fall, flash flooding is a real concern. This will be especially problematic where the ground is hard after the prolonged dry spell, making it difficult for the water to soak in.
Difficult driving conditions are expected with the chance that some roads could be closed.
Large hail and frequent lightning are also possible.
Northern Ireland will also see some showers but these are likely to be less intense with less thunder.
Many parts of Scotland will remain dry with sunny spells, although some showers are likely in the south-west later.
Thunderstorms to continue on Thursday
Thursday will bring another zone of thunderstorms, again affecting mostly England and Wales.
The Met Office has issued a further yellow weather warning, valid from 06:00 until 22:00 BST.
Widespread rainfall totals of 20-30mm (0.8-1.2in) are expected in the warning area within three hours, while some areas could see 50mm (2in) within the same timeframe.
There is a small chance that eastern-facing hills - exposed to easterly winds - could record 75mm (3in) during 12 hours, which would bring a significant flood risk.
The showers may eventually reach southern Scotland and Northern Ireland but are likely to weaken and become less intense as they drift northwards.
![A weather map showing the yellow thunderstorm area for Thursday, encompassing Northallerton, Settle, Leeds, Hull, Liverpool, Caernarfon, Derby, Grantham, Aberystwyth, Birmingham, Cambridge, Oxford, Cardiff and Bristol.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/dcda/live/8b71b7e0-a08b-11f1-84af-1fbec28b23b2.jpg)
Hailstones of 1-2cm could accompany Thursday's downpours, as well as thunder and lightning
Wettest weather in weeks for parts of southern UK
Despite a period of unsettled weather last week, some southern parts of the UK have still seen barely any rain recently.
Brize Norton in Oxfordshire has recorded just 0.4mm of rain so far this August, less than 1% of what it would normally expect during the month as a whole.
In July, it received only 1mm.
Kew Gardens recorded no rain at all in July, and only 1.8mm so far this month.
It means the rain we are expecting this week is likely to far outstrip what has fallen recently in some areas.
Why you may not see showers and thunderstorms on your weather app
Thunderstorms are often very hit-and-miss.
Some places can see flooding downpours while others, perhaps only a few miles away, avoid the heaviest rain and stay essentially dry.
Weather apps - including the BBC Weather app - can struggle in these scenarios.
Forecasters know that the conditions are ripe for storms to form, with warm humid air across the UK interacting with a zone of colder air pushing in from the west, higher in the atmosphere.
This generates low pressure and instability.
However, the computer weather models that drive weather apps will always struggle to pinpoint exactly where and when the biggest storms will spring up.
It is a bit like heating popcorn kernels in a pan.
You cannot know precisely which kernels will pop and in which order, while some kernels may not pop at all.
Some of the storms will also occur at night, which may mean they do not show up in the daily weather icons.
It is worth keeping an eye on the hourly weather symbols, as well as the percentage chances of rain, if you are making outdoor plans.
summary: Met Office yellow weather warnings for thunderstorms and potential flash flooding are in force across parts of the UK for Wednesday and Thursday. Heavy downpours could bring 20-30mm of rain within an hour in some areas, alongside risks of lightning, large hail, and difficult driving conditions. While these storms will bring the wettest weather in weeks to some southern areas that have experienced prolonged dry spells, their hit-and-miss nature means some locations will miss the rain entirely.
key_points: Met Office yellow thunderstorm warnings are active for Wednesday and Thursday, primarily covering England and Wales.
Flash flooding and travel disruptions are a concern due to heavy downpours, hard ground from dry spells, and potential rainfall totals reaching up to 50mm or more.
Additional hazards accompanying the storms include frequent lightning, large hail, and difficult driving conditions.
Weather apps may struggle to accurately pinpoint the exact locations of the storms because of their hit-and-miss nature.

title: UK to warn citizens to stock up on food amid threat from climate crisis and hostile states
author: Jessica Elgot; Kiran Stacey
content:
UK citizens will be told to stock up on tinned food and take steps to ensure they are prepared for national emergencies as part of a new government campaign to improve the nation’s resilience.
The new campaign from the Cabinet Office will set out ways people can prepare for extreme weather events and potential attacks from hostile states, including stocking up on bottled water, sources told the Guardian.
The aim will be to ensure most households have basic supplies and knowledge about how to cope in a crisis, in order to free up immediate government resources for the most vulnerable.
Planning for a number of disasters, from cyber-attacks to extreme heat and flooding, has increased over the past few months after a number of incidents both in the UK and across the world. The plans, first reported by the FT, also include an internal reassessment of government preparations for a military attack by a hostile state affecting Britain.
The Cabinet Office minister Louise Haigh, who is Andy Burnham’s de-facto deputy, is also understood to be coordinating crisis planning across departments in Whitehall to allow swifter assistance to affected communities.
![A man waters an allotment in Slough, Berkshire, using water cans on another hot day.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a5487a4ca1b5eb7cf59028b349f2750d9eae12d4/0_0_3187_1962/master/3187.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
During his campaign to become Makerfield MP, Burnham spoke repeatedly about the threat of flooding to communities and the inadequacy of government planning and response.
Burnham convened a Cobra meeting earlier this month to coordinate the government’s response to the heatwave, amid a threat of spreading wildfires and drought warnings.
The government was criticised, however, for its decision to send an emergency phone alert warning of wildfires last week, which charities and domestic abuse survivors said risked the safety of people who might be hiding secret phones.
Haigh’s predecessor, Darren Jones, had said that work was under way on the so-called “war book” on how international conflict might affect the UK.
The Cabinet Office said: “Safeguarding national security is the first priority of any government.
“We’re committed to raising awareness of simple steps households can take to make themselves more resilient, as well as driving forward the home defence programme to build our country’s preparedness for various threats.”
Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, warned shortly before he left office that Russia could attack a Nato country within four years, according to western intelligence assessments.
![Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Andy Burnham shaking hands.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d7f17112d3883ea0285adbc9a49311416ac22fdb/0_0_3000_2000/master/3000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Visiting Ukraine on Monday, Burnham accused the Kremlin of “outrageous threats” against the UK as Russia warned of an escalation in tensions after the UK’s decision to present Ukraine with newly declassified blueprints to allow Kyiv to improve its production of long-range missiles.
Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said the exchange would add “fuel to the fire” and scupper any moves towards a peace deal.
Peskov said: “Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime.
“Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire, and methodically and regularly hatches schemes to prevent even the slightest progress in the peaceful settlement process.”
Last week hackers linked to Iran were blamed for a cyber-attack that caused a British power plant to be temporarily shut down.
The incident involved a small-scale energy generator, according to the UK government. It added that at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system, but it marks an apparent escalation in the threat posed by Iran to UK infrastructure.
summary: The UK government is launching a new Cabinet Office campaign to improve national resilience by advising citizens to stock up on basic supplies like tinned food and bottled water. The initiative aims to help households cope with emergencies such as extreme weather and hostile state attacks, freeing up government resources for vulnerable populations. Planning has intensified following recent incidents including cyber-attacks, heatwaves, and rising geopolitical tensions.
key_points: A new government campaign will advise UK citizens to store tinned food and bottled water to prepare for emergencies.
The preparedness effort aims to help households handle crises like extreme weather and hostile state attacks, freeing up resources for the vulnerable.
Planning across Whitehall has increased following events including cyber-attacks, droughts, and military threats from hostile nations.
Recent incidents include an Iranian-linked cyber-attack that temporarily shut down a small-scale British power plant.

title: Thousands of new social homes promised for West Midlands
author: Isabella Boneham
content:
![Builders placing bricks onto a wall with a house with scaffolding in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/10f3/live/d781df20-a095-11f1-91dc-4919512f173f.jpg)
The West Midlands currently has 7,450 households living in temporary accommodation, according to the region's mayor
- Published
More than 3,000 social and affordable homes are going to be built in the West Midlands after the region was given Â£409m by the government.
The West Midlands' mayor said the money would be used along with his own housing funds to build thousands more homes that were affordable for local people.
Richard Parker said nearly 15,000 children in the region were living in temporary accommodation and he wanted that number "coming down quickly".
"I believe people deserve better and we will change that by giving people the housing stability and security they need to get on in life," he added.
David Hopper, from Coventry, said he had been homeless for two-and-a-half years following the death of his mother and a family fallout, but he now lived in a Midland Heart social rent apartment in the city.
"I was trying to rebuild my life and kept failing because I couldn't move on without my own home," he said.
"I now have one less thing to worry about and this is going to give me the strength to go forward."
![Richard Parker on the left wearing black glasses looks at David Hopper who is also wearing black glasses, a blue jumper while patting a gold-coloured dog on the head that is sitting in the middle on a grey chair.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1504/cpsprodpb/baa2/live/4eb1f5e0-a08b-11f1-84af-1fbec28b23b2.jpg)
David Hopper, from Coventry, told the mayor that he now lives in a social rent apartment that has changed his life
The West Midlands currently has 7,450 households, including 14,976 children, living in temporary accommodation, costing local councils tens of millions of pounds a year in additional housing costs, the mayor said.
A further 65,335 households are on social housing waiting lists.
The Â£400m announced on Tuesday is the first funding to be released from the region's Â£1.7bn Social and Affordable Homes Programme which runs until March 2035 and will see at least 10,000 affordable new homes built across the region over the decade.
The cash from the government is part of a plan from ministers to build 300,000 social and affordable homes across the country.
- ![Campaigner Linda Johnson holds a poster that says "Brinklow save our village". She is wearing a blue coat and pink scarf and has long blonde hair.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/9829/live/568a6c20-04fb-11f0-b61c-853344875b4d.jpg)
  - Published9 January 2025
 ![Promotional image for the housing target tracker. There is a young couple in the middle looking at some paperwork. Around them are various images of details from buildings and stylised charts. The palette is predominantly orange.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/9c8d/live/25af1a70-cdd7-11ef-87df-d575b9a434a4.png)
- ![A woman with long brown hair and wearing a blue coat, blue jumper, headband and sunglasses stands in front of a colourful mural depicting a large bee.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/1125/live/fd11df80-acc0-11ef-8c4f-d52b39c994e1.jpg)
summary: The West Midlands has received £409m from the government to build more than 3,000 new social and affordable homes. Announced by the region's mayor, the funding aims to address a crisis where 7,450 households are in temporary accommodation. This money is the first release from a £1.7bn programme running until March 2035 to build at least 10,000 affordable homes in the region.
key_points: The West Midlands received £409m from the government for social and affordable housing.
Nearly 15,000 children in the region currently live in temporary accommodation.
A further 65,335 households are on social housing waiting lists in the West Midlands.
The funding is part of a broader £1.7bn Social and Affordable Homes Programme running until March 2035.

title: Teacher accused of seducing pupil claims she had ‘painful’ sex condition
author: Telegraph Reporters
content:
![Sally-Anne Bowen arrives at court with Darren Scotchbrook, her partner of 36 years](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/25/TELEMMGLPICT000499492023_17876832202520_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqLNwheLb4aY0lsVcTg9uO6DNXp8BaBSlhEQJn-Rwr55Q.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Sally-Anne Bowen arrives at court with Darren Scotchbrook, her partner of 36 years](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/25/TELEMMGLPICT000499492023_17876832202520_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqLNwheLb4aY0lsVcTg9uO6DNXp8BaBSlhEQJn-Rwr55Q.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
A teacher accused of having sex with a pupil “20 to 30 times” has claimed that a rare condition made intercourse extremely painful for her at the time.
Sally-Anne Bowen, 65, is alleged to have indecently assaulted two teenage boys when they were aged around 14 to 15 and she was in her mid-20s.
Her trial at Harrow Crown Court heard that the chemistry teacher – then 25 – was said to have “engaged in flirtatious conduct” with the pupils and had sex with one of the boys “20 to 30 times” over five months.
She also kissed the second boy while allowing him to touch her breasts and place his hand near her crotch in a cafe as they ate lunch together, it is said.
On Tuesday, Darren Scotchbrook, her partner of 36 years, told a court he was “always quick” in bed to spare Ms Bowen pain because of her vaginal condition.
Jurors have been told a congenital condition prevented Ms Bowen having sex until she was 25, after which she generally avoided lengthy penetration or using condoms with Mr Scotchbrook.
The couple met at a pub in Catford run by Mr Scotchbrook’s parents in 1990, when he was about 20 and she was 28, jurors heard.
Recalling their first date on a boat on the Thames, Mr Scotchbrook said Ms Bowen did not want to have sex when they got home. “I was a bit upset about it. I spent £200 on dinner,” he said.
When the relationship developed sexually, he said: “It was completely different. She had a condition she was not aware of. It was obviously there. It was more of a process than lovemaking.”
Mr Scotchbrook said the couple have continued to have sex during their 36-year relationship, but added it was “built on much more than that”.
He said sex was “clearly” not as enjoyable as he would like it to be for Ms Bowen, who was often “reluctant”, and that it also left him “sore”.
Questioned by Madeleine Wolfe, prosecuting, he agreed he had sex with Ms Bowen throughout their relationship. Ms Bowen gave birth in 2002.
Asked whether Ms Bowen “willingly engaged in” sex “as frequently as weekly”, Mr Scotchbrook said: “Yes.”
Mark Kimsey, Ms Bowen’s barrister, read agreed evidence from Dr Adrian Lower, a consultant gynaecologist instructed by the defence, and Dr Ahmos Ghaly, instructed by the prosecution.
Both medical experts agreed Ms Bowen had a “longitudinal vaginal septum” that was diagnosed in 1990 and was not “resected” until an operation in 2017.
Mr Kimsey said the operation records did not specify the extent of the septum, but it was clear the right canal was larger and Ms Bowen could insert a tampon.
The doctors also concluded the alleged sexual activity with the first complainant was “feasible”.
Mr Kimsey added: “The experts agreed full penile vaginal penetration would be painful but possible to achieve in the right vaginal canal.”
Ms Bowen, of Hemel Hempstead, Herts, denies seven counts of indecent assault. She was earlier cleared on one further charge of indecent assault.
The trial continues.
summary: Sally-Anne Bowen, a 65-year-old former chemistry teacher, is on trial at Harrow Crown Court denying seven counts of indecent assault against two teenage boys when she was in her mid-20s. During the trial, her partner of 36 years testified that she suffered from a painful congenital condition known as a longitudinal vaginal septum, which was not surgically corrected until 2017. Medical experts agreed that while the condition would have made full penetration painful, the alleged sexual activity remained feasible.
key_points: Sally-Anne Bowen denies seven counts of indecent assault involving two teenage boys.
Her partner testified that a congenital vaginal condition made intercourse painful for her.
Medical experts confirmed she had a longitudinal vaginal septum until it was operated on in 2017.
Experts also concluded that the alleged sexual activity with the pupil was feasible despite the pain.

title: Mapped: Where thunderstorms and 75mm of rain could hit UK this week
author: Rebecca Whittaker
content:
Thunderstorms and heavy rain are expected across the UK this week as a wet and unsettled put an end to a hot and dry summer.
Five back-to-back heatwaves over the past few months has left 70 per cent of England and Wales in a drought. Although some parts of the UK have seen cooler weather and showers, a lot more rain is needed before these conditions start to ease.
However, showery conditions could return by Tuesday, with thunderstorm warnings issued across England and Wales on Wednesday and Thursday.
Despite the wet weather, temperatures are predicted to be on the rise as warmer air moves in, pushing temperatures to 26C.
![Thunderstorms will cover parts of England and Wales on Wednesday](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/25/10/21/Screenshot-2026-08-25-at-11-12-47.png)
Where will there be thunderstorms?
Yellow thunderstorm warnings are in place on Wednesday and Thursday across the West and East Midlands, as well as the North West, South East, South West and east of England, and parts of Wales. The Met Office has warned that lightning and hail could be widespread as the storms move northwards across both days.
Rain is expected to arrive in the South West and in south Wales on Tuesday, before more showers sweep across the south of England on Wednesday.
By Thursday, heavy downpours are predicted in the West Midlands before moving up towards Manchester and Leeds.
![Thunderstorms will return on Thursday](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/25/10/51/Screenshot-2026-08-25-at-11-14-59.png)
Heavy rain is also forecast on Thursday night in eastern England.
The Met Office said that 20 to 30mm of rainfall is expected to accumulate in three hours across the affected areas and up to 50mm in 12 hours can be expected in places.
There is a small chance that some places may see more than 50mm in three hours and more than 75mm over 12 hours, especially over east-facing high ground. Lightning and hail of 1-2cm will also be hazardous, the forecaster warned.
Homes and businesses could be flooded quickly, the forecaster said, with damage to some buildings from floodwater, lightning strikes or hail. Flooding and lightning could cause delays and cancellations to train and bus services.
The risk of spray and sudden flooding could also lead to road closures and difficult driving conditions, with a chance of power cuts for some parts of the country.
However, thunderstorms could hit Manchester and Newcastle later in the week on Sunday afternoon.
![Thunderstorms have been forecast in Manchester and Newcastle on Sunday](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/24/8/09/Screenshot-2026-08-24-at-08-26-46.png)
Will there be another heatwave?
Although warm and hot spells are still possible, they will likely be short-lived, with temperatures sitting near average.
Temperatures are set to reach 26C in London on Thursday and sit in the mid- to low-twenties for most of the UK over the week.
But towards the end of September, the Met Office suggests there could be hot spells in the South of England.
2026 is the first year on record to see three separate days where temperatures reached the 37C threshold, as well as the first year with four days at 36C or above.
Before 2026, the UK had recorded 37C or higher on only six occasions.
It also extends 2026’s record-breaking run of days above 35C.
For four months in a row, temperatures hit 35C in the UK on at least one day in May, June, July and now August.
July was also the driest month since records began in 1836 in both England and Wales, and southern England alone had its driest calendar month ever on record.
By 15 July this year, the UK had already recorded more days above 30C than in the whole of 1976, which was known for its long-lasting heatwave.
What is the long-range forecast?
By the Bank Holiday weekend, showers and longer spells of rain are expected to hit many parts of the UK, along with some strong winds, the Met Office said.
It added that thunderstorms and heavy bursts of rain are also forecast.
The weather is set to remain changeable through the first week of September, with above-average rainfall amounts for the time of year.
But some drier and more settled interludes and short-lived warm or hot spells are possible in the South of England.
Towards the end of September, drier weather could become more prevalent, especially in the South and the South East. In the North East more unsettled weather is forecast.
The Met Office said temperatures will probably be near normal at first but may become warmer later, with the possibility of some hot spells in the South.
summary: Thunderstorms and heavy rain are expected across parts of England and Wales this week, bringing a wet end to a hot and dry summer that left 70 percent of England and Wales in a drought. Yellow thunderstorm warnings have been issued for Wednesday and Thursday, with potential risks including flooding, lightning strikes, hail, and transport disruptions. Despite the wet weather, temperatures are predicted to reach up to 26C as warmer air moves in.
key_points: Yellow thunderstorm warnings are in place on Wednesday and Thursday for parts of the Midlands, North West, South East, South West, east of England, and Wales.
Rainfall accumulations of 20 to 30mm are expected in three hours, with up to 75mm possible over 12 hours in some areas.
